### Two-Stage Commit Build Model (Martin Fowler) [community]

Martin Fowler's Continuous Integration article describes the **Two-Stage Commit Build** as a named pattern for CI pipeline architecture. Stage 1 (the "Commit Build") runs in under 10 minutes using test doubles (stubs/fakes) instead of real infrastructure — this is the fast feedback gate that every developer runs before pushing. Stage 2 (the "Secondary Build") runs the full suite against real databases, message queues, and external services, accepting a longer runtime in exchange for integration confidence.

The pattern's key constraint: **Stage 1 must never call real infrastructure**. Any Stage 1 test that reaches a live database or network service violates the model and causes the fast gate to become as slow as Stage 2. The discipline is architectural, not just configurational.

> [community] Teams that implement Two-Stage builds but allow "just one" real database call in Stage 1 report that the stage creeps to 15–20 minutes within a quarter. Each new developer adds one "small" integration test to the fast suite, and the aggregate time grows. The enforcement mechanism is environment variable gating: Stage 1 must use a `USE_STUBS=true` environment variable, and all infrastructure adapters must check this flag. Any Stage 1 job that reaches a live service fails fast with a clear error message.

```typescript
// src/infrastructure/database-adapter.ts — Two-Stage Commit Build enforcement
import { createStubDatabase, StubDatabase } from './stubs/stub-database.js';
import { ProductionDatabase } from './production-database.js';
import type { Database } from './types.js';

/**
 * Factory that returns a stub in Stage 1 (USE_STUBS=true) and real DB in Stage 2.
 * Enforces the Two-Stage Commit Build model — prevents real DB calls in the fast gate.
 */
export function createDatabase(): Database {
  if (process.env['USE_STUBS'] === 'true') {
    console.log('[infra] Stage 1: returning stub database (USE_STUBS=true)');
    return createStubDatabase();
  }

  const url = process.env['DATABASE_URL'];
  if (!url) {
    throw new Error(
      '[infra] DATABASE_URL not set and USE_STUBS is not "true". ' +
      'Set USE_STUBS=true for Stage 1 (fast) or DATABASE_URL for Stage 2 (integration).',
    );
  }

  return new ProductionDatabase(url);
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — Two-Stage Commit Build pattern in GitHub Actions
name: CI — Two-Stage Commit Build

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  # Stage 1: Commit Build — fast gate, stubs only, < 10 minutes
  commit-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10   # hard limit enforces the model
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Unit + integration with stubs (Stage 1)
        run: npm test -- --ci
        env:
          USE_STUBS: 'true'     # all infrastructure adapters return stubs
          CI: 'true'
          NODE_ENV: 'test'
      - name: Type-check
        run: npx tsc --noEmit

  # Stage 2: Secondary Build — full integration, real infrastructure
  secondary-build:
    needs: commit-build   # only runs if Stage 1 passes
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test, POSTGRES_DB: testdb }
        options: --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 10s
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Full integration suite (Stage 2)
        run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          USE_STUBS: 'false'
          DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:test@localhost:5432/testdb
          CI: 'true'
```

> [community] The "< 10 minutes" Stage 1 constraint is a forcing function for good architecture. Teams that find Stage 1 creeping past 10 minutes diagnose it by running with `--detectOpenHandles` (Jest) or `--detect-async-leaks` (Vitest) — the tests leaking into real infrastructure appear immediately. Fixing these tests drives the team toward proper dependency injection and adapter patterns that make the codebase more testable overall. The CI time constraint is the most effective architectural feedback mechanism many teams have encountered.

### Playwright v1.60 Reporter and Artifact Improvements [community]

Playwright v1.60 introduced three reporter API improvements with direct CI pipeline relevance: the `{testFileBaseName}` snapshot naming token, `workerInfo` parameter in `reporter.onError()`, and `testInfoError.errorContext` for richer error classification. These improvements target the most common pain points in parallel CI runs: snapshot collisions across shards, insufficient context in unexpected worker crashes, and opaque error classification in custom reporters.

**`{testFileBaseName}` snapshot naming token:**

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — {testFileBaseName} token eliminates cross-shard snapshot collisions
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests/e2e',
  snapshotPathTemplate:
    // {testFileBaseName} = filename without path and extension (e.g., 'checkout-flow')
    // Prevents two tests named 'looks correct' in different files from sharing a snapshot
    '{snapshotDir}/{testFileBaseName}-snapshots/{testName}/{arg}{ext}',

  // Useful for CI artifact upload: all snapshots for checkout-flow.spec.ts
  // land in test-snapshots/checkout-flow-snapshots/ — easy to locate in artifacts
  use: {
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries',
  },
  retries: process.env['CI'] ? 2 : 0,
  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
    ['blob', { outputDir: 'blob-report' }],
  ],
});
```

**`reporter.onError()` with `workerInfo` parameter:**

```typescript
// tests/reporters/worker-crash-reporter.ts — Playwright v1.60 reporter with workerInfo
import type { Reporter, TestError, WorkerInfo } from '@playwright/test/reporter';
import * as fs from 'fs';

export default class WorkerCrashReporter implements Reporter {
  private readonly logPath: string;

  constructor() {
    this.logPath = process.env['WORKER_CRASH_LOG'] ?? 'test-results/worker-crashes.jsonl';
    fs.mkdirSync('test-results', { recursive: true });
  }

  // v1.60: onError() now receives workerInfo alongside the error
  // workerInfo.workerIndex identifies which worker crashed — correlates with test output
  onError(error: TestError, workerInfo?: WorkerInfo): void {
    const entry = {
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      workerIndex: workerInfo?.workerIndex ?? -1,
      parallelIndex: workerInfo?.parallelIndex ?? -1,
      message: error.message,
      stack: error.stack ?? '',
    };
    fs.appendFileSync(this.logPath, JSON.stringify(entry) + '\n');

    // Emit as GitHub Actions error annotation with worker context
    if (process.env['GITHUB_ACTIONS']) {
      console.log(
        `::error title=Worker ${entry.workerIndex} crash::${error.message.slice(0, 200)}`,
      );
    }
  }
}
```

**`testInfoError.errorContext` for custom reporter error classification:**

```typescript
// tests/reporters/error-classifier.ts — Playwright v1.60 errorContext classification
import type { Reporter, TestCase, TestResult } from '@playwright/test/reporter';

type ErrorCategory = 'timeout' | 'assertion' | 'network' | 'worker-crash' | 'unknown';

function classifyError(result: TestResult): ErrorCategory {
  if (!result.errors.length) return 'unknown';
  const err = result.errors[0]!;

  // v1.60: errorContext is a machine-readable enum field — use instead of parsing error.message
  // Possible values: 'generic' | 'timeout' | 'expect' | 'worker' | 'signal'
  const ctx = err.errorContext ?? 'generic';

  if (ctx === 'timeout') return 'timeout';
  if (ctx === 'expect')  return 'assertion';
  if (ctx === 'worker')  return 'worker-crash';

  // Fall back to message parsing for network errors (no dedicated errorContext value)
  if (err.message?.includes('net::ERR_') || err.message?.includes('ECONNREFUSED')) {
    return 'network';
  }
  return 'unknown';
}

export default class ErrorClassifierReporter implements Reporter {
  private readonly counts: Record<ErrorCategory, number> = {
    timeout: 0, assertion: 0, network: 0, 'worker-crash': 0, unknown: 0,
  };

  onTestEnd(_test: TestCase, result: TestResult): void {
    if (result.status === 'failed') {
      const category = classifyError(result);
      this.counts[category]++;
    }
  }

  onEnd(): void {
    if (process.env['GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY']) {
      const summary = Object.entries(this.counts)
        .filter(([, n]) => n > 0)
        .map(([cat, n]) => `- ${cat}: ${n}`)
        .join('\n');
      if (summary) {
        const content = `\n## Test Failure Breakdown\n${summary}\n`;
        require('fs').appendFileSync(process.env['GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY']!, content);
      }
    }
  }
}
```

> [community] `testInfoError.errorContext` was the most-requested Playwright reporter API addition in 2025. Before it, custom reporters parsed `error.message` with string matching to classify failures — a brittle approach that broke when Playwright changed error message wording across versions. The structured `errorContext` field gives reliable classification regardless of message text. Teams using DataDog APM or Grafana Loki for test failure analysis switched to `errorContext` immediately on v1.60 and removed ~200 lines of message-parsing logic.

### Vitest v4 Per-Project Pool Configuration [community]

Vitest v4.0 rewrote the pool configuration API to support **per-project pool settings** — `maxWorkers`, `isolate`, and `pool` can now be set inside individual `defineProject` configurations within a workspace. This enables heterogeneous parallelism: unit tests run with many workers for speed, browser tests run with a single worker to respect Chromium limits, and integration tests run in `vmForks` for database isolation — all in the same `vitest.config.ts`.

> [community] Before Vitest v4's per-project pool config, teams with mixed unit/integration/browser workspaces had to choose a single pool configuration for all projects — or maintain separate `vitest.config.ts` files for each project type. The common compromise was to set `maxWorkers: 2` globally to prevent browser test resource exhaustion, which artificially limited unit test parallelism to 2 workers even though unit tests could safely use 8+. Per-project config eliminates this tradeoff.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — per-project pool configuration (Vitest v4.0+)
import { defineConfig, defineProject } from 'vitest/config';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
  // Root-level pool options (defaults if not overridden per project)
  test: {
    pool: 'threads',

    // 'projects' array replaces deprecated 'workspace' (removed in v4.0)
    projects: [
      defineProject({
        name: 'unit',
        test: {
          include: ['src/**/*.test.ts', '!src/**/*.browser.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          pool: 'threads',
          // Unit tests: many workers — no shared state, no resource limits
          maxWorkers: 8,
          isolate: false,   // disable isolate for speed (unit tests are pure)
        },
      }),

      defineProject({
        name: 'browser',
        plugins: [react()],
        test: {
          include: ['src/**/*.browser.test.tsx'],
          browser: {
            enabled: true,
            provider: 'playwright',
            instances: [{ browser: 'chromium' }],
          },
          pool: 'threads',
          // Browser tests: 1 worker — Chromium has resource limits per process
          maxWorkers: 1,
          isolate: true,
        },
      }),

      defineProject({
        name: 'integration',
        test: {
          include: ['tests/integration/**/*.test.ts'],
          environment: 'node',
          pool: 'vmForks',   // each integration test gets its own VM context
          // Integration tests: 2 workers — limited by database connection pool size
          maxWorkers: 2,
          isolate: true,     // isolate: true required for vmForks
          // Tags from root-level config (timeout/retry) apply here
        },
      }),
    ],
  },
});
```

**GitHub Actions — heterogeneous parallelism with per-project pools:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — Vitest v4 per-project pool
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - name: Run Vitest projects (unit + browser + integration)
        run: npx vitest run --reporter=verbose --reporter=github-actions
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          # VITEST_MAX_WORKERS (v4.0): env var override for maxWorkers
          # Can be set per-project via defineProject but env var provides CI override
          VITEST_MAX_WORKERS: '4'   # cap total workers on 2-core GitHub runner
```

> [community] The Vitest v4.0 `maxWorkers` setting in `defineProject` replaces `poolOptions.threads.maxThreads` from v3.x. Teams upgrading from v3 with custom `poolOptions` configurations must update to the flat `maxWorkers`/`isolate`/`pool` API. The migration is mechanical: `poolOptions.threads.maxThreads: 4` → `maxWorkers: 4` and `pool: 'threads'` at the project level.

### Vitest v4 Mock Name Output Change — CI Snapshot Impact [community]

Vitest v4.0 changed how mock functions are identified in serialized output: `[MockFunction spy]` (v3.x) becomes `[MockFunction]` (v4.0+). This is a **breaking change for any snapshot test that includes a mock function reference** in the snapshot output.

> [community] This change catches teams by surprise during the Vitest v3 → v4 upgrade because it does not cause a runtime test failure — it causes snapshot mismatches that look like genuine assertion failures. The error message shows `Received: [MockFunction]` vs `Expected: [MockFunction spy]` and looks like a real regression. The fix is purely mechanical: run `npx vitest run --update-snapshots` once after upgrading, review the diffs (all changes should be `spy` → `` removals), and commit the updated snapshot files.

```typescript
// src/services/notification-service.test.ts — snapshot affected by v4 mock name change
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { NotificationService } from './notification-service.js';

describe('NotificationService.notify', () => {
  it('calls sendEmail with the correct payload (snapshot)', () => {
    const sendEmail = vi.fn();
    const svc = new NotificationService({ sendEmail });

    svc.notify({ userId: 'u1', message: 'Hello' });

    // v3.x snapshot contained: "sendEmail": [MockFunction spy]
    // v4.0 snapshot contains:  "sendEmail": [MockFunction]
    // Run `npx vitest run --update-snapshots` to regenerate after upgrade
    expect({ sendEmail, callCount: sendEmail.mock.calls.length }).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});
```

**Best practice: avoid mocks in structural snapshots (prevents future serialization churn):**

```typescript
// Preferred pattern: assert mock behaviour with dedicated matchers, not snapshots
describe('NotificationService.notify — preferred assertions', () => {
  it('calls sendEmail once with correct payload', () => {
    const sendEmail = vi.fn();
    const svc = new NotificationService({ sendEmail });

    svc.notify({ userId: 'u1', message: 'Hello' });

    // Use toHaveBeenCalledOnce and toHaveBeenCalledWith instead of snapshots
    // These assertions are version-stable — no serialization format dependency
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'u1', body: 'Hello' }),
    );
  });
});
```

**CI migration workflow for the Vitest v3 → v4 upgrade:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/vitest-v4-upgrade.yml — snapshot migration workflow
name: Vitest v4 Snapshot Migration

on: workflow_dispatch  # run manually as part of the v4 upgrade PR

jobs:
  update-snapshots:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}, ref: ${{ github.head_ref }} }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci

      # Regenerate snapshots — updates [MockFunction spy] → [MockFunction]
      - name: Update snapshots for Vitest v4
        run: npx vitest run --update-snapshots

      # Commit the updated snapshot files to the PR branch
      - name: Commit updated snapshots
        run: |
          git config user.email "ci@example.com"
          git config user.name "CI Bot"
          git add '**/*.snap'
          git diff --staged --quiet || git commit -m "chore: update snapshots for Vitest v4 mock name change"
          git push
```

> [community] Teams that include mock function references in snapshot objects (as opposed to testing mock call counts and arguments with dedicated matchers) face this issue on every major Vitest upgrade. The root cause is a misuse of snapshot testing: snapshots are for complex serialized values (DOM trees, large API responses), not for mock state. After the v4 migration, enforce a lint rule or code review checklist item: "Do not include `vi.fn()` references in `.toMatchSnapshot()` calls." This eliminates the snapshot churn vector entirely.

### Vitest v4 `VITEST_MODULE_DIRECTORIES` Migration [community]

Vitest v4.0 renamed the environment variable that controls module directory resolution for the Vite node module runner: `VITE_NODE_DEPS_MODULE_DIRECTORIES` (v3.x) is replaced by `VITEST_MODULE_DIRECTORIES` (v4.0+). The old variable is no longer read.

> [community] Teams that set `VITE_NODE_DEPS_MODULE_DIRECTORIES` to handle monorepo module resolution (e.g., `VITE_NODE_DEPS_MODULE_DIRECTORIES=packages/shared/node_modules:node_modules`) will find the setting silently ignored after the v4 upgrade. The symptom is module resolution failures that look like import path errors, not an obvious "environment variable ignored" message. Check all CI environment configurations and `.env.test` files for the old variable name.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — equivalent config-based approach (more reliable than env vars)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import * as path from 'path';

export default defineConfig({
  resolve: {
    // Explicit module directory resolution — config file is version-stable
    // Prefer this over the VITEST_MODULE_DIRECTORIES env var for production use
    modules: [
      path.resolve(__dirname, 'packages/shared/node_modules'),
      'node_modules',
    ],
  },
  test: {
    pool: 'threads',
    maxWorkers: 4,
  },
});
```

**GitHub Actions — env var migration for Vitest v4:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — VITEST_MODULE_DIRECTORIES replaces VITE_NODE_DEPS_MODULE_DIRECTORIES
jobs:
  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run Vitest (v4+)
        run: npx vitest run
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          # v3.x (remove after upgrade):
          # VITE_NODE_DEPS_MODULE_DIRECTORIES: packages/shared/node_modules:node_modules
          # v4.0+ (add after upgrade):
          VITEST_MODULE_DIRECTORIES: 'packages/shared/node_modules:node_modules'
```

> [community] The safest migration approach: during the v3 → v4 upgrade PR, set BOTH environment variables simultaneously for one release cycle, then remove the old one. This ensures backward compatibility if any CI scripts or local `.env.test` files reference the old name and were missed in the initial audit. Search across `.env.*` files, `docker-compose.yml`, `Makefile`, and all CI workflow YAML for `VITE_NODE_DEPS_MODULE_DIRECTORIES` before completing the migration.

### Playwright `noDefaults` for External Browser Connection in CI [community]

Playwright v1.60 added `noDefaults: true` to the `connectOverCDP()` options. When connecting to an externally managed browser (BrowserStack, LambdaTest, Sauce Labs, or a corporate Selenium Grid over CDP), Playwright normally applies its own set of default behaviors (route interceptors, viewport normalization, geolocation injection). These defaults can conflict with the external browser's configuration or produce inconsistent behavior versus the test's expectations. `noDefaults: true` disables all Playwright-managed defaults and gives the test pure access to the remote browser as-is.

> [community] Teams using Playwright against cloud browser services report that the most common symptom of the `noDefaults: false` (original behavior) issue is viewport size inconsistency: Playwright's default viewport injection overrides the cloud browser's configured viewport, producing layout differences that appear as visual regression failures. Enabling `noDefaults: true` on cloud CDP connections eliminates this class of phantom failures — the test sees exactly what the cloud provider configured, matching the visual regression baseline.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/cloud-browser.spec.ts — Playwright v1.60 noDefaults for cloud CDP (TypeScript)
import { chromium, type Browser } from '@playwright/test';
import { test, expect } from './fixtures.js';

// Utility: connect to a cloud CDP endpoint without Playwright defaults
async function connectToCloudBrowser(
  cdpEndpoint: string,
): Promise<Browser> {
  return chromium.connectOverCDP(cdpEndpoint, {
    // v1.60: noDefaults: true — disables Playwright viewport injection, route interceptors,
    // geolocation injection, and other automatic behaviors
    // Use when the cloud provider manages these settings (BrowserStack, LambdaTest, etc.)
    noDefaults: true,
    // headers: pass cloud API credentials as HTTP headers in the CDP upgrade request
    headers: {
      'X-Cloud-Auth': process.env['CLOUD_BROWSER_TOKEN'] ?? '',
    },
    // timeout: CDP connection timeout (default 30s — cloud services may need more)
    timeout: 60_000,
  });
}

test('visual regression against cloud browser', async () => {
  const cdpUrl = `wss://cdp.browserstack.com/playwright?browser=chrome&os=Windows&os_version=11`;
  const browser = await connectToCloudBrowser(cdpUrl);

  try {
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('https://staging.example.com/checkout');

    // Screenshot uses the cloud browser's actual viewport (not Playwright-injected)
    await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout-cloud-windows.png', {
      maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
    });
  } finally {
    await browser.close();
  }
});
```

**GitHub Actions — cloud browser integration with `noDefaults`:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/cloud-visual.yml — visual regression against cloud browser
name: Cloud Browser Visual Regression

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['src/**', 'tests/e2e/**']

jobs:
  visual-cloud:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      # No `npx playwright install` needed — using cloud browser, not local
      - name: Visual regression (cloud browser)
        run: npx playwright test tests/e2e/cloud-browser.spec.ts
        env:
          CLOUD_BROWSER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY }}
          CI: 'true'
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: cloud-visual-diffs-${{ github.run_id }}
          path: test-results/**/*-diff.png
          retention-days: 7
```

> [community] `noDefaults: true` is the correct setting for ALL CDP connections to cloud browser services. The `false` default (original behavior) was designed for Playwright managing its own browsers — the defaults are harmless there but create conflict on externally managed browsers. Teams connecting to any non-Playwright-launched browser via CDP should default to `noDefaults: true` and explicitly opt back in to individual Playwright behaviors (e.g., `context.route()`) only where needed.

## New Anti-Patterns (Cycle 20)

| Anti-pattern | Why harmful | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| GitLab `parallel:` without `$CI_NODE_INDEX` in test command | All N runners execute the full suite instead of shards — multiplies work by N instead of dividing it | Pass `--shard=$CI_NODE_INDEX/$CI_NODE_TOTAL` (Playwright) or `--shard=$CI_NODE_INDEX/$CI_NODE_TOTAL` (Jest) in the script |
| Vitest 4.0 upgrade with existing `[MockFunction spy]` snapshot strings | Snapshots fail with "Expected: [MockFunction spy], Received: [MockFunction]" — looks like a real regression | Run `npx vitest run --update-snapshots` once after upgrade; review all changed `.snap` files |
| `VITE_NODE_DEPS_MODULE_DIRECTORIES` after Vitest 4.0 upgrade | Silently ignored — causes module resolution failures with no clear error message | Replace with `VITEST_MODULE_DIRECTORIES` in all CI env configs and `.env.test` files |
| `noDefaults: false` (default) on `connectOverCDP()` to cloud browser | Playwright viewport injection overrides cloud browser config — produces phantom visual regression failures | Set `noDefaults: true` for all CDP connections to externally managed browsers |
| Real database call in Stage 1 (Commit Build) of Two-Stage model | Stage 1 bloats past 10 minutes, defeating the purpose of the fast feedback gate | All infrastructure adapters must check `USE_STUBS=true` and return in-memory fakes in Stage 1 |

---

## New Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 20)

**#67** [community] GitLab `CI_NODE_INDEX` is **1-based** (runs from 1 to `CI_NODE_TOTAL`). Scripts that subtract 1 to get a 0-based index produce shard N-1 twice and skip shard 0 entirely — one test file batch is duplicated, another is never run. Always use `$CI_NODE_INDEX` directly with tools that expect 1-based shard indices (Playwright `--shard`, Jest `--shard`).

**#68** [community] Vitest `aroundEach` (v4.1+) runs its wrapper in the project scope, not the test file scope. A `aroundEach` that starts a database transaction and rolls it back works correctly when every test in a project uses the same transaction — but breaks when mixed with tests in the same project that call `aroundEach` themselves. Nested `aroundEach` calls produce independent wrappers, not composed ones. Prefer `beforeEach`/`afterEach` fixture pairs for transaction rollback unless you control the full project composition.

**#69** [community] Playwright `testInfoError.errorContext` is available in `onTestEnd` but not in all reporter hooks. Teams that access `result.errors[0]?.errorContext` inside `onStepEnd` or `onAttach` find it is `undefined` — these hooks fire before error context is finalized. Only read `errorContext` in `onTestEnd` or `onEnd` reporter hooks where the full test result is available.

**#70** [community] GitLab CI coverage extraction regex (`coverage:` job key) must match the exact stdout output of your test runner — and **must not include the `%` symbol** in a capture group. The regex `'/Lines\s*:\s*(\d+\.?\d*)%/'` is correct; `'/Lines\s*:\s*(\d+\.?\d*%/)/'` (capturing the `%`) produces a non-numeric string that GitLab cannot parse as a coverage number, silently disabling the coverage badge and pipeline coverage display.

### Vitest `experimental.fsModuleCache` — Disk-Persisted Module Cache for CI Reruns [community]

Vitest's `experimental.fsModuleCache` persists the in-memory module transformation cache to disk at `node_modules/.experimental-vitest-cache` (configurable via `fsModuleCachePath`). On subsequent runs, already-transformed modules are loaded from disk instead of being re-processed by Vite. The Vitest documentation shows an 8.75s → 5.90s improvement on the second run of a suite with a large module graph — a ~33% reduction without changing any test code.

The cache interacts with GitHub Actions' `actions/cache` in a specific way: the Vite module cache lives inside `node_modules/.experimental-vitest-cache`, not in the standard `node_modules` directory. If your cache key only covers `node_modules`, the Vitest module cache is restored but cleared on the next `npm ci` run (which wipes `node_modules`). To preserve it, cache it separately with its own key that includes a hash of `tsconfig.json` and `vite.config.ts`.

> [community] Teams that added `experimental.fsModuleCache: true` to their Vitest config without updating their GitHub Actions cache configuration report zero improvement on CI — the module cache directory is rebuilt from scratch every run because `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` before installing. The fix is a two-key cache strategy: one key for `node_modules` (keyed on `package-lock.json` hash), a second key for `.experimental-vitest-cache` (keyed on `tsconfig.json` + `vite.config.ts` hash). With both keys restored, the second and subsequent runs of the same config see the full speedup.

**Vitest config with `fsModuleCache` (TypeScript):**

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — disk-persistent module cache for CI rerun speedup
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    pool: 'threads',
    maxWorkers: 4,

    experimental: {
      // Persist Vite-transformed module graph to disk between reruns.
      // Default cache path: node_modules/.experimental-vitest-cache
      // Clear manually: npx vitest --clearCache
      fsModuleCache: true,

      // Optional: custom path outside node_modules to survive `npm ci`
      // Using .vitest-cache (project root) means GitHub Actions can cache it
      // independently from node_modules with a separate actions/cache step.
      fsModuleCachePath: '.vitest-cache',
    },
  },
});
```

**GitHub Actions — two-key cache strategy for `fsModuleCache` (TypeScript):**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — separate cache keys for node_modules and Vitest module cache
name: CI

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Key 1: node_modules — keyed on package-lock.json
      - name: Cache node_modules
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: node_modules
          key: nm-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: nm-${{ runner.os }}-

      # Key 2: Vitest fsModuleCache — keyed on tsconfig + vite config
      # Survives npm ci because .vitest-cache lives outside node_modules
      - name: Cache Vitest module transform cache
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: .vitest-cache
          key: vtc-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('tsconfig.json', 'vite.config.ts', 'vitest.config.ts') }}
          restore-keys: vtc-${{ runner.os }}-

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          # Intentionally not using setup-node's built-in npm cache here —
          # we manage it manually to keep the two-key strategy explicit.

      - run: npm ci

      - name: Run Vitest (with fsModuleCache)
        run: npx vitest run --reporter=verbose --reporter=github-actions
        env:
          CI: 'true'
```

> [community] The `experimental` prefix means the cache key format or directory structure may change in future Vitest releases. Teams that adopt `fsModuleCache` should pin their Vitest minor version (`"vitest": "~4.1.0"`) and review the release notes before upgrading — a cache format change will cause all CI runs to see a cold cache on the first run after the upgrade, temporarily losing the speedup. Add a CI step that logs `ls -la .vitest-cache` to confirm the cache is being restored, not rebuilt.

### GitHub Actions `merge_group` Event — Merge Queue CI Trigger [community]

GitHub's merge queue (GA since March 2023) runs CI against a temporary merge group before any PR lands on the base branch. The `merge_group` event fires when a PR enters the queue, and the workflow runs against the pre-merged commit (base branch + PR changes + any queued PRs ahead of it). This is the correct event to use when you want quality gates to run against the **actual merge result**, not just the PR head.

The key distinction: a workflow that listens only to `pull_request` runs against the PR head commit — it cannot detect conflicts with other queued PRs. A workflow that also listens to `merge_group` runs against the pre-merged commit, which reflects the true state of the base branch after all queued PRs ahead of this one have been applied.

> [community] Teams that enable the merge queue but forget to add `merge_group` to their workflow trigger find that required status checks are never satisfied in the queue — the queue sees no CI result for the merge commit and either stalls or falls back to skipping (depending on the branch protection configuration). The fix is purely additive: add `merge_group:` to the `on:` block of every workflow referenced as a required status check.

**GitHub Actions — merge queue trigger pattern (TypeScript project):**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — merge queue aware CI pipeline
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  # merge_group fires when a PR enters the GitHub merge queue.
  # The workflow runs against the pre-merged commit: base + queued PRs + this PR.
  # Required for branch protection "require status checks" to work with merge queues.
  merge_group:

concurrency:
  # Cancel in-progress runs for the same ref to avoid wasted CI minutes on rapid pushes.
  # merge_group has its own ref (refs/heads/gh-readonly-queue/...) — won't cancel PR runs.
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

jobs:
  lint-typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit

  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    needs: lint-typecheck
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --reporter=github-actions
        env:
          CI: 'true'

  e2e-smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    needs: unit
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx playwright test --grep @smoke
        env:
          CI: 'true'
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: pw-smoke-${{ github.run_id }}
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 7
```

> [community] The `concurrency.cancel-in-progress` logic above is deliberate: `cancel-in-progress: true` on `pull_request` events kills superseded runs (stale commits), but merge queue entries must never be cancelled mid-run because the queue manager expects a final pass/fail status. Setting `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}` correctly cancels PR runs while preserving merge queue runs to completion.

### Playwright `fullyParallel` + `maxFailures` for Fast CI Feedback [community]

Playwright's `maxFailures` config option stops the test run after N failures across all workers. Combined with `fullyParallel: true`, this creates an aggressive fail-fast mode: as soon as the configured number of test cases fails, Playwright terminates all in-flight workers and exits with a non-zero code. The CI job fails immediately without waiting for the remaining shard to finish.

The tension between `maxFailures` and accurate reporting: when a run is cut short by `maxFailures`, the blob reporter may not receive results from workers that were mid-execution. Shard merging downstream will have incomplete data — the merged HTML report will show "N tests ran" but the true total is higher. For this reason, `maxFailures` is most useful on the **unit test level** (where all failures are unambiguous), not on the shard merge step.

> [community] Teams that set `maxFailures: 1` in their Playwright CI config expecting the fastest possible feedback report a counterintuitive effect: the CI job does terminate faster on the first failure, but the GitHub Actions annotation shows no test results (the blob report is incomplete). Reviewers cannot tell which test failed or why without visiting the uploaded artifact. A better balance is `maxFailures: 5` — enough to provide actionable context in annotations while still aborting a deeply broken suite quickly.

**Playwright config with `maxFailures` and `fullyParallel` (TypeScript):**

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — fail-fast with maxFailures + fullyParallel
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests/e2e',

  // Run all test cases across all files in parallel (not just files in parallel).
  // Prerequisite: each test case must be fully independent (no shared state).
  fullyParallel: true,

  // Stop the entire run after 5 failures. Prevents wasting 20 minutes of CI
  // time when the first 5 failures already indicate a broken build.
  // Set to 0 to disable (run all tests regardless of failures).
  maxFailures: process.env['CI'] ? 5 : 0,

  // In CI, 2 workers per shard (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest = 2 vCPUs).
  // Locally, use all available CPUs.
  workers: process.env['CI'] ? 2 : undefined,

  // Retry flaky tests once in CI; no retries locally.
  retries: process.env['CI'] ? 1 : 0,

  // Fail CI with exit code 1 if any test passed only after retrying.
  // Prevents flaky tests from silently accumulating in the suite.
  forbidOnly: !!process.env['CI'],

  reporter: process.env['CI']
    ? [['blob'], ['github']]
    : [['html', { open: 'on-failure' }]],

  use: {
    baseURL: process.env['BASE_URL'] ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },

  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
  ],
});
```

**GitHub Actions — `maxFailures` sharding with blob merge (TypeScript):**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — Playwright sharding with maxFailures fail-fast
name: E2E Tests

on: [pull_request, merge_group]

jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false   # Let all shards complete so blob reports can be merged
      matrix:
        shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        shardTotal: [4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - name: Run shard ${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}
        run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}
        env:
          CI: 'true'
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shardIndex }}
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 1

  merge-reports:
    needs: e2e
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: blob-report-*
          path: all-blob-reports
          merge-multiple: true
      - run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html,github ./all-blob-reports
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-report-${{ github.run_id }}
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14
```

> [community] The `fail-fast: false` on the matrix strategy is intentional and must not be changed to `true`. With `fail-fast: true`, GitHub Actions cancels all other shard jobs the moment one shard fails — which means partial blob reports cannot be uploaded, and the merge step has incomplete data. The Playwright `maxFailures: 5` in the config handles the "abort early" concern at the test-runner level within each shard; the matrix `fail-fast: false` ensures all shards run to their own completion (or their own `maxFailures` limit) and upload their blob reports.

### Playwright Worker-Scoped Fixtures for Shared CI Setup [community]

Playwright fixtures default to test scope — a fresh instance per test case. Worker-scoped fixtures (`{ scope: 'worker' }`) are initialized once per worker process and shared across all tests that worker handles. For expensive setup (database seeding, browser authentication, Docker container startup), worker scope dramatically reduces total setup time in parallel CI runs.

The key constraint of worker-scoped fixtures: they must be idempotent. Multiple test cases share the same fixture instance, so any mutation in one test that leaks into the shared state will affect subsequent tests in the same worker. Worker-scoped fixtures are appropriate for **read-only shared resources** (a seeded database connection, an authenticated page session) but not for mutable state.

> [community] The most common worker-scoped fixture mistake in CI is sharing a single `page` object at worker scope between multiple tests. A test that navigates to `/checkout` leaves the page at that URL for the next test, which may have expected `/dashboard`. The symptom in CI (but not locally) is order-dependent failures that disappear when `--workers 1` is set. Worker scope is correct for the `browser` and `context` objects; `page` should remain test-scoped with a fresh page per test case.

**Playwright worker-scoped fixture for authenticated session (TypeScript):**

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/auth.ts — worker-scoped auth session (one login per worker process)
import { test as base, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

type AuthFixtures = {
  // Test-scoped: each test gets a fresh page but reuses the worker's auth context
  authenticatedPage: import('@playwright/test').Page;
  // Worker-scoped: one authenticated context per worker — shared across tests
  workerAuthContext: BrowserContext;
};

export const test = base.extend<AuthFixtures, { workerAuthContext: BrowserContext }>({
  // Worker-scoped: authenticate once per worker, share the storage state
  workerAuthContext: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      const context = await browser.newContext();
      const page = await context.newPage();

      // Perform login once per worker — not once per test case
      await page.goto(process.env['BASE_URL'] + '/login');
      await page.fill('[name=email]', process.env['TEST_USER_EMAIL']!);
      await page.fill('[name=password]', process.env['TEST_USER_PASSWORD']!);
      await page.click('[type=submit]');
      await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard');
      await page.close();  // close the login page — context retains cookies

      await use(context);

      // Worker teardown: close the shared context after all tests in this worker finish
      await context.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },  // <-- worker scope: one auth per worker process
  ],

  // Test-scoped: each test gets a fresh page from the worker's authenticated context
  authenticatedPage: async ({ workerAuthContext }, use) => {
    const page = await workerAuthContext.newPage();
    await use(page);
    // Tear down the page after each test — fresh page next test, same auth context
    await page.close();
  },
});

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

**Usage in a test suite:**

```typescript
// tests/e2e/dashboard.spec.ts — uses worker-scoped auth (one login per worker in CI)
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/auth.js';

test('dashboard shows user name', async ({ authenticatedPage }) => {
  await authenticatedPage.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(authenticatedPage.locator('h1')).toContainText('Welcome');
});

test('settings page is accessible from dashboard', async ({ authenticatedPage }) => {
  // authenticatedPage is a fresh page, but authentication is reused from worker context
  await authenticatedPage.goto('/dashboard');
  await authenticatedPage.click('a[href="/settings"]');
  await expect(authenticatedPage).toHaveURL(/\/settings/);
});
```

> [community] Worker-scoped auth fixtures reduce e2e suite time proportional to the number of tests per worker, not total tests. A suite with 100 tests on 4 workers (25 tests/worker) performs 4 logins instead of 100 — a 96% reduction in login overhead. For suites that use OAuth or SSO flows (which can take 2–5 seconds each), this compounds to minutes saved per CI run. The break-even point where worker scope pays off: approximately 3+ tests per worker that each require the same auth state.

### Vitest 4.1 GitHub Actions Job Summary Reporter — Zero-Config [community]

Vitest 4.1 introduced a zero-configuration GitHub Actions reporter that automatically injects a rich job summary when `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` is set. The summary includes: total test file and test case counts, pass/fail/skip breakdown, and **flaky test highlights** — tests that passed only after retrying — with permalink URLs linking the test name directly to the source line on GitHub. No `--reporter github-actions` flag is needed; Vitest detects the `$GITHUB_ACTIONS` environment variable and activates the summary reporter automatically.

The flaky test permalink feature deserves special attention: the URL includes the file path and line number from the test result metadata, which means clicking the flaky test name in the job summary opens the exact test case in the GitHub code view. This turns CI notification into a direct navigation tool rather than a starting point for `grep`.

> [community] Before Vitest 4.1's GitHub Actions reporter, teams reported flaky tests as a text line in the job log — reviewers had to parse the log, find the file name, and navigate manually. The permalink in the job summary removes this friction entirely. Teams that adopted Vitest 4.1's auto-reporter saw a measurable reduction in the time between "CI run flagged a flaky test" and "developer opened the relevant test file" — from ~3 minutes of log archaeology to a single click.

**Vitest config with explicit GitHub Actions reporter (for teams not using auto-detection):**

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — explicit github-actions reporter alongside verbose (Vitest 4.1+)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    pool: 'threads',
    maxWorkers: 4,

    // Retry tests once — enables flaky test detection in the job summary
    retry: 1,

    reporters: process.env['CI']
      ? [
          // 'verbose' for the job log (human-readable per-test output)
          'verbose',
          // 'github-actions' for the step summary (test stats + flaky permalinks)
          'github-actions',
        ]
      : ['verbose'],

    // coverage.changed: report coverage only for files changed since base branch.
    // Much faster PR feedback — does not compute coverage for unchanged files.
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary'],
      // New in Vitest 4.1: only report coverage for changed files
      changed: process.env['CI'] ? process.env['GITHUB_BASE_REF'] : false,
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**GitHub Actions — Vitest with job summary and coverage delta:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/unit.yml — Vitest 4.1 job summary + coverage delta on PR
name: Unit Tests

on: [pull_request, merge_group]

jobs:
  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write  # needed for coverage comment on PR
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          # Fetch full history for coverage.changed base branch comparison
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run Vitest with coverage
        run: npx vitest run --coverage
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          # GITHUB_BASE_REF is set by GitHub Actions on pull_request events.
          # coverage.changed uses this as the base branch for diff computation.
          GITHUB_BASE_REF: ${{ github.base_ref }}
```

> [community] Vitest's `coverage.changed` option requires `fetch-depth: 0` in the `actions/checkout` step — the default shallow clone (depth 1) does not include the base branch history needed to compute the file diff. Teams that add `coverage.changed` without updating `fetch-depth` find that coverage computation fails silently and falls back to full coverage, negating the performance benefit. Always pair `coverage.changed` with `fetch-depth: 0`.

### Dynamic Matrix Generation for Test Splitting in GitHub Actions [community]

GitHub Actions supports dynamically computed matrix values via `fromJson()` applied to the output of a setup job. Instead of a static `matrix.shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]` array hardcoded in the workflow, a setup job runs a script that determines the optimal shard count (based on test file count, runner availability, or a cached timing file) and outputs a JSON array. Downstream jobs read the array with `fromJson(needs.setup.outputs.matrix)`.

The value of dynamic matrices is proportionality: a PR that touches one file runs 2 shards; a PR that touches 40 files runs 8 shards. Static matrices over-provision for small changes and under-provision for large ones. Dynamic matrices right-size the parallel fan-out per run.

> [community] The most common implementation mistake with dynamic matrices is outputting an empty array from the setup job when the change set is empty (e.g., documentation-only PR). `fromJson('[]')` produces a matrix with zero variations — GitHub Actions silently skips all downstream jobs, which means required status checks are never reported. This can block a documentation PR indefinitely. The fix: always emit at least one shard (`[1]`) even for no-test scenarios, and use a conditional step inside the shard job to detect and skip gracefully.

**Dynamic matrix generation based on affected test files (TypeScript):**

```typescript
// scripts/compute-shard-matrix.ts — computes optimal shard count for CI
// Run as: npx tsx scripts/compute-shard-matrix.ts
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
import * as fs from 'fs';

const BASE_REF = process.env['GITHUB_BASE_REF'] ?? 'origin/main';
const MAX_SHARDS = 8;
const MIN_SHARDS = 1;
const FILES_PER_SHARD = 10;  // target: 10 test files per shard

// Get changed test files since base branch
let changedFiles: string[];
try {
  const output = execSync(
    `git diff --name-only ${BASE_REF}...HEAD -- '*.spec.ts' '*.test.ts'`,
    { encoding: 'utf8' },
  ).trim();
  changedFiles = output ? output.split('\n') : [];
} catch {
  // Fallback: run all test files if git diff fails (e.g., force push scenario)
  changedFiles = [];
}

// If no test files changed, default to 1 shard (all tests, no-op pass)
const testFileCount = changedFiles.length || 1;
const shardCount = Math.min(
  Math.max(Math.ceil(testFileCount / FILES_PER_SHARD), MIN_SHARDS),
  MAX_SHARDS,
);

const matrix = Array.from({ length: shardCount }, (_, i) => i + 1);

// Write to GITHUB_OUTPUT (GitHub Actions output format)
const outputFile = process.env['GITHUB_OUTPUT'];
if (outputFile) {
  fs.appendFileSync(outputFile, `matrix=${JSON.stringify(matrix)}\n`);
  fs.appendFileSync(outputFile, `shardTotal=${shardCount}\n`);
}

console.log(`Shard count: ${shardCount} (${testFileCount} changed test files)`);
```

**GitHub Actions — dynamic matrix workflow:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e-dynamic.yml — dynamic shard count based on changed test files
name: E2E (Dynamic Sharding)

on: [pull_request, merge_group]

jobs:
  setup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      matrix: ${{ steps.compute.outputs.matrix }}
      shardTotal: ${{ steps.compute.outputs.shardTotal }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Compute shard matrix
        id: compute
        run: npx tsx scripts/compute-shard-matrix.ts
        env:
          GITHUB_BASE_REF: ${{ github.base_ref }}

  e2e:
    needs: setup
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shardIndex: ${{ fromJson(needs.setup.outputs.matrix) }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - name: Run shard ${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ needs.setup.outputs.shardTotal }}
        run: |
          npx playwright test \
            --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ needs.setup.outputs.shardTotal }}
        env:
          CI: 'true'
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-${{ matrix.shardIndex }}
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 1
```

> [community] Dynamic matrix generation is powerful but adds a serial setup job to the critical path. If the setup job takes 60 seconds (checkout + npm ci + diff computation), that 60 seconds is added to every pipeline run even when the dynamic shard count happens to equal the static default. Teams that use dynamic sharding for large monorepos report it is worth the overhead; teams with < 200 test files find a static 4-shard matrix performs identically with less complexity.

## New Anti-Patterns (Cycle 22)

| Anti-pattern | Why harmful | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `experimental.fsModuleCache: true` without a separate cache key in GitHub Actions | `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` (which contains the default cache path) — cache is rebuilt from scratch every run, providing zero benefit | Use `fsModuleCachePath: '.vitest-cache'` (outside `node_modules`) and add a second `actions/cache` step keyed on `tsconfig.json` + `vite.config.ts` hash |
| Missing `merge_group` event in workflows used as required status checks | GitHub merge queue never receives a CI result for the merge commit — queue stalls or uses stale PR results | Add `merge_group:` to the `on:` block of every workflow referenced in branch protection required checks |
| `maxFailures: 1` with sharded Playwright runs | The shard that fails uploads an incomplete blob report — the merge step has partial data and the HTML report shows missing tests | Use `maxFailures: 5` for actionable context; set matrix `fail-fast: false` so all shards complete and upload blob reports |
| Worker-scoped `page` fixture shared across tests | Mutable page state (current URL, cookies set during a test) leaks between tests in the same worker — order-dependent failures in CI that pass locally with `--workers 1` | Keep `page` at test scope; use worker scope only for `browser` and `context` (read-only auth state) |
| Dynamic matrix outputting empty array `[]` for documentation-only PRs | Required status checks are never reported — PR cannot merge | Always emit at least `[1]` from the setup job; use a no-op fast-pass inside the shard job when no tests need to run |
| `coverage.changed` without `fetch-depth: 0` in `actions/checkout` | Shallow clone lacks base branch history — diff computation silently fails and falls back to full coverage, negating the performance benefit | Always pair `coverage.changed` with `fetch-depth: 0` in the checkout step |

## New Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 22)

**#71** [community] Vitest `experimental.fsModuleCache` does not track plugin configuration in its cache keys. If a Vite plugin reads an environment variable (e.g., a feature flag injected at build time), the cached module may reflect the old flag value. Teams that use `define` or `envPrefix` in Vite config must include those values in the `fsModuleCachePath` cache key in GitHub Actions, or disable `fsModuleCache` for builds where `define` values change between runs.

**#72** [community] GitHub Actions `concurrency.cancel-in-progress: true` must not be applied to `merge_group` event runs. When a merge queue entry is cancelled mid-run, GitHub marks the required check as "cancelled" (not "failed"), which the queue manager treats differently depending on the branch protection config. On some configurations this silently allows the merge; on others it permanently blocks the queue entry. Use `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}` to restrict cancellation to PR events only.

**#73** [community] Playwright `fullyParallel: true` with worker-scoped fixtures behaves differently than expected when combined with `--shard`. Worker-scoped fixture setup runs once per worker per shard, not once per shard. A 4-shard configuration with 2 workers per shard performs 8 worker-scope setups total (2 per shard × 4 shards). Teams that expected worker-scoped auth to run exactly once per shard and measured setup overhead accordingly will see 2× more setups than anticipated. Plan for `workers × shards` worker-scope executions when sizing timeout budgets.

**#74** [community] Vitest `coverage.changed` with `GITHUB_BASE_REF` only works correctly on `pull_request` events. On `push` to main or `merge_group` events, `GITHUB_BASE_REF` is empty, causing `coverage.changed` to silently report zero changed files — resulting in an empty coverage report that appears to show 100% coverage. Guard the option: `changed: process.env['CI'] && process.env['GITHUB_BASE_REF'] ? process.env['GITHUB_BASE_REF'] : false`. Always run full coverage on merge-to-main and merge queue events.

**#75** [community] Dynamic matrix jobs with `fromJson(needs.setup.outputs.matrix)` produce GitHub Actions job names like `e2e (1)`, `e2e (2)`, etc. Branch protection required status checks are matched by **exact job name**. If the shard count changes (e.g., from 4 to 8 dynamic shards), the job names change and existing branch protection rules no longer match the new names. Use a separate sentinel job (`e2e-complete: needs: e2e`) with a stable name as the required status check, so the required check name never changes regardless of how many shards ran.

### Jest 30 `globalsCleanup` for CI Memory Stabilization

Jest 30 introduces the `globalsCleanup` option to address a class of CI memory leaks where custom global variables (timers, event listeners, singletons attached to `globalThis`) persist across test files within a single Jest worker. In CI, this accumulates over long suite runs, causing memory spikes that trigger OOM kills — most visibly on runners with 7 GB RAM. The option has three values: `'off'` (legacy behavior), `'soft'` (warn on leaked globals — new default), and `'on'` (automatically restore `globalThis` to its initial snapshot before each file). Teams migrating from Jest 29 to Jest 30 that see unexpected "leaked global" warnings should first audit which globals their test setup registers and either protect them explicitly (using `protectProperties`) or switch to `'on'` to enforce cleanup.

> [community] A team running a 2,400-test monorepo with Jest 29 reported intermittent OOM kills on their 7-GB GitHub Actions runner (standard `ubuntu-latest`). After upgrading to Jest 30 with `globalsCleanup: 'on'`, peak memory dropped from 6.2 GB to 1.8 GB — matching the 77% reduction reported in the Jest 30 benchmark. The root cause was a metrics singleton registered in `setupFilesAfterEnach` that accumulated event listener registrations across files because the same object reference persisted across files in a worker.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — Jest 30 globalsCleanup for CI memory stability
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  // Enable automatic globalThis cleanup between test files within a worker.
  // Prevents: timer accumulation, event listener leaks, singleton state bleed.
  // Requires Jest 30+.
  testEnvironmentOptions: {
    globalsCleanup: 'on',
  },

  // Barrel file optimizer — eliminates "import everything" tree-shaking gap
  // in Jest's module system. Up to 100x faster load for large barrel exports.
  // Requires: npm install --save-dev babel-plugin-transform-barrels
  transform: {
    '^.+\\.(ts|tsx)$': ['babel-jest', {
      plugins: ['babel-plugin-transform-barrels'],
    }],
  },

  // Native jest.config.ts (no ts-jest overhead for the config file itself)
  // Still use ts-jest for test file transformation.
  preset: 'ts-jest',
  testEnvironment: 'node',

  // Jest 30: retryTimes with delay — avoid thundering-herd on infrastructure
  // retries after first failure. waitBeforeRetry: 2000 gives flaky DB tests
  // time to recover before the retry attempt.
  // Set in test file: jest.retryTimes(2, { waitBeforeRetry: 2000 });
};

export default config;
```

**GitHub Actions — Jest 30 CI workflow with barrel optimizer (YAML):**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/unit.yml — Jest 30 with barrel optimizer and memory-safe flags
name: Unit Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci

      - name: Run Jest 30
        run: |
          npx jest \
            --ci \
            --maxWorkers=50% \
            --forceExit \
            --testPathPatterns "src/"
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          # Jest 30: NODE_OPTIONS heap size no longer needed for most suites
          # thanks to 77% memory reduction — remove if previously required
          # NODE_OPTIONS: --max-old-space-size=4096
```

### Vitest 4.1 Agent Reporter for AI CI Contexts

Vitest 4.1 ships a dedicated `agent` reporter that suppresses all output for passing tests and surfaces only failures with their full error context. This reporter is designed for AI-assisted CI workflows (Copilot, Claude, OpenCode) where the consuming agent reads `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` or stdio output to diagnose failures. The standard `verbose` reporter generates thousands of lines for a 500-test suite — most of which are `✓ should return correct value` lines that consume token context without adding information. The `agent` reporter reduces this to zero lines for a green run and structured failure output for red runs.

> [community] Teams integrating AI code-review bots with their CI pipelines report that switching from `verbose` to `agent` reporter reduces the token count fed to the review bot by 85–95% on green runs, directly cutting API costs and improving response quality on failure runs (the bot sees only failures, not 800 passing lines before them). The `agent` reporter output is also structured JSON-compatible, making it straightforward to pipe into a bot prompt.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — agent reporter for AI CI contexts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // In CI: use 'github-actions' for human job summary + 'agent' for AI bot
    // In local: use 'verbose' or 'dot'
    reporters: process.env['CI']
      ? [
          'github-actions',  // writes to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY (human-readable)
          'agent',           // writes failures-only to stdout (AI-consumable)
        ]
      : ['verbose'],

    // Vitest 4.1: test tags for stage-based CI filtering
    // Run only smoke tests on feature branches:
    //   npx vitest run --tags-filter="@smoke"
    // Run everything except slow tests on PR:
    //   npx vitest run --tags-filter="!@slow"
    // Boolean operators: and/&&, or/||, not/!, parentheses, wildcards
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yml — stage-based tag filtering with agent reporter
name: Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  smoke:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --tags-filter="@smoke"
        env:
          CI: 'true'

  full:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run
        env:
          CI: 'true'
```

### Vitest `--detect-async-leaks` as a CI Gate

Vitest 4.1 adds `--detect-async-leaks` (config: `detectAsyncLeaks: true`) which fails the test run when any test leaves open handles — unclosed database connections, unresolved timers, dangling fetch requests — between test executions. This is the Vitest equivalent of Jest's `--detectOpenHandles`, but integrated as a first-class CI gate rather than a debugging flag. Running it in CI catches the class of leaks that cause the next test to fail non-deterministically: a test that leaves a database connection open may hold a transaction lock that the next test needs.

> [community] A Node.js API team found that 12 of their 340 test cases left open `pg` (PostgreSQL) connections. With `--detect-async-leaks` disabled, these leaked connections accumulated silently and caused random `connection timeout` failures on the 8th+ consecutive test file in CI — appearing as flakiness. With the flag enabled, each culprit test was immediately identified by name. After fixing the connection cleanup in `afterEach`, the intermittent failures disappeared completely.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — async leak detection as a CI gate
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Fail the run if any test leaves open handles (DB connections, timers, etc.)
    // Requires Vitest 4.1+. Use only in CI or as an audit pass — it adds ~5-10%
    // overhead per test file due to the async handle tracking.
    detectAsyncLeaks: process.env['CI'] === 'true',

    // Vitest 4.1: aroundEach for transaction-scope test isolation
    // All tests in this project run inside a DB transaction that auto-rolls back.
    // Incompatible with tests that commit their own transactions — separate those
    // into a different Vitest project (workspace config).
  },
});
```

**TypeScript — `aroundAll` for one-time DB schema seeding with auto-teardown:**

```typescript
// src/__tests__/db-integration.test.ts — aroundAll for schema setup + teardown
import { describe, test, expect, aroundAll } from 'vitest';
import { createTestDatabase, dropTestDatabase } from '../test-utils/db';

// aroundAll (Vitest 4.1+): wraps the entire describe block.
// yield suspends execution — all tests in the block run before the finally clause.
// Replaces beforeAll/afterAll pairs; guarantees cleanup even on test failure.
describe('User repository', () => {
  aroundAll(async function* () {
    const db = await createTestDatabase('user_tests');
    try {
      yield; // All tests in this describe block execute here
    } finally {
      await dropTestDatabase(db);
    }
  });

  test('creates user', async () => {
    // db is available via module-level import — aroundAll controls lifecycle
    expect(true).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

### Docker BuildKit GHA Layer Cache (`type=gha,mode=max`) for Test Images

When test suites run inside Docker containers (e.g., Testcontainers, containerized integration tests, or multi-service acceptance suites), Docker layer caching dramatically reduces CI build time. GitHub Actions' native BuildKit cache backend (`type=gha`) stores layer blobs directly in GitHub's cache service — no external registry required. `mode=max` caches all intermediate layers (not just the final stage), which matters for multi-stage Dockerfiles where the test tooling stage changes rarely.

A common pattern: separate the "install dependencies" layer from the "copy source" layer. Because `package.json` and `package-lock.json` change rarely relative to source code, the dependency installation layer is nearly always a cache hit.

> [community] A team that containerized their integration test suite (PostgreSQL + Redis + app image) reduced the Docker build step from 4 minutes 20 seconds to 28 seconds on cache hit by moving to `type=gha,mode=max` and splitting the `COPY` instruction into two layers: one for `package*.json` (rarely changes) and one for `src/` (changes every commit). The savings compounded across parallel shards — with 4 shards each building independently, they saved 15+ minutes per PR run.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.test — multi-stage test image with cache-friendly layer order
FROM node:22-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
# Layer 1: copy manifests only — cached unless package-lock.json changes
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts

FROM node:22-alpine AS test
WORKDIR /app
# Layer 2: copy compiled deps from previous stage (cache hit if deps unchanged)
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
# Layer 3: copy source — invalidated on every commit but deps layer stays hot
COPY . .
CMD ["npx", "vitest", "run", "--reporter=github-actions"]
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/integration.yml — Docker BuildKit with GHA layer cache
name: Integration Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx (required for BuildKit cache)
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Build test image with GHA layer cache
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile.test
          push: false
          load: true
          tags: myapp-test:${{ github.sha }}
          # type=gha: store layers in GitHub Actions cache (no registry needed)
          # mode=max: cache all intermediate layers, not just final stage
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=test-image
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max,scope=test-image

      - name: Run integration tests inside container
        run: |
          docker run --rm \
            -e CI=true \
            -e DATABASE_URL=${{ secrets.TEST_DATABASE_URL }} \
            myapp-test:${{ github.sha }}
```

### SLSA Provenance Generation with GitHub Artifact Attestations

SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) level 2 provenance can be generated automatically for test artifacts and release builds using GitHub's `actions/attest-build-provenance` action (GA March 2025). This creates a signed SLSA provenance statement stored as a GitHub attestation, verifiable with `gh attestation verify`. For test pipelines, provenance on test binaries ensures that the binary actually tested matches what was deployed — closing the gap between "tests passed" and "tests passed on this exact binary."

> [community] Security-focused teams adopting SLSA provenance report an unexpected CI benefit: provenance attestations serve as a tamper-evident audit log of which binary was tested. When a production incident occurs, `gh attestation verify` against the deployment artifact confirms (or refutes) whether it was tested in CI. Teams that previously relied only on git SHA correlation found that environment-specific builds (different `NODE_ENV` or feature flag values) could produce a different binary from the same SHA — provenance attestation catches this class of drift.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/release.yml — SLSA provenance for test artifacts
name: Build and Attest

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write    # Required: OIDC token for signing provenance
  attestations: write # Required: write attestation to GitHub
  contents: read

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      artifact-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --ci

      - name: Build release artifact
        id: build
        run: |
          npm run build
          DIGEST=$(sha256sum dist/app.js | awk '{print $1}')
          echo "digest=sha256:$DIGEST" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "Built artifact digest: sha256:$DIGEST"

      - name: Generate SLSA provenance attestation
        uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v2
        with:
          subject-path: dist/app.js
          # Generates a signed SLSA provenance statement stored as a
          # GitHub attestation. Verify with:
          #   gh attestation verify dist/app.js --owner <org>
```

### GitHub OIDC Custom Properties for Attribute-Based CI Trust

GitHub Actions OIDC tokens (GA March 2025 for custom properties) now include `repo_property_*` claims that reflect repository custom properties. This enables attribute-based trust policies in cloud provider IAM (AWS, GCP, Azure) without per-repository allow-lists. A trust policy can grant deployment credentials only to repositories tagged `environment:production-capable` — eliminating the maintenance burden of updating IAM policies every time a new repository needs production access.

For test pipelines, this is most useful for granting access to test-only infrastructure (staging databases, test secrets stores) based on a repository property like `tier:internal` rather than enumerating every repository by name.

> [community] A platform team managing 80 repositories found that their AWS IAM OIDC trust policy (which allowed all repositories in the org) became a security concern when external contractors gained org membership. After adopting `repo_property_team:platform` as the claim filter, only 12 platform-owned repositories could assume the staging-access role — reducing the blast radius of a compromised workflow token by 85%. The migration required one pass to set custom properties on the allowed repos; no workflow changes were needed.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/integration.yml — OIDC with custom property claim filter
name: Integration Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  id-token: write  # Required for OIDC token issuance
  contents: read

jobs:
  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Configure AWS credentials via OIDC
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/TestInfraAccess
          aws-region: us-east-1
          # The IAM role's trust policy condition filters on:
          # "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub" matches "repo:myorg/*"
          # AND
          # "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:repo_property_tier" == "internal"
          # This means only repos with the 'tier:internal' custom property
          # can assume this role — no per-repo allow-list required.

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          # Credentials injected by the OIDC action above — short-lived tokens
          # scoped to this workflow run only. No long-lived secrets in repo.
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DATABASE_URL }}
```

**AWS IAM trust policy condition (JSON — not YAML):**

```json
{
  "Condition": {
    "StringLike": {
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:myorg/*:ref:refs/heads/*"
    },
    "StringEquals": {
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:repo_property_tier": "internal"
    }
  }
}
```

### Playwright `test.abort()` Guard-Rail Fixtures for Missing CI Credentials

Playwright v1.60 introduced `test.abort(message)` which can be called from fixtures, `beforeAll`, or route handlers to immediately abort the test (and mark it as failed) rather than silently skipping it or hanging until timeout. This is the correct pattern for CI guard-rail fixtures that check for required environment variables — a missing `TEST_API_KEY` should fail loudly with an actionable message, not time out after 30 seconds.

> [community] Before `test.abort()`, teams used `test.skip(condition, message)` to skip tests when credentials were absent. In CI, this produced green runs with 0 passing tests — which passed required status checks. Developers merged PRs without noticing that all tests were skipped because credentials were missing from the environment. `test.abort()` exits with code 1, which fails the required status check and surfaces the misconfiguration immediately.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — guard-rail fixture using test.abort()
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type RequiredEnv = {
  apiKey: string;
  baseUrl: string;
};

// Guard-rail fixture: abort immediately on missing credentials
// rather than skipping (which passes CI) or timing out (which wastes minutes)
export const test = base.extend<RequiredEnv>({
  apiKey: async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    const key = process.env['TEST_API_KEY'];
    if (!key) {
      await testInfo.abort('TEST_API_KEY environment variable is not set. ' +
        'Add it to your GitHub Actions secrets and reference it in the workflow.');
    }
    await use(key!);
  },

  baseUrl: async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    const url = process.env['BASE_URL'];
    if (!url) {
      await testInfo.abort('BASE_URL environment variable is not set. ' +
        'Set it to the staging environment URL in the workflow env: block.');
    }
    await use(url!);
  },
});

export { expect };
```

```typescript
// tests/api.spec.ts — using guard-rail fixtures
import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('POST /users creates a user', async ({ apiKey, baseUrl, request }) => {
  const response = await request.post(`${baseUrl}/users`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    data: { name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' },
  });

  expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
  const body = await response.json();
  expect(body).toMatchObject({ name: 'Alice' });
});
```
