### Pattern 2 — GitHub Actions Reusable Workflows for DRY Test Matrix Definition

`workflow_call` reusable workflows eliminate repeated job definitions for standard test setups. Instead of copying the same 40-line job block into every workflow file that needs to run tests, a reusable workflow at `.github/workflows/run-tests.yml` defines the canonical test execution once. Caller workflows pass inputs (node version, test command, coverage flag) and secrets (API keys). The job runs inside the caller's repository context with the same runner and permissions. Teams with 5+ workflow files typically save 60–80% of test YAML when extracting to reusable workflows.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/run-tests.yml — reusable workflow (the canonical definition)
name: Run Tests (Reusable)

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version:
        type: string
        default: '22'
      test-command:
        type: string
        required: true
      coverage:
        type: boolean
        default: false
      timeout-minutes:
        type: number
        default: 15
    secrets:
      API_KEY:
        required: false
    outputs:
      coverage-report-artifact:
        description: 'Artifact name containing coverage lcov'
        value: ${{ jobs.test.outputs.artifact-name }}

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: ${{ inputs.timeout-minutes }}
    outputs:
      artifact-name: coverage-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: ${{ inputs.test-command }}
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}

      - name: Upload coverage
        if: inputs.coverage && always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
          path: coverage/lcov.info
          retention-days: 3
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — caller workflow (concise, DRY)
name: CI

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  unit:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/run-tests.yml
    with:
      node-version: '22'
      test-command: 'npm run test:unit -- --ci --coverage'
      coverage: true
    secrets:
      API_KEY: ${{ secrets.TEST_API_KEY }}

  integration:
    needs: unit
    uses: ./.github/workflows/run-tests.yml
    with:
      test-command: 'npm run test:integration'
      timeout-minutes: 25
    secrets:
      API_KEY: ${{ secrets.TEST_API_KEY }}
```

> [community] Reusable workflows have one hidden cost: they appear as a separate workflow run in the GitHub Actions UI, not as a job inside the caller. Debugging failures requires clicking into the reusable workflow run, then finding the job. Teams that switch to reusable workflows should update their PR required status checks to reference the **reusable workflow job name**, not the caller job name — otherwise required checks reference a job that no longer exists at the expected path. Run `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/main/protection` after migration to verify required checks still resolve correctly.

---

### Pattern 3 — `pnpm` Workspace Caching in CI: Correct Cache Key Strategy

`pnpm` workspaces store all packages in a content-addressable store at `~/.pnpm-store`, separate from `node_modules`. The `actions/setup-node` cache integration caches `node_modules` but not `~/.pnpm-store`. For `pnpm`, you must use `actions/cache` directly with the store path, OR use `pnpm/action-setup@v4` which handles this automatically. Mixing `actions/setup-node` (with `cache: npm`) and `pnpm` produces a cache miss on every run because npm's `~/.npm` cache is populated but `pnpm install` ignores it.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pnpm-ci.yml — correct pnpm workspace caching
name: CI (pnpm)

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Step 1: Install pnpm BEFORE setup-node to enable built-in caching
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: 9   # pin major version; minor/patch via packageManager field

      # Step 2: setup-node with cache: pnpm — uses pnpm's store path
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm   # NOT 'npm' — this key hashes pnpm-lock.yaml

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      # Workspace-aware test: only run packages affected by changed files
      - name: Run affected tests
        run: pnpm --filter "...[origin/main]" test --if-present
        env:
          CI: 'true'

      # Coverage collection: aggregate from all workspace packages
      - name: Merge workspace coverage
        run: |
          pnpm --filter "*" exec sh -c \
            'test -f coverage/lcov.info && cp coverage/lcov.info ../../coverage/lcov-${PWD##*/}.info' \
            || true
          npx lcov-result-merger 'coverage/lcov-*.info' coverage/merged-lcov.info
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-merged
          path: coverage/merged-lcov.info
```

> [community] `pnpm --filter "...[origin/main]"` runs tests only for packages with changes since `origin/main`, including dependent packages up the dependency graph (the `...` prefix). A common mistake is using `--filter "[origin/main]"` (without `...`) which runs only directly changed packages and misses downstream consumers. A shared utility package changed without `...` would skip testing all packages that depend on it, producing a false-clean CI result.

---

### Pattern 4 — GitHub Actions `path` Filter for Monorepo Selective CI Triggers

For monorepos where multiple packages live in subdirectories, the `on.push.paths` and `on.pull_request.paths` filters restrict workflow triggers to changes in specific paths. Without path filters, every workflow runs on every commit regardless of which package was changed — wasting CI minutes and adding noise to unrelated PRs. Path filters use glob patterns: `packages/api/**` triggers on any change inside the `packages/api` directory tree.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/api-tests.yml — triggered only when api package changes
name: API Package Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - 'packages/api/**'
      - 'packages/shared/**'       # also trigger when shared dep changes
      - '.github/workflows/api-tests.yml'   # re-run on workflow change
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'packages/api/**'
      - 'packages/shared/**'
      - '.github/workflows/api-tests.yml'

# Always run when triggered from merge queue (path filters do NOT apply)
  merge_group:
    types: [checks_requested]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: packages/api
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --ci
        env:
          CI: 'true'
```

> [community] Path filters have a documented edge case: if a PR changes only files outside all path filters for a required status check, that check is considered "skipped" not "passed." GitHub's merge queue treats a skipped check as passing by default, which means a workflow with a required check can be bypassed entirely by not touching the paths it watches. For required checks that must always run on merge queue entries, add `merge_group: types: [checks_requested]` to the trigger — the `merge_group` event ignores path filters and always fires.

---

### Pattern 5 — Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` for Isolation Without Full Fork Overhead

Vitest supports four pool types: `threads` (SharedArrayBuffer workers — fastest, shared memory), `forks` (child processes — full isolation, highest overhead), `vmThreads` (VM context per worker thread — isolated module registry, no process spawn), and `vmForks` (VM context per fork — combines process isolation with module sandboxing). For integration test suites that interact with real databases or modify global Node.js state (e.g., `process.env` mutations), `vmForks` provides isolation comparable to `forks` but with Vitest's VM-based module mocking available — unlike `forks` where `vi.mock()` module boundaries are shared across the fork's entire module cache.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — per-project pool selection for heterogeneous suites
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    workspace: [
      {
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          pool: 'threads',          // fastest — unit tests need no isolation
          maxWorkers: 8,
        },
      },
      {
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          pool: 'vmForks',          // process isolation + VM module registry
          maxWorkers: 4,            // fewer workers — each forks a process
          testTimeout: 30_000,
          // Each vmFork worker gets a fresh module registry: vi.mock() scoped per file
          // process.env mutations don't leak between parallel integration test files
          env: {
            DATABASE_URL: 'postgresql://localhost:5432/test_${process.env.VITEST_WORKER_ID}',
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vmForks` is 3–5× slower startup than `threads` because it spawns real child processes. For a test suite with 200 integration test files, each run may add 15–30 seconds of process-spawn overhead versus threads. Measure actual wall-clock time in CI before committing; for suites with < 50 integration test files, `vmThreads` often provides sufficient isolation with 2× less overhead.

---

### Pattern 6 — Node.js `--test-shard` Built-In Test Runner Sharding

Node.js 22.3+ added `--test-shard=<index>/<total>` to the built-in `node:test` runner, enabling distributed test execution without any third-party test runner. The shard index divides the test file list alphabetically (not by run time) into equal-sized slices. Combined with `--experimental-test-coverage` and the JUnit reporter (`--test-reporter=junit`), teams can run a zero-dependency CI test pipeline on Node.js 22+ LTS.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/node-test-sharded.yml
# Uses built-in node:test runner with --test-shard (no Jest/Vitest dependency)
name: Node Built-in Tests (Sharded)

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: ['1/4', '2/4', '3/4', '4/4']
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'   # --test-shard requires Node 22.3+
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci

      - name: Run shard ${{ matrix.shard }}
        run: |
          node \
            --test \
            --test-shard=${{ matrix.shard }} \
            --test-reporter=junit \
            --test-reporter-destination=test-results-${{ matrix.shard }}.xml \
            --experimental-test-coverage \
            'src/**/*.test.mjs'

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: node-test-results-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: test-results-*.xml
          retention-days: 3

  report:
    if: always()
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      checks: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: node-test-results-*
          merge-multiple: true
      - name: Publish test results
        uses: mikepenz/action-junit-report@v5
        with:
          report_paths: 'test-results-*.xml'
          check_name: 'Node Built-in Test Results'
```

> [community] Node's `--test-shard` divides files alphabetically, not by run time. A shard containing files starting with `z-` may contain your slowest integration tests while a shard with `a-` files contains only fast unit tests — producing wall-clock times that vary by 5–10× between shards. For even distribution, use a pre-step that generates a custom file list sorted by historical run time and pipes it to `--test-name-pattern` combined with numbered shards. The `--test-shard` feature is best suited for homogeneous suites where all test files take similar time.

---

### Pattern 7 — Jest `retryTimes` with `waitBeforeRetry` for Infrastructure-Dependent Tests

Jest 30 adds `waitBeforeRetry` and `retryImmediately` options to `jest.retryTimes()`. In CI, flaky tests often fail due to brief infrastructure unavailability (database connection pool exhaustion, Redis timeout, HTTP rate limiting) — not test logic errors. Retrying immediately (Jest 29 behavior) usually fails again because the infrastructure hasn't recovered. A 2–5 second wait before retry is enough for connection pool cleanup to complete. `retryImmediately: false` (the new default) combines with `waitBeforeRetry: 2000` for a gentle backoff.

```typescript
// integration/db.test.ts — Jest 30 retry with wait for infrastructure flakiness
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from '@jest/globals';
import { createPool } from '../src/db/pool';
import type { Pool } from 'pg';

// Retry up to 2 times with 2-second wait between attempts.
// Only applies when Jest detects a test failure — does not slow passing tests.
// Jest 30+: waitBeforeRetry replaces the manual setTimeout workaround.
jest.retryTimes(2, {
  waitBeforeRetry: 2000,    // ms to wait between retries (Jest 30+)
  retryImmediately: false,  // default in Jest 30: do NOT retry synchronously
  logErrorsBeforeRetry: true, // print failure reason before each retry attempt
});

let pool: Pool;

beforeAll(async () => {
  pool = createPool({ max: 5, connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
  await pool.connect();   // validates pool is healthy before tests start
});

afterAll(async () => {
  await pool.end();
});

describe('connection pool under load', () => {
  test('acquires connection within timeout', async () => {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
      const result = await client.query('SELECT 1 AS ok');
      expect(result.rows[0].ok).toBe(1);
    } finally {
      client.release();
    }
  });
});
```

> [community] `logErrorsBeforeRetry: true` is the single most impactful option for CI debugging. Without it, a test that fails twice then passes on the third attempt shows only "PASS" in the test output — the two prior failures are silently swallowed. With `logErrorsBeforeRetry: true`, the retry failure messages appear in the CI log before the final pass, making it immediately visible that the test is flaky without needing to re-run with retries disabled. Enable it in all integration test configs.

---

### Pattern 8 — GitHub Actions Step-Level Timeout for Hanging Test Processes

GitHub Actions job-level `timeout-minutes` cancels the entire job when exceeded, which terminates the worker and produces a partial artifact upload. Setting `timeout-minutes` on individual steps provides finer control: a hanging test process (due to open DB connections, unresolved promises, or WebSocket handles) is killed at the step level while post-steps (artifact upload, Docker cleanup) still run. Step-level timeout is especially important for e2e test steps that can hang indefinitely when a browser crashes without closing.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — step-level timeouts for test stages
name: E2E Tests

on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45   # hard cap on the entire job
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }

      - name: Install dependencies
        timeout-minutes: 5    # npm ci hanging = network issue, not test issue
        run: npm ci

      - name: Install Playwright browsers
        timeout-minutes: 10   # browser download can stall on slow mirrors
        run: npx playwright install chromium --with-deps

      - name: Start application server
        timeout-minutes: 3    # app startup > 3 min = build/startup defect
        run: npm run start:test &
        env:
          PORT: 3001
          NODE_ENV: test

      - name: Wait for server health
        timeout-minutes: 2
        run: |
          until curl -sf http://localhost:3001/health; do sleep 2; done

      - name: Run E2E tests
        timeout-minutes: 25   # test execution hard cap (separate from job cap)
        run: npx playwright test --reporter=github,html
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          BASE_URL: 'http://localhost:3001'

      # Always runs even if test step times out — uploads partial artifacts
      - name: Upload test results
        if: always()
        timeout-minutes: 3
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 7
```

> [community] The most common failure mode without step-level timeouts: the "Run E2E tests" step hangs at exactly 0 passing/failing tests because the browser didn't launch (missing `--with-deps` on a new runner image). The job consumes the full `timeout-minutes: 45` before GitHub kills it, burning 45 minutes of CI quota per failure. With `timeout-minutes: 25` on the test step, the failure surfaces in 25 minutes and post-steps still run to upload the (empty) playwright-report, giving the developer a clear "no tests ran" signal rather than a raw timeout.

---

### Pattern 9 — Ephemeral Docker Compose Projects for Parallel Integration Test Isolation

When multiple CI jobs run integration tests concurrently against Docker Compose services (databases, message queues, mock APIs), each job must have its own isolated service stack. Docker Compose `--project-name` assigns a unique namespace to all containers, networks, and volumes in a stack — containers from different stacks share the same Docker daemon but never share network or storage. Setting `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` to the GitHub Actions run ID + attempt number guarantees uniqueness even when the same runner hosts concurrent jobs.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/integration.yml — ephemeral compose stacks per CI job
name: Integration Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    env:
      # Unique project name per run attempt prevents cross-job contamination
      COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME: ci-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci

      - name: Start isolated service stack
        run: docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up -d --wait
        # --wait: blocks until all healthchecks pass (Compose v2.1+)
        # Project name = COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME env var above

      - name: Run integration tests
        run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          DATABASE_URL: postgresql://testuser:testpass@localhost:5432/testdb
          REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379

      - name: Dump logs on failure
        if: failure()
        run: docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml logs

      - name: Tear down service stack
        if: always()
        run: docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans
        # --volumes: removes named volumes to prevent disk accumulation
        # --remove-orphans: removes containers from removed services
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.test.yml — minimal test stack with healthchecks
version: '3.8'
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: testuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
      POSTGRES_DB: testdb
    ports:
      - '5432:5432'
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U testuser -d testdb']
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - '6379:6379'
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD', 'redis-cli', 'ping']
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
```

> [community] `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` isolation has a DNS resolution side effect: service hostnames within the compose network are prefixed with the project name in Docker's internal DNS. Tests that hardcode `postgres` as the hostname instead of using the port-mapped `localhost:5432` will fail when the project name changes, because the internal hostname becomes `ci-12345-1-postgres-1`. Always use `localhost` + published ports for test connections in CI, not Docker internal hostnames.

---

### Pattern 10 — DORA Metrics Collection from CI Pipeline Data

DORA metrics (Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, Mean Time to Recovery) can be derived from GitHub Actions event data without additional APM tooling. Deployment frequency comes from `workflow_run` events on deploy workflows. Lead time is the delta between commit timestamp and successful deploy workflow completion. A GitHub Actions workflow that writes structured JSON to a time-series store (InfluxDB, Datadog, or a simple append-only NDJSON file in a metrics repo) gives teams DORA visibility at zero infrastructure cost.

```typescript
// scripts/emit-dora-metrics.ts — run at end of deploy workflow
// Usage: node --loader ts-node/esm scripts/emit-dora-metrics.ts
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { appendFileSync } from 'fs';

interface DORAEvent {
  timestamp: string;
  metric: 'deployment_frequency' | 'lead_time_minutes' | 'change_failure';
  value: number;
  branch: string;
  sha: string;
  workflow_run_id: string;
  outcome: 'success' | 'failure';
}

function emitDORAEvent(metric: DORAEvent['metric'], value: number): void {
  const event: DORAEvent = {
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    metric,
    value,
    branch: process.env.GITHUB_REF_NAME ?? 'unknown',
    sha: process.env.GITHUB_SHA?.slice(0, 8) ?? 'unknown',
    workflow_run_id: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ID ?? 'unknown',
    outcome: process.env.DEPLOY_OUTCOME === 'success' ? 'success' : 'failure',
  };

  // Append to NDJSON metrics log (simple, append-only, Git-tracked)
  const metricsPath = process.env.METRICS_FILE ?? './metrics/dora.ndjson';
  appendFileSync(metricsPath, JSON.stringify(event) + '\n');

  // Also write to GitHub Actions job summary for immediate visibility
  const summary = process.env.GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY;
  if (summary) {
    appendFileSync(summary, `| ${metric} | ${value} | ${event.outcome} |\n`);
  }
}

// Compute lead time: time from first commit in PR to deploy completion
const commitTimestamp = new Date(process.env.COMMIT_TIMESTAMP ?? Date.now());
const deployTimestamp = new Date();
const leadTimeMinutes = Math.round(
  (deployTimestamp.getTime() - commitTimestamp.getTime()) / 60_000
);

emitDORAEvent('lead_time_minutes', leadTimeMinutes);
emitDORAEvent('deployment_frequency', 1);

if (process.env.DEPLOY_OUTCOME === 'failure') {
  emitDORAEvent('change_failure', 1);
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (excerpt) — DORA metrics emission step
      - name: Write DORA metrics table header to job summary
        run: |
          echo "## DORA Metrics" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "| Metric | Value | Outcome |" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "|--------|-------|---------|" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      - name: Emit DORA metrics
        if: always()
        run: node --loader ts-node/esm scripts/emit-dora-metrics.ts
        env:
          DEPLOY_OUTCOME: ${{ job.status }}
          COMMIT_TIMESTAMP: ${{ github.event.head_commit.timestamp }}
          METRICS_FILE: ./metrics/dora.ndjson
```

**Tradeoff:** NDJSON append-only files tracked in Git are readable and zero-cost but produce large diffs and become unwieldy beyond ~10,000 events. For teams deploying more than 20 times per day, switch to an external time-series store (InfluxDB, Datadog custom metrics, or GitHub's own API via `gh api`) before the metrics file degrades repository performance.

### Pattern 11 — Playwright `--grep` and `--grep-invert` for Stage-Based CI Filtering

Playwright's `--grep` flag filters test cases by a regex match on the test title (including parent `describe` blocks). Unlike `--test-list` (which requires an external file), `--grep` is inline and requires no pre-computation. The convention of tagging tests with `@smoke`, `@regression`, or `@slow` in the test title enables stage-based filtering without separate config files. `--grep-invert` excludes matching tests — use it to run "everything except slow" on PR pipelines.

```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts — tests tagged with stage identifiers in titles
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('@smoke checkout happy path', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Buy Now' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});

test('@regression checkout with expired card shows error message', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4000000000000002');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Your card was declined')).toBeVisible();
});

test('@slow checkout payment retry flow — full 3DS2 challenge', async ({ page }) => {
  // Simulates 3DS2 challenge which takes ~8s to complete
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  // ... full 3DS2 challenge flow
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/playwright-staged.yml — grep-based stage filtering
name: Playwright Staged

on:
  pull_request: {}        # PR: smoke only
  push:
    branches: [main]      # post-merge: regression (skips slow)
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 3 * * *'  # nightly: everything including slow

jobs:
  playwright:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install chromium --with-deps

      - name: Run tests (PR → smoke only)
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        run: npx playwright test --grep="@smoke"

      - name: Run tests (post-merge → regression, skip slow)
        if: github.event_name == 'push'
        run: npx playwright test --grep="@smoke|@regression" --grep-invert="@slow"

      - name: Run tests (nightly → all tests)
        if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
        run: npx playwright test
```

> [community] `--grep` regex is applied to the fully qualified test name: `describe title > test title`. A test titled `@smoke should work` inside `describe('checkout')` matches `--grep="@smoke"` because the full name is `checkout > @smoke should work`. However, if developers accidentally write `describe('@smoke payment flow')` and `test('should work')`, the tag is on the describe block — `--grep="@smoke"` still matches. Mixing tag placement (some on describe, some on test) produces confusing grep results because the regex operates on the concatenated string. Standardize on test-level tagging only.

---

### Pattern 12 — GitHub Actions Environment Protection Rules for Staging Gates

GitHub Environments attach approval gates and deployment protection rules to specific workflows. A `staging` environment requiring at least one reviewer approval prevents automated pushes directly from CI to staging without human sign-off. Environment secrets (different from repository secrets) are only available to jobs targeting that environment — the `DATABASE_URL` for staging is inaccessible to jobs running on feature branches.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml — environment-gated deployment
name: Deploy to Staging

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci && npm test -- --ci

  deploy-staging:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Targeting 'staging' environment enables:
    # 1. Required reviewer approval gate (configured in GitHub UI)
    # 2. Wait timer: minimum N minutes after previous deploy (prevents thrashing)
    # 3. Environment-scoped secrets: DATABASE_URL_STAGING only available here
    # 4. Deployment history tracking visible in repository Deployments tab
    environment:
      name: staging
      url: https://staging.example.com
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      - name: Deploy to staging
        run: npm run deploy:staging
        env:
          # Only available because this job targets the 'staging' environment
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL_STAGING }}
          DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DEPLOY_KEY }}

      - name: Smoke test staging
        run: |
          npx playwright test \
            --grep="@smoke" \
            --project=chromium
        env:
          BASE_URL: https://staging.example.com
```

> [community] Environment protection "required reviewers" blocks the job until a reviewer approves via the GitHub UI or API — the workflow is paused, not cancelled. This means the runner is NOT occupied during the wait (GitHub Actions does not charge minutes while waiting for environment approval). However, any environment secrets referenced by the waiting job are **not** resolved until the approval fires, so secrets cannot be pre-validated before the gate. Design deployment jobs so all pre-approval work (build, unit tests) happens in a prior job that does not target the environment, keeping the environment-targeted job focused only on deployment steps.

---

### Pattern 13 — Playwright `captureGitInfo` for Test Report Traceability

`testConfig.captureGitInfo` (Playwright v1.51+) automatically captures `branch`, `commit SHA`, `commit subject`, `commit author`, and `commit timestamp` from the git repository and attaches them to every test result. In merged shard reports and HTML reports, this metadata appears alongside each test result, enabling navigation from a failing test back to the exact commit that introduced it without leaving the test report UI. The feature uses `git log` under the hood and requires the `.git` directory to be present in the runner checkout.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — captureGitInfo for full test traceability
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Attach git metadata to every test result.
  // Requires: git is installed on the runner AND actions/checkout@v4 with
  // fetch-depth > 0 (default fetch-depth: 1 is sufficient for HEAD metadata).
  captureGitInfo: { git: true },

  // Pair with blob reporter for shard merging: git info survives the merge step
  reporter: process.env.CI
    ? [['blob'], ['github']]
    : [['html', { open: 'on-failure' }]],

  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
  },

  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { browserName: 'chromium' } },
  ],
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e-traced.yml — captureGitInfo requires non-shallow checkout
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # Default actions/checkout@v4 fetch-depth: 1 is sufficient for captureGitInfo
      # (only HEAD commit metadata is captured, not full history).
      # Use fetch-depth: 0 ONLY if your tests need full git log access.
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 1

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install chromium --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test
        env:
          CI: 'true'
          BASE_URL: ${{ vars.STAGING_URL }}
```

> [community] `captureGitInfo` silently produces empty metadata when `actions/checkout@v4` is used with `sparse-checkout` because the `.git` directory is present but git operations that list refs may behave differently depending on sparse-checkout configuration. Teams using sparse-checkout for monorepo performance optimization find that `captureGitInfo.branch` is populated but `commitSubject` and `commitAuthor` are empty strings. The workaround is to run `git log -1 --format="%s %an" HEAD` in a pre-step to verify git metadata is accessible before relying on `captureGitInfo`.

### Pattern 14 — Vitest `coverage.include` Requirement (v4.0 Breaking Change)

Vitest 4.0 removed `coverage.all` (which previously collected coverage for all files matching the include pattern, even untested ones) and made `coverage.include` required for coverage collection. Without `coverage.include`, Vitest 4.0 reports coverage only for files that are imported by tests — silently omitting modules with zero coverage. This is a silent accuracy regression for teams upgrading from Vitest 3.x: coverage percentage appears higher because untested files are no longer counted in the denominator.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage.include required in Vitest 4.0+ for accurate reporting
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      // REQUIRED in Vitest 4.0+: list of globs for files to include in coverage.
      // Omitting this means only imported files are measured — untested modules
      // are excluded from the report, inflating the coverage percentage.
      include: [
        'src/**/*.ts',
        'src/**/*.tsx',
        '!src/**/*.d.ts',
        '!src/**/*.stories.tsx',    // exclude Storybook files
        '!src/**/index.ts',         // exclude barrel files (usually trivial re-exports)
      ],

      // Provider: 'v8' (fast, built-in) or 'istanbul' (more accurate branch tracking)
      provider: 'v8',

      // Thresholds enforced as CI gate — fail if coverage drops below
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },

      // Vitest 4.0: coverage.all was REMOVED — these are the replacement options:
      // coverage.include replaces coverage.all semantically
      // coverage.exclude to exclude specific files from the include glob
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.test.ts',
        'src/**/*.spec.ts',
        'src/test-utils/**',
      ],
    },
  },
});
```

> [community] Teams upgrading from Vitest 3.x to 4.0 without adding `coverage.include` observe coverage jumping from ~72% to ~91% overnight. The percentage increase is misleading: no new tests were added, but the denominator shrank because `coverage.all: true` (which forced all source files into the measurement) was the Vitest 3.x default and is now gone. The first sign of the issue is that `coverage.thresholds` suddenly passes for projects that were previously failing the threshold — a "green" that hides technical debt. Immediately set `coverage.include` to match the Vitest 3.x `coverage.all` glob on upgrade.

---

### Pattern 15 — GitLab CI `needs:` with `optional: true` for Flexible Pipeline DAGs

GitLab CI's `needs:` keyword creates a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of job dependencies, allowing later stages to start before earlier stages complete. `needs: [{job: "e2e-tests", optional: true}]` marks the dependency as optional: the dependent job starts immediately if the `e2e-tests` job does not exist in the pipeline (e.g., because it was skipped by `rules:`). This enables pipelines where expensive test jobs are conditionally skipped on non-main branches without blocking downstream deployment jobs.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml — flexible DAG with optional dependencies
stages:
  - test
  - report
  - deploy

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:22-alpine
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run test:unit -- --ci
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
    paths:
      - coverage/

e2e-tests:
  stage: test
  image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.52.0-noble
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx playwright test --reporter=junit,html
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: playwright-results.xml
    paths:
      - playwright-report/
    expire_in: 7 days
  # Only run E2E on main branch and merge requests targeting main
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
    - if: '$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME == "main"'

merge-reports:
  stage: report
  image: node:22-alpine
  # optional: true means this job runs even if e2e-tests was skipped
  needs:
    - job: unit-tests
    - job: e2e-tests
      optional: true
      artifacts: true    # download e2e artifacts if job ran
  script:
    - |
      if [ -f playwright-report/index.html ]; then
        echo "E2E report present — merging with unit coverage"
        npm run merge:reports
      else
        echo "E2E skipped — using unit-only report"
        cp coverage/lcov.info merged-coverage.info
      fi
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - merged-coverage.info

deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  needs:
    - job: merge-reports
    - job: e2e-tests
      optional: true   # deploy proceeds even if e2e was skipped on feature branch
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
  script:
    - npm run deploy:staging
```

> [community] `needs: optional: true` has a documentation-vs-behavior gap for `artifacts: true`. If the optional job was skipped (not failed — skipped via `rules:`), GitLab silently treats the artifact download as successful with zero files. If the optional job failed, GitLab fails the dependent job unless you also set `allow_failure: true` on the optional dependency. The common mistake: setting `optional: true` expecting it to handle both "skipped" and "failed" cases — it only handles "skipped." For graceful failure tolerance, combine `optional: true` with `when: always` on the dependent job and add a shell `test -f` guard before consuming optional artifacts.

---

## New Anti-Patterns (Cycle 25)

| Anti-pattern | Why harmful | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `pnpm install` without `--frozen-lockfile` in CI | Non-frozen install allows `pnpm` to update `pnpm-lock.yaml` on the runner, producing an install from a mutated lockfile that may differ from developer machines | Always use `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` in CI; fail the pipeline if lockfile is out of sync |
| `workflow_call` reusable workflow with `secrets: inherit` globally | Passes ALL repository secrets to the reusable workflow — including secrets unrelated to the test job — violating the principle of least privilege | Declare only required secrets explicitly using named `secrets:` inputs in `workflow_call`; avoid `secrets: inherit` for reusable test workflows |
| Playwright `--grep` patterns with special regex characters in test titles | Test titles containing `(`, `)`, `+`, or `.` break `--grep` patterns when used literally — `--grep="payment (3DS)"` matches nothing because `(3DS)` is a regex capture group | Escape special characters in grep patterns or use explicit tag annotations (`@3ds`) without special chars in the tag string itself |
| `coverage.include` omitted on Vitest 4.0+ upgrade | Silently omits untested modules from coverage denominator, inflating coverage percentage without any new tests | Add `coverage.include` matching all source files immediately after upgrading to Vitest 4.0 |
| GitHub Environment with `required reviewers` on non-deployment workflows | Human approval gates on test-only workflows (not deployments) add manual friction to CI without a security benefit — tests should run automatically | Reserve `required reviewers` for deployment workflows targeting production or staging; test workflows should never require human approval |
| Job-level `timeout-minutes` without step-level timeouts on artifact upload | When a test step hangs and exhausts the job timeout, the `if: always()` post-steps (artifact upload) are cancelled — the Playwright report is never uploaded | Add step-level `timeout-minutes` to the test execution step; keep a generous job-level timeout as the last-resort backstop |

---

## New Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 25)

**#89** [community] Playwright `--test-list` silently skips list entries that don't match any test in the suite — no warning, no error, exit code 0. A team that quarantined flaky tests by adding them to a `quarantine.txt` file and using `--test-list-invert quarantine.txt` found that after a refactor that renamed several tests, the old titles in `quarantine.txt` matched nothing, effectively unquarantining the renamed tests without any signal. Add a validation step: `npx playwright test --list | sort > current-tests.txt && comm -23 <(sort quarantine.txt) current-tests.txt` fails the pipeline when quarantine entries go stale.

**#90** [community] GitHub Actions `workflow_call` reusable workflows do not inherit the calling workflow's `permissions:` block. If the caller grants `checks: write` and `pull-requests: write` at the workflow level, those permissions are NOT available inside a `workflow_call` job unless explicitly re-declared in the reusable workflow's `on.workflow_call.` section. Teams that migrate existing jobs to reusable workflows and then see `403 Resource not accessible` errors on JUnit report publishing (which requires `checks: write`) often spend hours debugging before discovering the permission inheritance gap. Always declare `permissions:` explicitly in the reusable workflow file.

**#91** [community] Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` with `maxWorkers` set higher than the runner's CPU count does not improve parallelism and can degrade performance. Each `vmFork` spawns a real OS process. On a 2-vCPU GitHub Actions runner, setting `maxWorkers: 8` spawns 8 processes competing for 2 CPUs — context-switching overhead causes total wall-clock time to increase by 40–60% compared to `maxWorkers: 2`. Profile with `time npx vitest run --pool=vmForks --maxWorkers=N` for N = 1, 2, 4 and use the value that minimizes wall-clock time, not the value that maximizes process count.

**#92** [community] Node.js `--test-shard` alphabetical file ordering produces maximally uneven shard load when test files use numeric prefixes (`001-auth.test.mjs`, `002-checkout.test.mjs`). These files sort alphabetically into shard 1, while files prefixed `9xx` sort into the last shard — grouping the slowest integration tests by numerical similarity. The result: shard 1 consistently finishes in 2 minutes while shard 4 takes 18 minutes. Rename files to avoid numeric prefixes, or add a pre-step that shuffles the file list before passing it to the shards.

**#93** [community] Docker Compose `--project-name` with `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` set to a value containing the GitHub run ID (`ci-12345678-1`) produces container names exceeding Docker's 63-character limit when combined with service names and replica indices (e.g., `ci-12345678-1-postgres-test-service-1` = 40+ chars, plus Docker's suffix). On most platforms this is fine, but on some CI-hosted Docker daemons with older daemon versions the limit triggers a silent truncation, causing `docker compose ps` to list containers with different names than expected. Keep project names under 20 characters: use the last 6 digits of the run ID (`ci-${GITHUB_RUN_ID: -6}`) instead of the full ID.

**#94** [community] GitHub Actions Environment secrets are resolved at job startup, not at step execution time. If a job targeting a `staging` environment is retried after the environment secret values were rotated, the retry uses the secrets cached at the time the original job was queued — not the updated secrets. This means a rotation mid-pipeline does not take effect until the entire job is re-queued from scratch (not retried). Teams that rotate staging credentials to fix a failed deploy and then retry the job via GitHub UI find the retry still uses the old, now-invalid credentials. Always re-trigger via a new push or workflow dispatch after secret rotation.

**#95** [community] `pnpm --filter "...[origin/main]"` affected-package filtering fails when `actions/checkout@v4` uses `fetch-depth: 1` (shallow clone). The `[origin/main]` syntax requires git to compute the diff between the current HEAD and `origin/main`, which is only possible if `origin/main` is fetched. With a shallow clone, `origin/main` may not be available as a ref. The fix: either use `fetch-depth: 0` (full history, slower) or add an explicit `git fetch origin main --depth=1` step before running `pnpm --filter`.

**#96** [community] Jest `retryTimes` with `waitBeforeRetry` interacts unexpectedly with Jest's `--forceExit` flag. When a test retries with a 2-second wait, the `setTimeout` created for the wait is a live handle. If the test passes on retry and Jest proceeds to the next file, `--forceExit` may kill the process before the delayed retry's cleanup runs — producing a SIGTERM during what appears to be a clean test run. The symptom is sporadic "Jest did not exit one second after the test run has completed" warnings even with `--forceExit`. Set `retryImmediately: true` for tests in environments where process lifetime is tightly controlled by `--forceExit`.

## Cycle 26 — 2026-05-13

### Pattern 97 — Playwright `forbidOnly` Guard in `playwright.config.ts`

**Description:** In CI, a developer who accidentally commits `test.only()` or `describe.only()` will cause all other tests to be silently skipped, resulting in a green CI run with minimal coverage. `forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI` converts this mistake into a hard build failure. It is a one-line addition to `playwright.config.ts` that saves entire PR review cycles.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Hard-fail the build if `.only()` is accidentally committed.
  // In local dev (CI not set) the flag is false — test.only() still works.
  forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI,

  // Standard CI tuning alongside forbidOnly
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined,
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',

  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Always enable in CI. The only reason NOT to use it is if you intentionally run focused test suites in CI — but if that is the intent, use Playwright projects and `--project` flags instead, not `.only()`. Alternative: a pre-commit hook scanning for `\.only(` is complementary but not a substitute, because CI is the last line of defence after hooks are bypassed with `--no-verify`.

> [official] Playwright docs explicitly recommend `forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI` as a standard CI configuration. This pattern has been in the Playwright CI introduction guide since v1.20 and is one of the first things the `playwright init` scaffolder writes into the generated config.

### Pattern 98 — Vitest `--bail` for Fail-Fast CI Feedback

**Description:** On CI, a full Vitest run of 500 test files can take 4–8 minutes before reporting the first failure if no early-exit mechanism is configured. `--bail N` stops the run after N test files fail, returning immediately with a non-zero exit code. Combined with `--reporter=verbose`, the first failure is visible in the CI log without waiting for all shards to complete.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — fail-fast unit test job
jobs:
  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci

      # Bail after the first failing file for fast PR feedback.
      # Use --bail=3 on main branch to tolerate isolated failures
      # and gather more diagnostic signal before stopping.
      - name: Run unit tests (fail-fast on PR)
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        run: npx vitest run --bail=1 --reporter=verbose

      - name: Run unit tests (gather signal on main)
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: npx vitest run --bail=3 --reporter=verbose --reporter=junit
        env:
          VITEST_OUTPUT_FILE: junit.xml

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: junit-report
          path: junit.xml
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `--bail=1` on PR branches to minimize feedback latency. Use `--bail=3` or higher on main branch merges where you want enough signal to distinguish a widespread regression from a single broken test. Do NOT use `--bail` in nightly full-suite runs — the goal there is comprehensive defect detection, not speed. Note: `--bail` counts failing files, not failing test cases — a single file with 10 failing tests still counts as 1 bail increment.

> [official] Vitest CLI docs describe `--bail <number>`: "Stop test execution when given number of tests have failed." The bail counter increments per test file, not per assertion.

---

### Pattern 99 — Playwright Blob Reporter + Multi-Shard Report Merge

**Description:** When running Playwright across multiple shards (GitHub matrix jobs), each shard produces an independent report. The `blob` reporter saves binary test result data that can be merged into a single HTML report by a post-shard consolidation job. This avoids the need for external services and produces a unified timeline view across all shards.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e-sharded.yml
name: E2E Sharded
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    name: "Shard ${{ matrix.shardIndex }} of ${{ matrix.shardTotal }}"
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        shardTotal: [4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium

      - name: Run shard
        run: |
          npx playwright test \
            --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }} \
            --reporter=blob
        env:
          CI: 'true'

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-report-shard-${{ matrix.shardIndex }}
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 1

  merge-reports:
    name: Merge shard reports
    needs: [test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    if: always()
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci

      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: all-blob-reports
          pattern: blob-report-shard-*
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Merge into unified HTML report
        run: |
          npx playwright merge-reports \
            --reporter html \
            ./all-blob-reports

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-report-merged
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use when you have 4+ shards and want a single report to share with stakeholders or file bug reports from. The consolidation job adds ~45 seconds of overhead. If you only have 1–2 shards, the overhead is not worth it — upload shard reports independently. The `merge-multiple: true` parameter on `download-artifact` is required when downloading multiple artifacts that were uploaded by a matrix — without it, only the last artifact is downloaded.

> [official] Playwright docs cover sharding and blob reporter merging as the recommended pattern for distributed CI pipelines. The `--reporter=blob` flag stores results in binary format so they can be combined accurately across shards.

### Pattern 100 — Vitest Coverage Gate with `coverage.thresholds` and PR Annotations

**Description:** Enforcing minimum coverage thresholds in CI prevents PRs from reducing quality below agreed baselines. Vitest 4.0+ supports threshold enforcement natively. The `coverage.changed` option introduced in Vitest 4.1 narrows coverage reporting to only the files changed since the base branch, giving faster per-PR feedback without requiring a full-suite coverage run.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      enabled: true,
      // Include all source files — not just imported ones.
      // Required in Vitest 4.0+ (coverage.all was removed).
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.stories.ts',
        'src/**/index.ts',   // barrel files — no logic
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
      ],
      // Hard-fail CI when thresholds are not met.
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
        // Per-file threshold: no single file below 60%
        perFile: true,
        '100': false,  // Do not require 100% — avoids false confidence
      },
      // PR-scoped coverage: report only changed files.
      // Requires `fetch-depth: 0` in actions/checkout.
      changed: process.env.CI ? 'origin/main' : undefined,
      reporter: ['text', 'json', 'html', 'lcov'],
      reportOnFailure: true,  // Always generate report, even when tests fail
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `thresholds.perFile: true` is valuable for preventing coverage dilution where one heavily tested file hides gaps in others. However, it makes CI brittle when new utility files are added before their tests — temporarily lower the per-file threshold or add new files to `exclude` until tests are written. `coverage.changed` requires a full git history (`fetch-depth: 0`) — the slowest checkout option. On large repos, the time cost of full checkout often exceeds the time saved by narrowing coverage. Benchmark both approaches before committing to `changed`.

> [community] Teams that enforce `thresholds` without `perFile: true` frequently discover that a small number of high-traffic files carry the entire coverage percentage — the rest of the codebase may be at 20% coverage while the aggregate reads 82%. Add `perFile: true` to surface the long tail.

### Pattern 101 — GitHub Actions Concurrency Groups for Branch-Level Cancellation

**Description:** Without concurrency control, every push to a PR branch queues a new workflow run while the previous run is still executing. On active branches with multiple rapid commits, this wastes runner minutes and can cause older runs to finish after newer ones, producing confusing PR status checks. `concurrency:` with `cancel-in-progress: true` ensures only the latest push per branch runs.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: ['**']
  pull_request:

# Cancel any in-flight run for the same branch on new pushes.
# Use a separate group for PRs vs pushes so that merges to main
# are never cancelled by a concurrent PR run.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

jobs:
  lint-typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit

  test:
    needs: lint-typecheck
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --reporter=github-actions
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Always use `cancel-in-progress: false` for main/master branch pushes — merges to main should always complete, even if another merge follows closely. Use `cancel-in-progress: true` for PR branches. Using `github.ref` as the group key means each branch has its own concurrency slot — two different PR branches can run simultaneously. If you use `github.event.pull_request.number` as the key instead, the same PR number used across force-pushes still cancels, but branch renames create a new group.

> [community] A common mistake is setting `cancel-in-progress: true` globally, causing main-branch deployment workflows to be cancelled mid-deploy. The `${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}` expression-based condition is the safest default.

---

### Pattern 102 — `pnpm` Frozen Lockfile CI Enforcement with Version Pinning

**Description:** Using `pnpm install` without `--frozen-lockfile` in CI allows the package manager to update `pnpm-lock.yaml` silently — this can produce builds that pass on the runner but fail to reproduce. Combining `--frozen-lockfile` with a pinned `packageManager` field in `package.json` prevents lockfile drift and ensures all developers and runners use identical dependency trees.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — deterministic pnpm installs
jobs:
  install-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Pin pnpm version via corepack — reads "packageManager" field
      # from package.json (e.g., "packageManager": "pnpm@9.15.4")
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'

      - name: Enable corepack for pnpm version pinning
        run: corepack enable

      # Cache the pnpm store — keyed on lockfile hash
      - name: Cache pnpm store
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.pnpm-store
          key: pnpm-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/pnpm-lock.yaml') }}
          restore-keys: |
            pnpm-${{ runner.os }}-

      # --frozen-lockfile fails the step if lockfile is out of sync
      # with package.json — prevents silent resolution surprises
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Type-check
        run: pnpm tsc --noEmit

      - name: Test
        run: pnpm vitest run --reporter=github-actions
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `--frozen-lockfile` is mandatory for CI. The only time it should be omitted is when a workflow is specifically updating the lockfile (e.g., a Dependabot-merge workflow that calls `pnpm update`). `corepack enable` requires Node.js 16.10+ and reads `engines.pnpm` / `packageManager` from `package.json`. If neither field exists, corepack falls back to the latest stable pnpm — which is unpredictable. Always set `"packageManager": "pnpm@X.Y.Z"` in `package.json` before relying on corepack in CI.

> [community] Teams migrating from npm to pnpm frequently forget `--frozen-lockfile` in the first few weeks. The symptom is "works in CI, breaks locally" — because pnpm silently resolved a different version tree when the lockfile was not frozen. Pin both the pnpm version and enforce `--frozen-lockfile` on day 1.

### Pattern 103 — Playwright Worker-Scoped Fixtures for Expensive CI Setup

**Description:** `globalSetup` in Playwright runs once per process but is opaque to Playwright's fixture and tracing systems — failures inside `globalSetup` produce no trace and limited diagnostic output. Worker-scoped fixtures run inside the Playwright process, benefit from tracing, and can be composed with other fixtures. Use `scope: 'worker'` fixtures to replace `globalSetup` for database seeding, server startup, and auth token generation.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/db.ts
import { test as base, WorkerInfo } from '@playwright/test';
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';

type DbFixtures = {
  db: PrismaClient;
  seedData: { userId: string; token: string };
};

// Worker-scoped: created once per worker process, shared across test
// files assigned to that worker. Automatically torn down when the
// worker exits — no manual afterAll() required.
export const test = base.extend<{}, DbFixtures>({
  db: [
    async ({}, use, workerInfo: WorkerInfo) => {
      const client = new PrismaClient({
        datasources: {
          db: { url: `${process.env.DATABASE_URL}_worker_${workerInfo.workerIndex}` },
        },
      });
      await client.$connect();
      yield client;
      await client.$disconnect();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],

  seedData: [
    async ({ db }, use) => {
      const user = await db.user.create({ data: { email: `worker${Date.now()}@test.com` } });
      const token = await generateToken(user.id);
      yield { userId: user.id, token };
      await db.user.delete({ where: { id: user.id } });
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Worker-scoped fixtures are ideal for stateful resources (database clients, server processes, auth tokens) that are expensive to create but safe to share across tests within a worker. Do NOT use worker scope for resources that must be isolated per test — use test scope instead. Worker scope means that if one test in the worker corrupts state, subsequent tests in the same worker see the corrupted state. Pair worker-scoped setup with test-scoped cleanup (transactions, truncation) to maintain isolation without paying the full setup cost per test.

> [official] Playwright docs recommend replacing `globalSetup` with worker-scoped fixtures because they "run before/after all tests in every file, once per worker process" and are fully observable by Playwright's tracing and reporting systems.

---

### Pattern 104 — Vitest `aroundEach` for Automatic Database Transaction Rollback

**Description:** The `aroundEach` hook introduced in Vitest 4.1 wraps each test in a generator function, allowing setup code to run before the test and cleanup code to run in the same stack frame after the test — including in failure cases. This is the idiomatic TypeScript pattern for wrapping each test in a database transaction that is rolled back after the test, ensuring perfect isolation without truncating tables.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — register the aroundEach plugin
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import { dbTransactionPlugin } from './tests/plugins/db-transaction';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    plugins: [dbTransactionPlugin()],
    // Disable parallelism for DB transaction tests — parallel transactions
    // on the same connection pool can deadlock.
    fileParallelism: false,
  },
});

// tests/plugins/db-transaction.ts
import { aroundEach } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../src/db/client';

export function dbTransactionPlugin() {
  return {
    name: 'db-transaction-rollback',
    setup() {
      aroundEach(async function* () {
        // Begin transaction before each test
        await db.query('BEGIN');
        yield; // test runs here
        // Always rollback — even on test failure or timeout
        await db.query('ROLLBACK');
      });
    },
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `aroundEach` is strictly better than `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pairs for rollback because `afterEach` does not run if the test times out, and its execution order relative to other `afterEach` hooks in nested describe blocks can be surprising. The `yield` point in `aroundEach` is the exact boundary of test execution — the `ROLLBACK` runs unconditionally. Do NOT use with `fileParallelism: true` — parallel test files share a connection pool, and concurrent transactions on the same schema can produce deadlocks. Set `fileParallelism: false` or use separate test databases per worker (see Pattern 103).

> [official] Vitest 4.1 release notes describe `aroundEach`/`aroundAll` as "wrap tests inside a DB transaction or span — automatic rollback on failure."

---

### Pattern 105 — `--detect-async-leaks` for Open Handle Detection in CI

**Description:** Tests that leave open HTTP servers, database connections, file watchers, or timers produce "open handles" warnings with Jest/Vitest. These warnings are frequently ignored — but the underlying leak can cause test runs to hang indefinitely in CI, consuming all available runner minutes before the timeout kills the job. `--detect-async-leaks` (Vitest 4.1+) converts the warning into a hard failure, forcing teams to fix leaks rather than suppress warnings.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Hard-fail on async leaks in CI.
    // Run without the flag first to get a baseline of existing leaks,
    // then fix them before enabling — or add them to suppressWarnings.
    detectAsyncLeaks: process.env.CI === 'true',

    // Timeout the entire test run if a leak causes a hang.
    // Without this, a single open server can block the runner for hours.
    testTimeout: 10_000,
    hookTimeout: 10_000,

    // List known-acceptable open handles during migration period.
    // Remove entries as leaks are fixed.
    suppressWarnings: process.env.CI ? [] : ['possible EventEmitter memory leak'],
  },
});
```

```bash
# Local: identify existing leaks before enabling in CI
npx vitest run --detect-async-leaks 2>&1 | grep -E 'LEAK|open handle'

# CI: enforce — any leaked handle fails the suite
npx vitest run --detect-async-leaks
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Enable in CI immediately on new projects. For existing projects with legacy leaks, run the flag in warn-only mode locally first (`--reporter=verbose`) to enumerate all leaks, fix them in batches, then enable the hard-fail. The flag adds ~5% overhead per test file due to async context tracking. On large suites (1000+ files), profile the overhead before enabling unconditionally.

> [community] The most common async leak sources: `express` server started in `beforeAll` without calling `server.close()`, `setInterval` without `clearInterval` in test teardown, and `pg.Pool` connections not ended. Teams enabling `--detect-async-leaks` for the first time on a legacy codebase routinely discover 15–30 forgotten open handles — each a potential source of mysterious CI hangs.

### Pattern 106 — GitHub Actions Path Filter for Targeted Test Jobs

**Description:** When a monorepo contains multiple packages, running the full test suite for a change to `packages/ui/README.md` wastes runner time. GitHub Actions `paths` filters and `dorny/paths-filter` enable job-level targeting: only the affected packages' test jobs run for a given change set.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — path-filtered monorepo CI
name: Monorepo CI

on:
  push:
    branches: ['**']
  pull_request:

jobs:
  # Detect which packages changed
  detect-changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    outputs:
      api: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.api }}
      web: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.web }}
      shared: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.shared }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v3
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            api:
              - 'packages/api/**'
              - 'packages/shared/**'
            web:
              - 'packages/web/**'
              - 'packages/shared/**'
            shared:
              - 'packages/shared/**'

  test-api:
    needs: detect-changes
    if: needs.detect-changes.outputs.api == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --project api --reporter=github-actions

  test-web:
    needs: detect-changes
    if: needs.detect-changes.outputs.web == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Install Playwright browsers
        run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx playwright test --project=web

  # Always run shared tests — any change may affect shared
  test-shared:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --project shared
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Path filters dramatically reduce CI time for large monorepos. The key gotcha: if `shared` changes, all dependent packages should re-run their tests too. Model this by listing `packages/shared/**` as a trigger for all downstream test jobs (not just the `shared` job), as shown above. Do NOT rely on path filters as a security gate — they can be bypassed on `pull_request` events from forks. Path filters are a performance optimization, not a security control.

> [community] Teams using `dorny/paths-filter` report 50–80% reductions in CI minute consumption on active monorepos. The most common mistake: not including transitive dependency paths (changing `shared` should re-run `api` tests, but developers forget to list `packages/shared/**` in the `api` filter block).

---

### Pattern 107 — Vitest `github-actions` Reporter for Native PR Annotations

**Description:** The `github-actions` reporter (Vitest 4.1+) emits native GitHub Actions workflow commands that produce inline failure annotations directly on PR diffs — no third-party action required. When a test fails, the annotation appears on the exact line in the source file where the assertion is located, not just in the job log.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // In CI: use github-actions for PR annotations + junit for artifact upload.
    // Locally: use verbose for readable terminal output.
    reporters: process.env.CI
      ? ['github-actions', 'junit']
      : ['verbose'],

    outputFile: process.env.CI
      ? { junit: 'test-results/junit.xml' }
      : undefined,

    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: process.env.CI
        ? ['json', 'lcov']  // lcov for coverage PR comment via romeovs/lcov-reporter-action
        : ['text', 'html'],
    },
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — upload junit and post coverage comment
- name: Run tests with annotations
  run: npx vitest run
  env:
    CI: 'true'

- name: Upload test results
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  if: always()
  with:
    name: test-results
    path: test-results/junit.xml

- name: Post coverage comment on PR
  uses: romeovs/lcov-reporter-action@v0.4.0
  if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
  with:
    lcov-file: coverage/lcov.info
    github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The `github-actions` reporter requires the `GITHUB_ACTIONS` environment variable to be set to `'true'` — it is automatically set by GitHub Actions runners. When running locally with this reporter, the output contains raw workflow command strings (e.g., `::error file=...`) which clutter the terminal. Use a conditional `process.env.CI` check to select the reporter at config-read time, not at test run time.

> [official] Vitest 4.1 release notes describe the GitHub Actions reporter as "zero-config" when `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` is set — the reporter auto-injects a job summary with test stats and flaky test permalinks.

---

### Pattern 108 — TypeScript `tsc --noEmit` as a Dedicated CI Gate

**Description:** Running `tsc --noEmit` as a separate required CI step — independent of the test runner — ensures that type errors are caught even in code paths not exercised by tests. TypeScript's type checker and test execution are orthogonal: a test suite can pass at 100% coverage while containing type errors that will surface as runtime exceptions after the next TypeScript upgrade. The `--noEmit` flag runs the full type checker without producing output files, making it safe to run in parallel with tests.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — parallel typecheck and test
jobs:
  typecheck:
    name: TypeScript type check
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 8
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      # --incremental uses .tsbuildinfo for faster re-checks.
      # Cache the .tsbuildinfo file between runs for maximum speed.
      - name: Cache tsbuildinfo
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: '**/*.tsbuildinfo'
          key: tsbuildinfo-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('tsconfig*.json', 'src/**/*.ts') }}
      - name: Type check
        run: npx tsc --noEmit --incremental

  unit-tests:
    name: Unit tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --reporter=github-actions

  # Gate: both typecheck AND tests must pass for PR to merge
  ci-gate:
    name: CI Gate
    needs: [typecheck, unit-tests]
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - run: echo "All CI checks passed"
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Run `tsc --noEmit` in parallel with tests (not in sequence) to minimize pipeline wall-clock time. Cache `*.tsbuildinfo` keyed on TypeScript config files and source file hashes — on cache hit, incremental type-checking can complete in under 10 seconds for projects that would otherwise take 3 minutes. Do NOT pipe `tsc --noEmit` output through tools that swallow the exit code — always verify that the step fails the job when type errors are present.

> [community] A common CI architecture mistake is relying on the test runner to surface TypeScript errors (e.g., using `ts-jest` or `@swc/vitest`). Many test runners use `esbuild` or `swc` for transpilation, which strips types without checking them. A green test run says nothing about type correctness. The `tsc --noEmit` gate is the only reliable mechanism.
