### Pattern 109 — Playwright `captureGitInfo` for Traceable Test Reports

**Description:** Playwright v1.51+ supports `captureGitInfo: true` in the project config, which automatically embeds branch name, commit SHA, PR number, and author information into the HTML and blob reports. This makes reports self-describing — when investigating a failure from a stored report weeks later, the exact commit and context are embedded in the report without consulting the CI log.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Embed git context into every report
  captureGitInfo: { commit: true, diff: false },

  // Combined with blob reporter for shard merging
  reporter: process.env.CI ? [
    ['blob', { outputDir: 'blob-report' }],
    ['github'],  // Native GitHub Actions annotations
  ] : [
    ['html', { open: 'on-failure' }],
  ],

  use: {
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `captureGitInfo` requires the runner to have git installed and the repository to be a git checkout (not a source archive). It adds negligible overhead. Set `diff: false` unless you need the diff embedded — `diff: true` can significantly increase report size for large changesets. The embedded metadata is visible in the HTML report's "Environment" tab and in blob report metadata, making it searchable when using Playwright's dashboard integrations.

> [official] Playwright v1.51 release notes introduce `captureGitInfo` as a configuration-level option to "auto-capture branch/SHA/PR metadata in test reports."

---

### Pattern 110 — Playwright `webServer.reuseExistingServer` for Local vs. CI Dev

**Description:** The `webServer` config option in `playwright.config.ts` starts a development server before tests run. Setting `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI` lets developers reuse an already-running local dev server while CI always starts a fresh server — avoiding port conflicts in CI without requiring manual server management locally.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    // Local dev: reuse an existing running server (faster iteration).
    // CI: always start fresh (avoids stale state from previous runs).
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    // Timeout for the server to become ready
    timeout: 120 * 1000,
    // Capture stdout/stderr for debugging server startup failures
    stdout: 'pipe',
    stderr: 'pipe',
    // v1.57+: capture dynamic port from stdout using a regex
    // Use when the dev server prints "Listening on :PORT"
    // wait: /Local:\s+http:\/\/localhost:(\d+)/,
  },

  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI` is the recommended default for most projects. If your dev server has a long startup time (>30 seconds), consider separating the server start into a dedicated GitHub Actions step that runs before the Playwright step, using `wait-on` to poll until ready — this makes the startup time visible in the CI timeline rather than buried inside the Playwright step. Do NOT use `reuseExistingServer: true` in CI — it can match a server started by a parallel job on a shared runner, producing cross-job pollution.

> [community] Teams debugging "connection refused" failures in Playwright CI often discover the issue is a dev server that prints its port to stderr rather than stdout. Playwright's server readiness check reads stdout by default. Redirect stderr to stdout (`2>&1`) in the `command` field, or use the `wait` regex pattern (v1.57+) that can match output from either stream.

---

### Pattern 111 — Vitest Workspace Projects for Multi-Environment Monorepo CI

**Description:** Vitest's workspace projects allow a single `vitest run` invocation to execute tests across multiple packages and environments simultaneously — each package in its own isolated Vite instance. This eliminates the need for multiple CI jobs per package on small-to-medium monorepos and consolidates coverage reporting.

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts (root of monorepo)
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  // Backend API — Node.js environment
  {
    extends: './packages/api/vitest.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'api',
      root: './packages/api',
      environment: 'node',
      include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
    },
  },

  // Frontend — jsdom environment
  {
    extends: './packages/web/vitest.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'web',
      root: './packages/web',
      environment: 'jsdom',
      include: ['src/**/*.test.tsx'],
      setupFiles: ['./src/test-setup.ts'],
    },
  },

  // Shared utilities — run in both environments
  {
    test: {
      name: 'shared-node',
      root: './packages/shared',
      environment: 'node',
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name: 'shared-browser',
      root: './packages/shared',
      environment: 'jsdom',
    },
  },
]);
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — single job runs all workspace projects
- name: Run all workspace tests
  run: npx vitest run --reporter=github-actions

# Run only specific projects on path-filtered branches
- name: Run API tests only
  if: steps.filter.outputs.api == 'true'
  run: npx vitest run --project api --reporter=github-actions
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Vitest workspace is ideal for monorepos where packages share a build pipeline (same Vite config, same TypeScript setup). It is NOT appropriate for packages that require drastically different Vite configurations or conflicting plugin versions — those should remain in separate CI jobs. Workspace projects all run in the same process, so a crashing test in one project can kill the entire workspace run; set `bail` carefully.

> [official] Vitest docs state: "All projects must have unique names; otherwise, Vitest will throw an error." Name each project explicitly using the `test.name` field to avoid collisions and to enable `--project` filtering.

### New Anti-Patterns (Cycle 26)

| Anti-pattern | Why harmful | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Vitest `coverage.all: true` on Vitest 4.0+ | `coverage.all` was removed in Vitest 4.0 — the option silently does nothing, leaving untested files excluded from coverage denominator | Replace with `coverage.include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}']` — the explicit include list is now required |
| Playwright `workers: 1` without `fullyParallel` on large suites | Setting `workers: 1` serializes all tests onto one worker — combined with the default file-level parallelism, a 200-spec suite takes 3–4× longer than necessary | Set `workers: 1` only when debugging flakiness; use `fullyParallel: true` with `workers: '50%'` for normal CI runs |
| Caching Playwright browser binaries | Playwright docs explicitly state that the restore-cache time is comparable to fresh download time — caching browser binaries adds cache management complexity without measurable benefit | Use `npx playwright install --with-deps` without a cache step; only cache `node_modules` and `.tsbuildinfo` |
| `actions/upload-artifact` without `if: always()` on test artifact steps | When tests fail and the job exits non-zero, post-steps without `if: always()` are skipped — the Playwright HTML report is never uploaded for the exact run that needs debugging | Always add `if: always()` to artifact upload steps for test reports and coverage |
| Multi-reporter array without `outputFile` in Vitest CI | Using `reporters: ['github-actions', 'junit']` without `outputFile: { junit: '...' }` causes both reporters to write to stdout — the JUnit XML is lost in the CI log | Always pair `junit` reporter with `outputFile.junit` pointing to a file path |

### New Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 26)

**#97** [community] Playwright `retries: 2` combined with `trace: 'on-first-retry'` does NOT record a trace for the initial (non-retry) run. If a test fails on the first attempt and passes on retry (flaky), the trace covers only the retry — not the original failure. Reproducing flakiness from the trace is impossible because the failure state is never recorded. Use `trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries'` (Playwright v1.54+) to record every attempt and retain all traces when any attempt fails.

**#98** [community] `actions/cache@v4` with a `hashFiles` key on `pnpm-lock.yaml` produces a cache miss on every run in monorepos that use workspace protocols (`"workspace:*"`) if pnpm updates the lock file during `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`. The root cause: `--frozen-lockfile` exits with code 1 when the lockfile needs updating, but the cache key was already computed before the install step. The fix: run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` strictly and treat a non-zero exit as a lockfile sync failure — add a workflow step that runs `pnpm install` (without `--frozen-lockfile`) and commits the updated lockfile, triggered only when the lockfile sync check fails.

**#99** [community] GitHub Actions matrix jobs with `strategy.fail-fast: true` (the default) cancel all in-flight shard jobs when any shard fails. If shard 3 fails after 8 minutes and shards 1, 2, 4 are still running, they are cancelled — and the merge-reports job (which runs `if: always()`) sees only the blob report from the completed shards plus the failed shard. The merged report is incomplete. Teams debugging failures from an incomplete merge often receive misleading data. Set `fail-fast: false` on Playwright shard matrices to let all shards complete, producing a complete merged report for the failed run.

**#100** [community] Vitest `--shard=X/Y` distributes test files alphabetically by default. A project that prefixes spec files with feature names (`auth.spec.ts`, `billing.spec.ts`, `cart.spec.ts`) produces maximally even shards only when file sizes are similar. When one spec file contains 300 test cases and the rest contain 10–30 each (a common pattern for a core authentication module), all 300-case tests land in shard 1 because `auth` sorts first alphabetically, causing a 10:1 time imbalance. Solution: measure per-file test duration with `--reporter=json` and rename or split files to balance shard duration rather than test count.

**#101** [community] TypeScript `--incremental` with cached `.tsbuildinfo` can produce false-positive type check passes when the cache key does not include all `tsconfig.json` files in a project reference chain. In a monorepo where root `tsconfig.json` references `packages/*/tsconfig.json`, a change to `packages/api/tsconfig.json` (e.g., adding a new `paths` alias) does not change the root `tsconfig.json` hash — so the cache key does not invalidate, and `tsc --incremental` uses the stale `.tsbuildinfo`, missing the new type errors introduced by the path alias change. Cache key should include all `tsconfig*.json` files: `hashFiles('**/tsconfig*.json', 'src/**/*.ts')`.

**#102** [community] `npx playwright install --with-deps` installs system-level dependencies (libnss3, libatk1.0) that require `sudo` on some Linux distributions. On GitHub Actions runners with Ubuntu 24.04, `--with-deps` works without sudo because the runner user has passwordless sudo. On self-hosted runners with restricted user permissions, the command fails silently with a non-zero exit code and no browser is installed — tests then fail with "browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist" rather than a more informative install error. On self-hosted runners, either pre-install browser dependencies in the runner image or run the install step as a privileged user.

## Cycle 27 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 112 — Playwright `maxFailures` for CI Resource Conservation

**Description:** In CI, a broken test suite with dozens of failures can exhaust runner time and cloud budget before reporting. `maxFailures` (equivalent to `--max-failures` on the CLI) stops the Playwright run after a configurable number of failures, returning early with a non-zero exit code. Unlike `retries`, which retry individual tests, `maxFailures` is a global circuit-breaker across the entire run. This is especially important on sharded workflows where a widespread regression would otherwise let all 4 shards run to completion before anyone learns the build is broken.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Stop after 10 failures in CI to avoid burning runner minutes.
  // Locally (CI not set) run everything to collect full signal.
  maxFailures: process.env.CI ? 10 : undefined,

  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined,
  fullyParallel: true,

  use: {
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
});
```

```yaml
# Equivalent CLI usage in .github/workflows/e2e.yml
- name: Run e2e tests
  run: npx playwright test --max-failures=10
  env:
    CI: 'true'
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `maxFailures: 10` on PR branches where speed matters most. On nightly runs or main-branch merges, either increase the limit (50+) or remove it entirely so the full defect picture is captured. Do NOT combine with `fail-fast: true` in the GitHub matrix strategy — that cancels sibling jobs at the matrix level, while `maxFailures` operates within a single runner. The two are complementary, not duplicates.

> [official] Playwright docs document `maxFailures` under `testConfig`: "The maximum number of test failures for the whole test suite run. After reaching this number of failures, Playwright Test will stop scheduling new tests and wait for the currently running tests to finish. Defaults to zero, which means run all tests."

---

### Pattern 113 — Vitest `--changed` Flag for PR-Scoped Unit Tests

**Description:** Vitest's `--changed` flag runs only the test files that are related to files modified since a given git ref. On a PR with 3 changed source files, only the test files that import those sources are executed — trimming a 400-file unit suite to 15 files with zero configuration beyond a base ref. This is the unit-test equivalent of Playwright's `--only-changed` feature (pillar 26) and can be combined with shard distribution for very large affected sets.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — PR-scoped unit test job
jobs:
  unit-changed:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          # Fetch the base branch so --changed can diff against it
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'npm'

      - run: npm ci

      # Run only tests related to changed files since the PR base
      - name: Run changed tests
        run: |
          npx vitest run \
            --changed=origin/${{ github.base_ref }} \
            --reporter=github-actions \
            --reporter=json \
            --outputFile=vitest-results.json

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: vitest-changed-results
          path: vitest-results.json
          retention-days: 7
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `--changed` is powerful on PR workflows where developer productivity depends on fast feedback. It is NOT a substitute for a full suite run — always trigger the full suite on main branch merges and scheduled nightly runs. A key gotcha: `--changed` relies on git history to compute the dependency graph; if a file has no test that imports it, `--changed` will return zero tests even if the change is critical. Pair with a full suite gate on merge to catch such blind spots.

> [official] Vitest CLI docs: `--changed [base]` — "Run tests only for changed files. If no value is provided, it will run tests against uncommitted changes (including staged and unstaged). To run tests against changes made in the last commit, you can use `--changed HEAD~1`."

---

### Pattern 114 — GitHub Actions `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress` for PR Branches

**Description:** By default, every push to a PR branch triggers a new workflow run while the previous run continues. On active PRs with frequent commits (rebasing, fixups), this wastes runner minutes — 5 concurrent runs for one PR, 4 of which are obsolete. Adding a `concurrency` block at the workflow level cancels the in-progress run when a new one starts on the same ref, ensuring at most one active CI run per branch at any time.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: ['**']
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

# Cancel in-progress runs on the same branch when a new push arrives.
# Use a unique group per PR number (or branch name for pushes).
# The conditional expression prevents cancelling runs on the main branch.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

jobs:
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Always use on feature branch and PR workflows. The key detail is `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}` — this expression evaluates to `false` on the main branch, which prevents cancelling the in-progress main-branch CI run when another push arrives. Without this guard, two fast pushes to main would cancel the first run's deployment steps mid-flight.

> [community] A common mistake is setting `cancel-in-progress: true` globally without the branch guard. Teams report cancelled deployment jobs on main when multiple PRs land in quick succession during a merge queue. The conditional expression on the `cancel-in-progress` key is the fix — but it is not in most copy-pasted concurrency examples online.

---

### Pattern 115 — Playwright `--project` Flag for Stage-Based CI Filtering

**Description:** Playwright's `--project` flag selects a named subset of configured test projects. By defining projects for `smoke`, `regression`, `visual`, and `api` test tiers, different CI stages can selectively execute the right subset without maintaining multiple `playwright.config.ts` files. This replaces `testIgnore` glob hacks and tag-based filtering for coarse-grained stage separation.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'smoke',
      testMatch: /.*\.smoke\.ts/,
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'regression',
      testMatch: /.*\.spec\.ts/,
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'visual',
      testMatch: /.*\.visual\.ts/,
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        // Slow network + small viewport to catch layout regressions
        viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 },
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'api',
      testMatch: /.*\.api\.ts/,
      use: { baseURL: process.env.API_BASE_URL },
    },
  ],
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — run different projects at different pipeline stages
- name: Smoke tests (PR gate — fast)
  run: npx playwright test --project=smoke

- name: Regression tests (merge gate)
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  run: npx playwright test --project=regression --project=api

- name: Visual regression (nightly)
  if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
  run: npx playwright test --project=visual
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Project-based filtering is preferable to `testIgnore` glob lists because each project can have its own device, timeout, and retry settings. The tradeoff is that `testMatch` patterns must remain mutually exclusive to avoid running the same test in multiple projects unintentionally. Use a file-naming convention (`.smoke.ts`, `.spec.ts`, `.visual.ts`) enforced by ESLint or a pre-commit hook.

> [official] Playwright docs on projects: "Projects are useful to run tests in multiple configurations. For instance, consider running tests against multiple browsers." Projects are also the correct mechanism for multi-stage filtering — not `testIgnore` or `.only()`.

---

### Pattern 116 — Vitest V8 Coverage with `coverage.changed` for PR Delta Reporting

**Description:** Vitest v4.1+ supports `coverage.changed`, which reports coverage only for source files that have changed since the base branch. On a PR that modifies 5 files, the coverage report focuses on those 5 files instead of the entire codebase, making the coverage signal actionable for reviewers. Paired with the `github-actions` reporter, this produces inline PR annotations showing uncovered lines in changed files.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'json', 'json-summary'],
      // Report coverage only for files changed since the base branch.
      // The value is a git ref — matches Vitest --changed flag semantics.
      changed: process.env.CI ? `origin/${process.env.BASE_BRANCH ?? 'main'}` : undefined,
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/*.stories.ts'],
      thresholds: {
        // Only enforce thresholds on changed files when using coverage.changed
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- name: Run tests with coverage
  run: npx vitest run --coverage
  env:
    CI: 'true'
    BASE_BRANCH: ${{ github.base_ref }}

- name: Upload coverage report
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  if: always()
  with:
    name: coverage-report
    path: coverage/
    retention-days: 7
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `coverage.changed` dramatically reduces coverage report noise on large codebases where total coverage is stable but individual PR changes are small. The limitation is that it does NOT report on files that should have new tests added but do not appear in the changed-files list (e.g., shared utilities that a new feature depends on). Always run full-coverage analysis on scheduled nightly runs to track overall coverage trends.

> [official] Vitest docs (v4.1): "coverage.changed — Run coverage for changed files only. Similar to `--changed` option. Accepts boolean, string (git rev), or an array of strings."

---

### Pattern 117 — Docker Playwright Image Pinning for Reproducible CI Environments

**Description:** When running Playwright tests in Docker (CircleCI, GitLab CI, Jenkins, self-hosted GitHub runners), the official Playwright Docker image `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` must be pinned to a specific version tag. Using `latest` causes silent browser version drift between CI runs — tests pass with Playwright v1.48 but fail after the image silently updates to v1.52 with a changed browser behavior. Pinning the image version to match your installed `@playwright/test` package version is mandatory.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e-docker.yml — using the Playwright Docker image as a container
name: E2E Tests (Docker)
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  e2e:
    # Run tests inside the pinned Playwright container
    container:
      image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.52.0-noble
      options: --ipc=host

    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          # Note: cache: 'npm' is less effective inside Docker containers
          # because the cache key changes with every container image version

      - run: npm ci
        # Browsers are pre-installed in the Docker image — skip playwright install
        # DO NOT run: npx playwright install --with-deps (already in image)

      - name: Run e2e tests
        run: npx playwright test --reporter=blob

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: playwright-blob-report
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 3
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The Docker approach eliminates the `npx playwright install --with-deps` step (90–120 seconds saved per job) and guarantees browser version consistency. The downside is that the image is large (~1.8GB compressed) and must be updated manually when upgrading `@playwright/test`. Keep the image version and npm package version in sync — a mismatch causes `browserType.launch` to fail with a version assertion error.

> [official] Playwright Docker docs: "It is recommended to always pin your Docker image to a specific version if possible, to avoid breaking changes in future Docker image releases." The `--ipc=host` flag is required because Chrome uses shared memory between the browser and renderer processes; without it, Chrome may crash on memory-intensive pages.

---

### Pattern 118 — GitHub Actions `actions/setup-node` `cache` Option for `node_modules`

**Description:** The `actions/setup-node` action includes a built-in `cache` option that handles `package-lock.json` or `yarn.lock` hashing and `node_modules` restoration without needing a separate `actions/cache` step. Compared to manual `actions/cache` configuration, this approach is less error-prone, automatically handles monorepo lock files, and aligns cache key computation with the exact tool being used (npm, yarn, or pnpm).

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — using setup-node built-in cache
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          # Built-in cache: hashes package-lock.json automatically.
          # Supports 'npm', 'yarn', and 'pnpm'.
          cache: 'npm'
          # For monorepos where the lock file is not at the root:
          # cache-dependency-path: 'apps/web/package-lock.json'

      - run: npm ci  # Fast if cache restored, full install if miss

      # TypeScript build info caching — separate from node_modules
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: '**/.tsbuildinfo'
          key: tsbuildinfo-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/tsconfig*.json', 'src/**/*.ts') }}
          restore-keys: |
            tsbuildinfo-${{ runner.os }}-

      - run: npm test
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the `setup-node` built-in cache for `node_modules` — it is simpler and less error-prone than a manual `actions/cache` step. Use a separate `actions/cache` step for `.tsbuildinfo` files, since the built-in cache key is scoped to the lock file only and does not account for TypeScript config changes. Do NOT cache Playwright browser binaries — the official docs confirm that the time to restore the cache is comparable to a fresh download with `--with-deps`.

> [community] Teams frequently add a manual `actions/cache` step for `node_modules` on top of `setup-node` with `cache: 'npm'`, resulting in double caching and confusing cache-miss behaviour. The `cache` option in `setup-node@v4` already wraps `actions/cache` internally — adding another cache step for the same path creates a race condition between two cache keys for the same directory.

---

### Pattern 119 — Playwright `workers: 1` in CI vs. Sharding for Stability

**Description:** Playwright recommends setting `workers: 1` in CI for stability — a single worker serialises all tests, preventing browser-instance interference on shared runners. However, `workers: 1` on a 500-spec suite can take 30+ minutes. The correct approach is to combine `workers: 1` (or `workers: 2`) per shard with matrix-based horizontal sharding: each shard runs serially, but 4 shards run concurrently across 4 machines, giving both stability and speed.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — stable CI configuration with horizontal scale via sharding
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Limit workers per machine for stability; scale horizontally via sharding.
  // CI sets workers=1 for maximum stability on shared runners.
  // Local dev gets 50% of available CPUs.
  workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : '50%',

  // Retry flaky tests twice in CI; fail immediately locally for fast dev feedback
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  // Fail-fast on CI after 10 failures; run everything locally
  maxFailures: process.env.CI ? 10 : undefined,

  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries',
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — horizontal scale via matrix sharding
jobs:
  e2e:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        shardTotal: [4]
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}
        env:
          CI: 'true'
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `workers: 1` per shard is appropriate for CPU-bound or stateful e2e tests that interact with a shared database or third-party service (race conditions between parallel browser instances cause non-deterministic failures). For stateless or well-isolated e2e tests, `workers: 2` per shard doubles throughput with no stability cost. Do NOT use a single machine with `workers: 8` as a substitute for 4 machines with `workers: 2` — the runner's CPU contention degrades browser performance unpredictably.

> [official] Playwright CI docs: "We recommend setting workers to 1 in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility. For horizontal scaling, use test sharding across multiple jobs."

---

### Pattern 120 — Vitest `pool: 'forks'` vs. `pool: 'threads'` in CI

**Description:** Vitest runs test files in isolated environments using one of three pool strategies: `forks` (child processes — default, highest isolation), `threads` (worker threads — faster but shared memory), or `vmForks`/`vmThreads` (VM context isolation). In CI, `forks` is the default and most stable, but `threads` can be 20–40% faster on suites that have no side effects between files. Choosing the wrong pool causes either reliability issues (`threads` with impure module state) or unnecessary slowness (`forks` when not required).

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — explicit pool selection based on test characteristics
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // 'forks' (default): separate Node.js processes — highest isolation,
    //   slower startup, safe for tests with process.env mutations or
    //   module-level state.
    // 'threads': worker threads — faster, lower memory, but tests share
    //   the same module registry if isolate:false.
    pool: process.env.CI_FAST ? 'threads' : 'forks',

    poolOptions: {
      threads: {
        // Control worker count explicitly in CI for predictable resource usage
        maxWorkers: process.env.CI ? 4 : undefined,
        minWorkers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined,
        // Disable per-file isolation when tests are known to be pure
        isolate: true,
      },
      forks: {
        maxForks: process.env.CI ? 4 : undefined,
        minForks: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined,
      },
    },

    // Run coverage in forks pool regardless of test pool
    // (coverage instrumentation is incompatible with vmThreads)
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Start with `forks` (the default) and switch to `threads` only after verifying your test suite has no module-level side effects (no `process.env` mutations in test setup, no global singleton state, no `jest.mock` equivalent that patches module registry). The performance gain from `threads` is most pronounced in suites with many small unit tests (~100ms each) where process startup overhead dominates. For integration tests with external I/O, pool type matters less — I/O wait time dominates.

> [community] A common CI gotcha: teams switch from `forks` to `threads` chasing a 30% speedup, but then see intermittent failures caused by two test files mutating `process.env.DATABASE_URL` concurrently. Worker threads share the same `process.env` object — mutations are not isolated between files unless `isolate: true` is set (which re-creates the module registry per file, eliminating much of the speed gain). The rule of thumb: if you use `process.env` mutation in test setup files, stay on `forks`.

### Pattern 121 — TypeScript `--incremental` Cache in CI with Correct Cache Keys

**Description:** TypeScript's `--incremental` flag persists compilation state in `.tsbuildinfo` files, making subsequent `tsc --noEmit` runs 60–80% faster by re-checking only changed files. In CI, this acceleration is only available if `.tsbuildinfo` is cached across runs — and the cache key must include all `tsconfig*.json` files and source files, not just the lock file. An incorrect cache key produces stale `.tsbuildinfo` hits that return false-positive type-check passes.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/typecheck.yml — incremental tsc with correct cache keys
jobs:
  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'npm'

      - run: npm ci

      # Cache .tsbuildinfo — key includes ALL tsconfig files AND source files.
      # A change to any tsconfig.json (paths, strict flags, references) must
      # bust the cache to prevent stale incremental compilation.
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: |
            **/.tsbuildinfo
            **/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo
          key: |
            tsc-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/tsconfig*.json', 'src/**/*.ts', 'src/**/*.tsx') }}
          restore-keys: |
            tsc-${{ runner.os }}-

      # Run type-check using --incremental (reads .tsbuildinfo if cache hit)
      - name: Type check
        run: npx tsc --noEmit --incremental
```

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json — ensure incremental is enabled
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "incremental": true,
    "tsBuildInfoFile": ".tsbuildinfo",
    "noEmit": true,
    "strict": true
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Incremental type-checking is high value on large TypeScript codebases (50k+ lines) where a cold `tsc --noEmit` takes 60–120 seconds. The cache key complexity is the main cost — it requires `hashFiles` over all TypeScript sources, which adds a few seconds of hash computation. Use `--libReplacement false` (TypeScript 5.8+) alongside `--incremental` to skip `@typescript/lib-*` package lookups for an additional 5–10% speed improvement.

> [community] The canonical gotcha (documented as real-world gotcha #101 in this guide): a change to a nested `tsconfig.json` (e.g., adding a `paths` alias in `packages/api/tsconfig.json`) does NOT change the root `tsconfig.json` hash. If the cache key only covers the root config, `tsc --incremental` uses the stale `.tsbuildinfo` and silently misses the new type errors. The fix is `hashFiles('**/tsconfig*.json', ...)` — the glob must cover all config files in the project tree.

### Pattern 122 — `act` for Local GitHub Actions Workflow Validation

**Description:** `nektos/act` is an open-source tool that runs GitHub Actions workflows locally using Docker. With the `--validate` and `--strict` flags added in v0.2.79, `act` can validate workflow YAML for syntax errors, invalid event triggers, unknown action references, and expression evaluation errors before pushing to GitHub. This eliminates a CI iteration loop where developers push to a branch just to see if the workflow YAML is correct.

```bash
# Install act (macOS/Linux)
brew install act
# or
curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nektos/act/master/install.sh | bash

# Validate all workflows in .github/workflows/ without running them
act --validate

# Strict mode: treat warnings as errors (recommended for CI-as-code review)
act --strict --validate

# Dry-run a specific workflow to check step evaluation
act push --dryrun --workflows .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — a workflow to validate locally with act
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, 'feat/**']
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `act` is most valuable for teams that iterate rapidly on workflow files (adding new jobs, updating action versions, tuning matrix strategies). The Docker overhead means actual job execution is slower than GitHub's runners, but for YAML validation the overhead is negligible. Not all GitHub Actions are supported locally — custom enterprise actions and environment secrets may not work with `act`. Use `--validate` and `--dryrun` as quick sanity checks; use the actual CI run for full verification.

> [official] `nektos/act` v0.2.79 release notes: "`--validate` validates the actions file without running any actions. `--strict` makes validation warnings into errors." These flags make `act` usable as a pre-push lint step for workflow files.

### Pattern 123 — Playwright `test.describe.serial()` for Interdependent Test Sequences

**Description:** Most Playwright tests should be fully independent — each test case sets up and tears down its own state. However, some UI flows represent genuine multi-step sequences where each step depends on the previous (e.g., a checkout flow: add-to-cart → enter-address → payment → order-confirmed). For these, `test.describe.serial()` guarantees sequential execution within the group and ensures the entire group retries together when any step fails.

```typescript
// checkout-flow.spec.ts — genuinely sequential user journey
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// serial() guarantees these tests run in order.
// If step 2 fails, steps 3 and 4 are skipped (not independently re-run).
// The entire block retries together when retries > 0.
test.describe.serial('Checkout flow', () => {
  let orderNumber: string;

  test('step 1: add product to cart', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-badge')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  test('step 2: proceed to checkout', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout/);
  });

  test('step 3: complete payment', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();
    const confirmation = page.getByTestId('order-number');
    await expect(confirmation).toBeVisible();
    orderNumber = await confirmation.textContent() ?? '';
  });

  test('step 4: verify order in account history', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/account/orders');
    await expect(page.getByText(orderNumber)).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `test.describe.serial()` is appropriate ONLY when the test steps genuinely represent a state machine where skipping to step 3 without completing step 2 is meaningless. For tests that only appear sequential because they share setup (e.g., all tests log in first), use worker-scoped fixtures to share the login state instead of `serial()`. The Playwright documentation explicitly warns: "It is usually better to make your tests isolated, so they can be efficiently run and retried independently."

> [community] Teams misuse `serial()` as a workaround for shared global state (e.g., a single test database that all tests read and write). The correct fix is database isolation per test using transactions or per-test seed/teardown. Using `serial()` to avoid fixing the state isolation problem turns a parallelizable suite into a single-threaded one — a 4× slowdown on a 4-worker CI setup.

---

### Pattern 124 — Vitest `reportCoverage` Thresholds as CI Gate

**Description:** Vitest's `coverage.thresholds` configuration causes the CI job to exit with a non-zero code when coverage falls below the specified percentages. This converts coverage from a passive metric (shown in a report) into an active gate (blocks merge if coverage drops). Combined with `coverage.changed` (pattern 116), the threshold gate applies specifically to the changed files in a PR, not the entire codebase.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage gate that blocks CI on threshold violation
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',

      // Files that must always be included in the coverage denominator.
      // Without this, untested files are excluded and coverage appears higher.
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        'src/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}',
        'src/**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}',
        'src/**/index.ts',       // re-export barrels skew line count
      ],

      reporter: ['text', 'json-summary', 'lcov'],

      // Thresholds: CI exits non-zero if ANY threshold is violated.
      // Set per-file thresholds to catch individual files with zero coverage.
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 85,
        statements: 80,
        // Per-file thresholds prevent a single well-tested file from
        // masking uncovered new files added in the same PR.
        perFile: true,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — coverage gate step
- name: Run tests with coverage gate
  run: npx vitest run --coverage
  # The step exits non-zero if thresholds are violated — CI fails here.

- name: Upload coverage to PR comment
  uses: davelosert/vitest-coverage-report-action@v2
  if: always()
  with:
    json-summary-path: coverage/coverage-summary.json
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `perFile: true` is the critical addition — without it, a new file with 0% coverage can be masked by existing files with 95% coverage, keeping the aggregate above the threshold. The downside of `perFile: true` is that it can block PRs for adding non-testable files (type declaration files, config files). Use the `exclude` list to exempt these files. Avoid setting thresholds above 90% for `branches` — branch coverage is naturally lower because error paths and defensive checks are hard to exercise in unit tests.

> [community] Teams often set `lines: 80` without `perFile: true` and are surprised when a PR that adds a 200-line uncovered module still passes the coverage gate because the aggregate stays above 80%. Adding `perFile: true` immediately exposes these gaps — expect a one-time wave of coverage debt surfacing when first enabling this option.

---

### Pattern 125 — GitHub Actions `if: always()` on Test Artifact Upload Steps

**Description:** GitHub Actions post-job steps (artifact uploads, report publishing) only run if the preceding steps succeed, by default. When a test job fails, the report artifact is the most valuable debugging asset — but it is never uploaded because the failed test step caused the job to exit non-zero, skipping the upload step. Adding `if: always()` to every artifact upload step ensures the report is available regardless of test outcome.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — always-upload artifact pattern
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium

      # This step exits non-zero on test failure — job is "failed" after this point
      - name: Run e2e tests
        run: npx playwright test --reporter=html,blob
        env:
          CI: 'true'

      # if: always() ensures this runs even after the test step fails.
      # Without it, the HTML report is never uploaded for failing runs.
      - name: Upload Playwright HTML report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: playwright-report-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14

      # Blob report for shard merge — also needs if: always()
      - name: Upload blob report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ github.run_id }}
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 1
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Apply `if: always()` to every test artifact upload step without exception. The only reason to omit it is deliberate cost control on high-frequency pipelines where artifact storage cost is a concern — even then, use `if: failure()` rather than removing `if: always()`, so you upload only when something goes wrong. Include the `github.run_attempt` in artifact names to distinguish retried run artifacts from original run artifacts.

> [community] This is one of the most frequently reported CI debugging pain points: a test fails in CI, the developer opens the Actions run to download the Playwright HTML report, and the artifact is missing because the upload step was skipped. The fix is a one-line addition (`if: always()`) but it is absent from many copy-pasted workflow templates. Adding `if: ${{ always() }}` (with curly braces) also works and is slightly more explicit about the expression evaluation context.

---

### Pattern 126 — Playwright `use.baseURL` with Dynamic Environment Resolution

**Description:** Playwright tests that hardcode `http://localhost:3000` in `page.goto()` calls cannot be reused across environments (dev, staging, preview). Setting `use.baseURL` in `playwright.config.ts` and using relative URLs in tests (`page.goto('/')`) makes the same test suite run against any deployment target. Combined with `webServer`, the config can spin up the local dev server for local runs and point to a deployed URL in CI without changing test code.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — environment-aware baseURL
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

// Resolve the target URL from environment:
// 1. CI preview deployments set PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL to the PR preview URL
// 2. CI main builds use the staging URL
// 3. Local development spins up a local dev server
const baseURL =
  process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL ??
  (process.env.CI ? 'https://staging.myapp.example.com' : 'http://localhost:3000');

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    baseURL,
    // Capture traces on first retry for debugging environment-specific failures
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },

  // Only start the local dev server when not pointing at an external URL
  webServer: baseURL.startsWith('http://localhost')
    ? {
        command: 'npm run dev',
        url: baseURL,
        reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
        timeout: 120_000,
      }
    : undefined,
});
```

```typescript
// tests/home.spec.ts — uses relative URLs, works in all environments
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('home page loads', async ({ page }) => {
  // Relative URL — resolved against baseURL from config
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/My App/);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** This pattern is essential for multi-environment deployments (PR preview environments, staging, production canary). The key convention to enforce is that ALL `page.goto()` calls in test files use relative paths — a single absolute URL in a test file breaks environment portability. Use an ESLint rule or a Playwright lint plugin to flag absolute `localhost` URLs in spec files.

> [community] Teams that add Playwright tests to a project with existing `localhost:3000` hardcodes spend significant time debugging "tests pass locally but fail in CI" issues where the root cause is that CI has no dev server running on port 3000. The `webServer` + `use.baseURL` pattern solves this at the framework level — once configured, developers cannot accidentally write environment-specific tests without violating the relative-URL convention.

### New Anti-Patterns (Cycle 27)

| Anti-pattern | Why harmful | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `strategy.fail-fast: true` (default) on Playwright shard matrix | Cancels sibling shards when any shard fails — the blob-report merge job receives an incomplete set of reports, producing a misleading partial merged report | Set `fail-fast: false` on all Playwright shard matrices; let all shards complete for a full report |
| Hardcoding `http://localhost:3000` in test files | Tests cannot run against staging, preview, or production environments without modifying test code | Set `use.baseURL` in `playwright.config.ts` and use only relative URLs in all `page.goto()` calls |
| Using `test.describe.serial()` to work around shared database state | Converts a parallelizable suite into a single-threaded sequential one — 4× or more slowdown on multi-worker CI | Fix the root cause: isolate database state per test using transactions, per-test seed/teardown, or Testcontainers |
| Caching `.tsbuildinfo` with only `package-lock.json` in the cache key | A tsconfig change (new `paths` alias, changed `strict` setting) does not bust the cache — `tsc --incremental` uses stale build info and misses new type errors | Include all `tsconfig*.json` files in the `hashFiles()` expression for the `.tsbuildinfo` cache key |
| Omitting `if: always()` on artifact upload steps | Playwright HTML report and coverage artifacts are not uploaded for failing runs — the exact run that needs debugging has no artifacts | Add `if: always()` to every test artifact upload step |

### New Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 27)

**#103** [community] Playwright `--shard=X/Y` distributes tests by file count, not by test count or estimated duration. A monorepo with one `auth.spec.ts` containing 80 test cases and nine other spec files with 5–10 cases each will place `auth.spec.ts` in shard 1 (alphabetically first) regardless of its size. Shard 1 takes 4× longer than all other shards, creating a critical-path bottleneck that negates the parallelism benefit. Measure per-file test duration with `--reporter=json`, then rename, split, or reorganize spec files to balance shard duration rather than shard file count. Alternatively, use Playwright's `--shard` in combination with the `--only-changed` flag to further reduce the per-shard load on PR runs.

**#104** [community] GitHub Actions `concurrency.cancel-in-progress: true` set globally (without the `${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}` guard) cancels the in-progress main-branch CI run when a second push lands before the first completes. In teams using a merge queue, this is catastrophic: the merge queue lands PR #1, starts the CI run, then PR #2 lands 30 seconds later and cancels PR #1's post-merge CI — leaving the main branch in an unverified state. Always scope `cancel-in-progress` to exclude the default branch using the conditional expression.

**#105** [community] Vitest `pool: 'threads'` with `isolate: true` (the default) recreates the module registry for every test file, which negates most of the speed advantage over `pool: 'forks'`. The only way to realise the full threads speedup is `isolate: false` — but this means all test files share module state, and any test that mutates a module-level singleton (including `process.env`) can affect subsequent tests in the same worker. Teams that switch to `threads` without reading the `isolate` docs see either mysterious intermittent failures (from shared state) or no speedup at all (from `isolate: true` overhead).

**#106** [community] `actions/upload-artifact@v4` silently succeeds (exit code 0) even when the `path:` glob matches zero files. If `playwright-report/` does not exist (because the test run crashed before Playwright could write the report), the upload step completes without error and the artifact entry in the GitHub UI shows "0 files". Teams debugging a crash spend minutes downloading and unzipping an empty artifact before realising the report was never generated. Add an explicit file-existence check before the upload step: `ls -la playwright-report/ || echo "No report directory"`.

**#107** [community] Vitest `coverage.changed` combined with `--shard` produces incorrect per-shard coverage data when the shards are later merged with `--merge-reports`. Each shard computes `changed` coverage independently against the base ref — but the merged report aggregates raw hit counts, not the `changed` file filter. The result is that the merged report shows coverage for ALL files, not just the changed ones, making the `coverage.changed` PR-scoped intent meaningless in the merged output. Use `coverage.changed` only on non-sharded coverage runs, or accept that the merged coverage report will show full-suite coverage.

## Cycle 28 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 127 — GitHub Actions Reusable Workflows for Cross-Repo Test Consistency [official]

**Description:** Reusable workflows (distinct from composite actions) expose an entire job graph as a callable unit. A central `platform` repository publishes the canonical CI workflow; product repositories call it with `uses: org/platform/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml@main`. Every product repo then gets lint, typecheck, unit, and integration in a maintained workflow without owning the YAML. Changes to CI policy (new gates, updated runner images, cache key changes) propagate to all callers on next invocation.

```yaml
# org/platform/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml — canonical reusable workflow
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version:
        type: string
        default: '20'
        required: false
      run-e2e:
        type: boolean
        default: false
        required: false
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN:
        required: false

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint

  typecheck:
    needs: lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit

  unit:
    needs: typecheck
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --ci --coverage

  e2e:
    if: ${{ inputs.run-e2e }}
    needs: unit
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npm run test:e2e
```

```yaml
# product-repo/.github/workflows/ci.yml — caller
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  ci:
    uses: org/platform/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml@main
    with:
      node-version: '22'
      run-e2e: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Ideal for organisations with 5+ Node.js repositories that share the same CI structure. When NOT to use: repositories with highly specialised CI requirements (native addons, multi-language builds, unusual service dependencies) will fight the abstraction. Named alternative: composite actions (step-level reuse within a single workflow vs. job-level reuse across repos). Limitation: reusable workflows cannot be nested more than 4 levels deep; caller secrets must be explicitly passed — they do not inherit automatically.

> [community] The most common reusable workflow adoption failure: platform teams publish the workflow but forget to version-pin callers. Every product repo uses `@main` and inherits breaking changes instantly. Add a versioned release tag strategy (e.g., `@v1`, `@v2`) and communicate migration timelines before releasing workflow changes that alter job names or outputs. [official]

---

### Pattern 128 — OpenID Connect (OIDC) Token Exchange for Cloud Credentials in CI [official]

**Description:** OIDC eliminates long-lived cloud credentials (AWS access keys, GCP service account JSON) stored as GitHub secrets. The CI job requests a short-lived JWT from GitHub's OIDC provider, then exchanges it with the cloud provider for temporary credentials. Credentials are scoped to the job, expire automatically, and cannot be extracted and reused outside the pipeline.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — AWS credentials via OIDC (no long-lived keys)
name: CI with OIDC AWS

on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  id-token: write    # required for OIDC token request
  contents: read

jobs:
  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Exchange GitHub OIDC token for temporary AWS credentials
      - name: Configure AWS credentials via OIDC
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/GitHubActionsCI
          role-session-name: ci-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
          aws-region: us-east-1
          # Credentials expire after 1 hour — sufficient for any CI job
          role-duration-seconds: 3600

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }

      - run: npm ci

      # Test code can now use AWS SDK with automatic credential resolution
      - run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          # Explicit region; no keys needed — credentials in env from OIDC action
          AWS_DEFAULT_REGION: us-east-1
```

```typescript
// tests/integration/s3-upload.test.ts — uses ambient OIDC-issued credentials
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand, DeleteObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

// SDK auto-discovers credentials from environment — works with OIDC-issued creds
const s3 = new S3Client({ region: process.env['AWS_DEFAULT_REGION'] ?? 'us-east-1' });
const TEST_BUCKET = process.env['TEST_BUCKET'] ?? 'my-test-bucket';
const TEST_KEY = `ci-test-${Date.now()}.txt`;

describe('S3 upload integration', () => {
  afterAll(async () => {
    // Clean up — delete the test object after the suite
    await s3.send(new DeleteObjectCommand({ Bucket: TEST_BUCKET, Key: TEST_KEY }));
  });

  it('uploads a file and verifies it exists', async () => {
    const result = await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
      Bucket: TEST_BUCKET,
      Key: TEST_KEY,
      Body: Buffer.from('hello ci'),
      ContentType: 'text/plain',
    }));
    expect(result.$metadata.httpStatusCode).toBe(200);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use OIDC for any test that requires cloud resources (S3, DynamoDB, GCS, Azure Blob). When NOT to use: local development where OIDC is unavailable — provide a fallback profile or localstack equivalent. Named alternatives: stored IAM access key secrets (insecure, requires manual rotation), Vault dynamic secrets (works but adds infrastructure dependency). Key requirement: the IAM role trust policy must match the GitHub OIDC claim — `repo:org/name:*` or scoped to specific branch/environment. [official]

---

### Pattern 129 — Playwright `--only-changed` for Sub-10-Second PR Feedback [official]

**Description:** `playwright test --only-changed` runs only the spec files that have changed since a specified base ref. Combined with a fast unit test gate, this gives PR authors first-pass browser feedback within 30–60 seconds rather than waiting for the full shard matrix.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — ultra-fast PR gate using --only-changed
name: PR Fast Gate

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  changed-e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 8
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          # Fetch origin/main for diff base
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }

      - run: npm ci

      - name: Cache Playwright browsers
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/ms-playwright
          key: pw-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}

      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium

      # Only run spec files changed since the PR base — exits 0 if no specs changed
      - name: Run changed e2e specs
        run: |
          npx playwright test \
            --only-changed=origin/main \
            --reporter=line \
            --pass-with-no-tests
        env:
          CI: 'true'

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: changed-e2e-report-${{ github.run_id }}
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 7
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — tune for fast changed-spec runs
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Fast timeout for the quick PR gate — changed specs should be focused
  timeout: 20_000,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,
  // Run changed specs in parallel within the single runner
  fullyParallel: true,
  workers: process.env.CI ? '50%' : undefined,
  reporter: [
    ['line'],
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [{ name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } }],
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Best for teams where developers write spec files alongside feature code. When NOT to use: architectural changes that affect many existing spec files — the changed filter will miss regressions in unmodified specs. Name the job clearly ("PR Fast Gate") so developers understand it is a subset check; the full suite still runs nightly. Named alternative: Vitest `--changed` flag for unit test equivalent. [official]

### Pattern 130 — `test.step()` Structured Sub-Steps for Playwright CI Reports [official]

**Description:** Playwright v1.39+ `test.step()` wraps logical sub-operations within a single test case, naming them individually in the HTML report and trace viewer. In CI, this eliminates cryptic "assertion failed" messages — the report shows exactly which step failed within a long multi-action test.

```typescript
// tests/e2e/checkout.spec.ts — structured steps for CI report clarity
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('complete checkout flow — guest user', async ({ page }) => {
  // Each step appears as a named node in the Playwright HTML report and trace
  await test.step('Navigate to product page', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Widget Pro' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('Add product to cart', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('status', { name: 'Cart' })).toContainText('1');
  });

  await test.step('Proceed to checkout as guest', async () => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue as guest' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout/);
  });

  await test.step('Fill shipping details', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Jane Doe');
    await page.getByLabel('Address').fill('123 Main St');
    await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Springfield');
    await page.getByLabel('Postal code').fill('12345');
  });

  await test.step('Submit order and verify confirmation', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL(/\/order-confirmation/, { timeout: 15_000 });
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

```typescript
// Reusable step helper — wraps repetitive interactions for consistent CI output
async function fillAddressForm(
  page: import('@playwright/test').Page,
  address: { name: string; street: string; city: string; zip: string },
): Promise<void> {
  await test.step(`Fill address for ${address.name}`, async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill(address.name);
    await page.getByLabel('Address').fill(address.street);
    await page.getByLabel('City').fill(address.city);
    await page.getByLabel('Postal code').fill(address.zip);
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Essential for long multi-action e2e tests where a failure in step 4 of 8 is otherwise reported as a generic assertion error. When NOT to use: short unit-style Playwright tests with 2–3 assertions — the step wrapping adds noise without benefit. Named alternative: splitting into separate `test()` blocks (cleaner isolation but higher runner overhead per test). [official]

### Pattern 131 — Reusable Test Data Factories with Zod Validation in CI [community]

**Description:** Test data factories produce valid, type-safe test objects with sensible defaults. Using Zod schemas as the single source of truth for both runtime validation and factory shape ensures factories cannot produce objects that fail API validation — eliminating a class of "test passes but creates invalid data" CI failures.

```typescript
// tests/factories/user.factory.ts — Zod-backed factory with CI-safe defaults
import { z } from 'zod';

// Shared schema — identical to what the API validates at runtime
export const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  name: z.string().min(1).max(100),
  role: z.enum(['admin', 'user', 'viewer']),
  createdAt: z.date(),
  active: z.boolean(),
});

export type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

// Counter for unique IDs across test runs within a process
let _seq = 0;
const seq = () => ++_seq;

// Factory: produces a validated User with overridable defaults
export function makeUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  const raw = {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    email: `user-${seq()}@ci-test.example.com`,
    name: `Test User ${seq()}`,
    role: 'user' as const,
    createdAt: new Date('2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'),  // frozen date for determinism
    active: true,
    ...overrides,
  };
  // Parse throws if the merged object violates the schema — catches invalid overrides
  return UserSchema.parse(raw);
}

// Specialised factories for common test scenarios
export const makeAdminUser = (overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User =>
  makeUser({ role: 'admin', ...overrides });

export const makeInactiveUser = (overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User =>
  makeUser({ active: false, ...overrides });
```

```typescript
// tests/unit/user-service.test.ts — using the factory in CI
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { UserService } from '../../src/services/user-service';
import { makeUser, makeAdminUser } from '../factories/user.factory';

describe('UserService.canEdit', () => {
  const service = new UserService();

  it('returns true when admin edits any user', () => {
    const admin = makeAdminUser();
    const target = makeUser();
    expect(service.canEdit(admin, target)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('returns false when regular user edits another user', () => {
    const actor = makeUser({ id: 'actor-id' });
    const target = makeUser({ id: 'target-id' });
    expect(service.canEdit(actor, target)).toBe(false);
  });

  it('returns true when user edits their own record', () => {
    const user = makeUser({ id: 'same-id' });
    expect(service.canEdit(user, { ...user })).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Factories pay for themselves on teams with 50+ test cases — the initial setup (schema, factory, helpers) takes 30–60 minutes but eliminates ad-hoc `{ id: '1', name: 'test' }` objects scattered across files. When NOT to use: tiny projects with fewer than 20 tests where inline objects are readable enough. Named alternatives: `@faker-js/faker` (random data without schema validation), `fishery` library (factory pattern without Zod coupling). [community]

> [community] The most impactful aspect of Zod-backed factories: when the API schema changes (a field becomes required, or its type changes), the factory's `UserSchema.parse()` call fails at test time rather than at the API call site — the compile error points directly to the factory, not to 30 scattered usages. Teams that adopt this pattern find schema drift in test data within minutes of a schema change rather than hours later during flaky integration failures.

---

### Pattern 132 — `pnpm` Workspaces with `--filter` for Targeted CI in Monorepos [community]

**Description:** `pnpm` workspaces integrate natively with monorepo CI patterns via `--filter`, `--filter-prod`, and `--changed` flags. Unlike `npm workspaces`, `pnpm` computes a correct topological dependency order and exposes the change graph without a separate orchestrator tool. For small-to-medium monorepos (3–20 packages) that do not need Nx or Turborepo, `pnpm` native filtering provides 70–85% of the CI efficiency at near-zero configuration cost.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — pnpm workspace targeted CI
name: CI (pnpm workspaces)

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  affected:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      packages: ${{ steps.detect.outputs.packages }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # needed for --filter with git ref

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with: { version: 9 }

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: pnpm

      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Detect changed packages
        id: detect
        run: |
          PKGS=$(pnpm -r --filter="...[origin/main]" exec pwd \
            | xargs -I{} basename {} \
            | jq -Rnc '[inputs]')
          echo "packages=$PKGS" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
          echo "Changed packages: $PKGS"

  test:
    needs: affected
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        package: ${{ fromJSON(needs.affected.outputs.packages) }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with: { version: 9 }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      # Run only the changed package and its local dependencies
      - name: Test ${{ matrix.package }}
        run: pnpm --filter="${{ matrix.package }}..." run test
```

```bash
# Local development equivalents
# Test only a specific package
pnpm --filter=@myorg/api run test

# Test a package and all of its dependents (regression check)
pnpm --filter="...@myorg/core" run test

# Test only packages changed since main (same as CI detection above)
pnpm -r --filter="...[origin/main]" run test

# Build in topological order — dependencies built before consumers
pnpm -r --filter="...[origin/main]" run build
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `pnpm` native filtering for monorepos that are already using `pnpm` and have 20 or fewer packages. When NOT to use: very large monorepos (50+ packages) where Nx Cloud DTE or Turborepo remote caching provides orders-of-magnitude better CI throughput. Named alternatives: Nx `affected`, Turborepo `--filter=...[origin/main]`, `lerna --since`. [community]

> [community] A common pnpm CI pitfall: the `--filter="...[origin/main]"` syntax requires a full git history fetch to compute the diff. Shallow clones (`fetch-depth: 1`) silently produce an empty filter result — all packages appear unchanged — and the `--filter` run exits 0 with no tests executed, giving a false green. Always set `fetch-depth: 0` in any CI job that uses pnpm's `--filter` with a git ref.
