### Pattern 305 — GitHub Actions `workflow_call` Reusable Workflow with `secrets: inherit` for DRY Cross-Repository CI Orchestration [official]

`workflow_call` triggers allow a workflow file to be invoked from another workflow, enabling a central "CI template" repository to define the canonical build/test/deploy pipeline while product repositories call it with a single `uses:` reference. Adding `secrets: inherit` on the caller side forwards all caller secrets to the reusable workflow without explicitly enumerating them, which eliminates the maintenance burden of keeping `secrets:` parameter lists in sync when new environment secrets are added. The reusable workflow can declare `inputs:` for version pins, environment names, or feature flags, keeping variability explicit while boilerplate stays centralized. This pattern is the GitHub Actions equivalent of GitLab CI's `include: project:` template inheritance and is recommended by GitHub's own internal platform teams for organizations running more than five product repositories against the same CI standard.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — product repository (caller)
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    uses: my-org/ci-templates/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml@main
    with:
      node-version: '22'
      coverage-threshold: 80
      run-e2e: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' }}
    secrets: inherit
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write

# .github/workflows/node-ci.yml — ci-templates repository (callee)
name: Node CI Template
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version:
        type: string
        default: '20'
      coverage-threshold:
        type: number
        default: 70
      run-e2e:
        type: boolean
        default: false
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN:
        required: false  # still declarable even with inherit; documents expected secrets

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
        env:
          NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
      - run: npm test -- --coverage --coverageThreshold='{"global":{"lines":${{ inputs.coverage-threshold }}}}'
      - if: inputs.run-e2e
        run: npm run test:e2e
```

**Tradeoff.** `secrets: inherit` silently forwards every caller secret to the reusable workflow, including secrets the callee does not need — this violates the principle of least privilege for secret exposure. A compromised step inside the reusable workflow could exfiltrate any inherited secret. For high-security pipelines (signing keys, production OIDC tokens), explicitly enumerate `secrets:` in the reusable workflow's `on.workflow_call.secrets` block and pass them by name from the caller; `secrets: inherit` is appropriate only for low-sensitivity secrets like NPM tokens and package registry credentials where the risk of over-exposure is acceptable. [official]

### Pattern 306 — Playwright `--shard` + GitHub Actions `strategy.matrix` with `--reporter=blob` for Horizontally Scaled E2E Parallelism [official]

Playwright's native sharding splits the test suite into N equal partitions by file, with each shard running independently on its own runner. Combining this with GitHub Actions matrix strategy and `--reporter=blob` produces per-shard blob reports that a final merge job aggregates into a single HTML report and JUnit XML — providing full suite visibility without running all tests on a single runner. The pattern scales linearly: doubling the shard count halves wall-clock E2E time, bounded only by test-count-per-shard minimums (Playwright recommends at least 5 tests per shard to avoid setup overhead dominating). For suites exceeding 500 test cases in a monorepo, this is the canonical approach documented in Playwright's CI guides for reaching sub-10-minute E2E feedback on push.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml
name: E2E Tests
on: [push]
jobs:
  e2e:
    name: E2E Shard ${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
        shardTotal: [6]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: |
          npx playwright test \
            --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }} \
            --reporter=blob
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shardIndex }}
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 1

  merge-reports:
    needs: e2e
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: always()
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: all-blob-reports/
          pattern: blob-report-*
          merge-multiple: true
      - run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter=html,junit ./all-blob-reports
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-html-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14
```

**Tradeoff.** Sharding by file count (Playwright's default) produces uneven shard durations when a small number of test files contain disproportionately long tests — a single 5-minute test file will cause one shard to run 3× longer than others, defeating the parallelism benefit. Use `--reporter=json` on a baseline run to collect per-file durations, then pass `--shard` alongside a custom `--project` filter or split files manually into even time buckets. Alternatively, Playwright's `--shard` respects `testDir` globs, so splitting tests into subdirectories by domain and running each subdirectory as a separate shard gives more control over load distribution. [official]

### Pattern 307 — GitLab CI `trigger:` with `strategy: depend` for Cross-Project Pipeline Fan-Out with Status Propagation [official]

GitLab CI's `trigger:` keyword launches a downstream pipeline in another project or in a child `yaml` file, enabling monorepo build graphs and cross-service integration tests. Adding `strategy: depend` makes the triggering job wait for the downstream pipeline to complete and reflects its final status — pass, fail, or cancel — back to the upstream job, so the parent pipeline's overall status correctly represents the full fan-out result. Without `strategy: depend`, the trigger job succeeds immediately after launching the downstream pipeline, and failures in downstream services are invisible to the parent pipeline's merge-request status checks. This pattern is essential for microservice monorepos where a change to a shared library must trigger and validate dependent service pipelines before the MR can be merged.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml — monorepo root pipeline
stages:
  - build
  - integration-test
  - deploy

build-shared-lib:
  stage: build
  script:
    - cd packages/shared-lib && npm run build
  artifacts:
    paths: [packages/shared-lib/dist/]
    expire_in: 1 hour
  rules:
    - changes: [packages/shared-lib/**/*]

trigger-service-a-tests:
  stage: integration-test
  needs: [build-shared-lib]
  trigger:
    project: my-org/service-a
    branch: $CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME
    strategy: depend       # wait and mirror downstream status
  variables:
    SHARED_LIB_SHA: $CI_COMMIT_SHA
    UPSTREAM_PIPELINE_ID: $CI_PIPELINE_ID
  rules:
    - changes: [packages/shared-lib/**/*]

trigger-service-b-tests:
  stage: integration-test
  needs: [build-shared-lib]
  trigger:
    project: my-org/service-b
    branch: main
    strategy: depend
  variables:
    SHARED_LIB_SHA: $CI_COMMIT_SHA
  allow_failure: true      # service-b tests are advisory; don't block MR
  rules:
    - changes: [packages/shared-lib/**/*]
```

**Tradeoff.** `strategy: depend` creates a hard coupling between the parent pipeline's duration and the downstream pipeline's execution time — if service-a runs a 20-minute integration suite, the triggering job in the parent pipeline blocks for 20 minutes, counting against the parent's total CI wall time. For pipelines with many downstream triggers, this can serialize what should be parallel work. Mitigate by running triggers in parallel within the same stage (they are parallel by default) and only using `strategy: depend` for pipelines whose failure should block the MR; use the default (fire-and-forget) for advisory or monitoring pipelines. Also note that `strategy: depend` on a cross-project trigger requires the triggering token to have at least `read_pipeline` access on the downstream project. [official]

### Pattern 308 — Vitest `vi.mock()` with Factory Function and `vi.importActual` for Partial Module Mocking Without Manual Re-export [official]

When a module exports ten functions but only two need to be mocked, re-exporting all ten manually inside a `vi.mock()` factory is fragile and breaks when the real module adds new exports. The idiomatic Vitest pattern uses `vi.importActual()` inside the factory to spread the real module's exports, then overrides only the specific functions under test. This preserves the real implementations for untested paths while replacing the target functions with `vi.fn()` spies, and it automatically adapts to new real-module exports without updating the mock. The pattern is analogous to Jest's `jest.mock()` with `jest.requireActual()` but uses top-level `await` inside the factory since Vitest factories can be `async`.

```typescript
// user-service.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

// Factory runs before module graph is initialized — vi.importActual is safe here
vi.mock('../lib/email-client', async (importActual) => {
  const actual = await importActual<typeof import('../lib/email-client')>();
  return {
    ...actual,                          // preserve real parseEmailAddress, validateDomain, etc.
    sendEmail: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'mock-id-123' }),
    sendBulkEmail: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ sent: 0, failed: 0 }),
  };
});

import { sendEmail } from '../lib/email-client';
import { registerUser } from '../services/user-service';

describe('registerUser', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it('sends welcome email on successful registration', async () => {
    await registerUser({ email: 'test@example.com', name: 'Alice' });
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'test@example.com', subject: expect.stringContaining('Welcome') })
    );
  });

  it('does not send email when registration fails validation', async () => {
    await expect(registerUser({ email: 'not-an-email', name: '' })).rejects.toThrow();
    expect(sendEmail).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.mock()` hoisting means the factory executes before any imports in the test file, which is why `vi.importActual()` is needed — the real module is not yet in scope as a regular import. A common mistake is using a module-level variable inside the factory (e.g., to reference a shared mock returned from a helper), which fails with "variable used before initialization" because the variable declaration is hoisted but not yet assigned when the factory runs. The fix is to define mock return values inside the factory itself or use `vi.mocked(sendEmail).mockReturnValue(...)` in `beforeEach` after the mock is set up. Also note that `importActual` returns a `Promise`, so the factory must be `async` — synchronous factories cannot use it. [official]

### Pattern 309 — Jest `--testPathPattern` + `--forceExit` + `--detectOpenHandles` for Diagnosing Hung CI Runs in Node.js Integration Test Suites [official]

Integration test suites that interact with databases, message queues, or HTTP servers frequently hang in CI after all test cases pass because open handles — database connection pools, `setInterval` timers, or TCP connections — prevent Node.js from exiting cleanly. `--forceExit` masks this by killing the process after the test run, while `--detectOpenHandles` identifies the specific resource preventing exit, emitting a stack trace with the allocation site. The diagnostic workflow is: first run with `--detectOpenHandles` (without `--forceExit`) in a local or slow CI environment to capture the stack, fix the resource leak in `afterAll`, then remove `--detectOpenHandles` from the permanent CI config since it adds ~200ms overhead per test file. Running with both flags simultaneously in permanent CI configuration is a red flag that the underlying leak has been deferred rather than fixed.

```json
// package.json — tiered Jest configuration for integration tests
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:unit": "jest --testPathPattern=src/.*\\.unit\\.test\\.ts --passWithNoTests",
    "test:integration": "jest --testPathPattern=src/.*\\.integration\\.test\\.ts --runInBand --forceExit",
    "test:integration:debug": "jest --testPathPattern=src/.*\\.integration\\.test\\.ts --runInBand --detectOpenHandles --verbose",
    "test:ci": "jest --ci --coverage --testPathPattern=src/.*\\.(unit|integration)\\.test\\.ts --forceExit"
  },
  "jest": {
    "testEnvironment": "node",
    "globalSetup": "<rootDir>/test/global-setup.ts",
    "globalTeardown": "<rootDir>/test/global-teardown.ts",
    "setupFilesAfterFramework": ["<rootDir>/test/setup.ts"],
    "testTimeout": 30000,
    "openHandlesTimeout": 5000
  }
}
```

```typescript
// test/global-teardown.ts — correct handle cleanup pattern
import { getDbPool } from '../src/db/pool';
import { getRedisClient } from '../src/cache/redis';

export default async function globalTeardown() {
  // Must end all persistent connections to allow Jest to exit cleanly
  await getDbPool().end();
  await getRedisClient().quit();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `--runInBand` (required for integration tests sharing a real database) serializes all test files onto a single process, eliminating the parallelism benefit of Jest's default worker pool. On a suite of 50 integration test files averaging 2 seconds each, `--runInBand` produces a 100-second serial run. Alternatives: use `--maxWorkers=2` with per-worker database schema isolation (each worker gets its own schema, seeded in `globalSetup`), or use Testcontainers to spin up a fresh database container per worker. The `--maxWorkers` approach is 2-4× faster but requires non-trivial schema isolation logic; `--runInBand` is simpler and sufficient for suites under ~60 seconds total. [official]

### Pattern 310 — GitHub Actions `actions/cache` with `restore-keys` Fallback Chain for Dependency Cache Hit Rate Optimization [official]

The `restore-keys` parameter in `actions/cache` defines an ordered list of cache key prefixes to fall back to when the exact primary key is not found. A well-structured fallback chain enables partial cache hits — restoring a cache from a previous lockfile state rather than starting cold — dramatically reducing install time even when `package-lock.json` has changed. The canonical three-level chain is: exact lockfile hash (perfect hit), OS-only prefix (any prior cache for this OS), platform-only (broadest fallback). Each level trades cache freshness for hit probability; the `npm ci` or `yarn install` after a partial hit only downloads the delta packages not present in the restored cache, which is typically 90% faster than a cold install when only one or two dependencies changed.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — three-level cache fallback chain
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'

      - name: Cache node_modules
        id: cache-node
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: |
            ~/.npm
            node_modules
          # Primary key: exact match — only valid if lockfile unchanged
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-node22-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          # Fallback 1: same OS + Node version, any lockfile — partial hit
          # Fallback 2: OS only — cross-version partial hit (Node major upgrade)
          # Fallback 3: bare prefix — last resort; still faster than cold npm cache
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-node22-
            ${{ runner.os }}-node-
            ${{ runner.os }}-

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci --prefer-offline
        # --prefer-offline uses npm's cache even for partial hits;
        # avoids network calls for packages already in ~/.npm

      - run: npm test -- --coverage
      - run: npm run build
```

**Tradeoff.** Caching `node_modules` directly (rather than only `~/.npm`) risks subtle cache poisoning when a package's install script (`postinstall`) produces platform-specific native binaries — a cached `node_modules` with Linux-compiled `.node` files will silently fail on a macOS or Windows runner if the OS-prefixed fallback key ever matches cross-platform. Always include `${{ runner.os }}` as the first segment of every cache key and all `restore-keys`. Additionally, `node_modules` caches can become stale if a package author pushes a new version with the same semver range resolved at install time — use `npm ci` (which validates against `package-lock.json`) rather than `npm install` after a cache restore to ensure lockfile integrity. [official]

### Pattern 311 — Vitest `globalSetup` + `provide` / `inject` API for Sharing Expensive Resources Across All Test Files Without Global State [official]

Vitest's `globalSetup` lifecycle hook runs once per Vitest process (outside any worker), making it suitable for starting a database container, an HTTP server, or a WebSocket service that all test files share. Prior to Vitest 2.x, the only way to pass the resulting port or connection string to test files was via `process.env`, which pollutes the global environment and does not compose well. The `provide` / `inject` API (stable in Vitest 2.0) allows `globalSetup` to call `provide('dbUrl', url)` and any test file to call `inject('dbUrl')` with full type safety — values are serialized across the worker boundary, so only JSON-serializable data is supported (connection strings, ports, flags — not class instances or Promises).

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globalSetup: './test/global-setup.ts',
    pool: 'forks',        // required for provide/inject — vmThreads does not support cross-context injection
    poolOptions: {
      forks: { singleFork: false },
    },
  },
});

// test/global-setup.ts
import { type GlobalSetupContext } from 'vitest/node';
import { createTestDatabase } from './test-db';

let dbContainer: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createTestDatabase>>;

export async function setup({ provide }: GlobalSetupContext) {
  dbContainer = await createTestDatabase();
  provide('testDbUrl', dbContainer.connectionString);
  provide('testDbPort', dbContainer.port);
}

export async function teardown() {
  await dbContainer?.stop();
}

// src/repositories/user-repo.integration.test.ts
import { inject } from 'vitest';

const dbUrl = inject('testDbUrl');  // type-safe; inferred from provide() call in globalSetup

describe('UserRepository', () => {
  it('creates and retrieves a user', async () => {
    const repo = new UserRepository(dbUrl);
    const user = await repo.create({ name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' });
    expect(user.id).toBeDefined();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `provide` / `inject` only serializes JSON-safe values, so complex objects (database connection pool instances, Testcontainer objects, EventEmitter instances) cannot be passed directly — only the string URL or port number. Each worker that calls `inject` receives a copy of the serialized value, meaning each worker must independently create its own connection pool using the injected URL. This is the correct design (connection pools are per-process), but it means `globalSetup` is responsible only for infrastructure lifecycle (start/stop the container), not for creating shared application-level resources. Teams that attempt to pass a shared pg `Pool` instance via `provide` discover that it is serialized as `{}` and the test silently uses an undefined pool, causing cryptic "cannot read property 'query' of undefined" errors. [official]

### Pattern 312 — GitHub Actions `pull_request_target` + Environment Protection Rule for Safe Fork PR Secret Access [official]

`pull_request` events from forked repositories do not have access to secrets, preventing fork contributors from running integration tests that require API keys or deployment credentials. `pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository (with secret access) but executes code from the fork's HEAD, creating a significant supply-chain risk if the workflow checks out and runs fork code with privileged secrets. The safe pattern combines `pull_request_target` with an environment protection rule requiring manual approval from a repository maintainer before the privileged job runs — the `environment: integration-tests` gate ensures no fork code executes with secrets until a human reviews the fork's changes.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/integration-fork.yml
name: Integration Tests (Fork PRs)
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, labeled]

jobs:
  # Unprivileged lint runs immediately — no secret access, safe to use fork code
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}  # fork code, no secrets
      - run: npm ci && npm run lint

  # Privileged integration tests require manual approval via environment gate
  integration:
    needs: lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Environment 'integration-fork-tests' has a protection rule:
    # "Required reviewers: [maintainers team]"
    # A maintainer must approve before this job runs with secrets
    environment: integration-fork-tests
    # Only run when 'safe to test' label is applied by a maintainer
    if: contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'safe to test')
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.TEST_DATABASE_URL }}
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.INTEGRATION_API_KEY }}
```

**Tradeoff.** The "safe to test" label approach requires a maintainer to manually label each fork PR before integration tests run, adding friction to the contributor experience and creating a workflow where the label must be removed and re-applied on subsequent commits to re-trigger the workflow (GitHub does not re-run `pull_request_target` on push if the label is already present). An alternative is to use the environment protection rule alone (without the label gate) and rely entirely on the manual approval prompt in the GitHub Actions UI. Choose the label approach when you want the intent ("a maintainer has reviewed this fork's code") to be visible in the PR's label history; choose the approval-only approach when you want a lighter-weight gate with less label management overhead. [official]

### Pattern 313 — GitLab CI `artifacts:reports:coverage_report` with `cobertura` Format for Merge Request Coverage Visualization [official]

GitLab can render per-line coverage overlays directly in the merge request diff view when a job uploads a Cobertura XML report via `artifacts:reports:coverage_report`. This eliminates the need for a separate coverage PR comment bot — GitLab natively shows coverage status per changed line (covered, uncovered, or partially covered) in the MR diff, and displays the overall coverage percentage delta in the MR overview. The pattern works with any coverage tool that produces Cobertura XML (Istanbul/nyc, Vitest's `--reporter=cobertura`, Jest with `coverageReporters: ['cobertura']`) and requires no GitLab configuration beyond the job definition.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml — coverage with MR diff visualization
test:
  stage: test
  image: node:22-alpine
  script:
    - npm ci --ignore-scripts
    - npm test -- --coverage --coverageReporters=cobertura --coverageReporters=text-summary
  coverage: '/Lines\s*:\s*(\d+\.?\d*)%/'   # regex extracts overall % for GitLab pipeline badge
  artifacts:
    when: always
    expire_in: 1 week
    reports:
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml
    paths:
      - coverage/lcov.info   # also upload lcov for external tools (SonarQube, Codecov)

# vitest.config.ts equivalent
# test: {
#   coverage: {
#     provider: 'v8',
#     reporter: ['cobertura', 'text-summary', 'lcov'],
#     reportsDirectory: 'coverage',
#   }
# }
```

**Tradeoff.** GitLab's Cobertura MR diff visualization has a file-count limit (1000 files per report in GitLab.com SaaS; configurable on self-managed) — monorepos with large test suites that generate coverage for thousands of source files will silently truncate the report, causing some files to show no coverage data in the diff. To work around this, scope coverage collection to changed files only using `--collectCoverageFrom` (Jest) or `coverage.include` patterns filtered by the MR's changed file list; this also speeds up coverage collection by 30-70% in large monorepos. Additionally, the `coverage:` regex field for pipeline badge extraction is matched against job log output, not the Cobertura XML — ensure your coverage reporter emits a human-readable summary line matching the regex pattern. [official]

### Pattern 314 — Playwright `page.route()` + `page.routeFromHAR()` for Deterministic API Response Replay in E2E Tests [official]

`page.routeFromHAR()` loads a pre-recorded HAR (HTTP Archive) file and intercepts matching network requests, replaying the recorded responses without hitting real backends. This is Playwright's first-class API mocking solution for E2E tests — unlike `page.route()` with manual response stubs, HAR replay captures the full realistic response structure (headers, status codes, timing, body encoding) from a real recording session, ensuring test responses match what the application actually handles in production. New in Playwright 1.60, `tracing.startHar()` / `tracing.stopHar()` enables recording HAR files inline during test runs in `--update-snapshots` mode, creating a self-updating mock system where running the suite against a live backend generates fresh HAR files.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'with-mocks',
      use: { /* uses HAR replay — fast, deterministic */ },
    },
    {
      name: 'record-hars',
      use: { /* hits real backend — run manually to refresh HAR files */ },
    },
  ],
});

// tests/dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

test.describe('Dashboard — HAR replay mode', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    // Replay recorded API responses; fallback: 'abort' prevents accidental live calls
    await page.routeFromHAR(
      path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures/dashboard-api.har'),
      {
        url: '**/api/**',         // only intercept API routes; static assets hit real server
        update: false,            // set true with UPDATE_HARS=1 env var to re-record
        fallback: 'abort',        // abort (not 'continue') to catch unrecorded routes
        notFound: 'fallback',
      }
    );
  });

  test('renders KPI cards with mocked data', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-kpi')).toHaveText('$1,234,567');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('user-count-kpi')).toHaveText('42,891');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** HAR files contain full response bodies and headers, and committed HAR files in a `fixtures/` directory become stale as the backend API evolves — a response schema change that adds a required field will cause the application to crash or render incorrectly against the old HAR response, while all Playwright tests continue to pass because they replay the stale data. Establish a HAR refresh cadence (e.g., regenerate HAR files weekly against a staging environment in a dedicated CI job) and add HAR file age assertions (`mtime` check in a test hook) that warn when HAR files are older than 30 days. Alternatively, use `update: process.env.UPDATE_HARS === '1'` to enable on-demand refreshes without code changes. [official]

### Pattern 315 — Vitest `test.each` with Tagged Template Literal Syntax for Human-Readable Parameterized Test Case Tables [official]

`test.each` accepts a tagged template literal that renders as a markdown-style table in source, making parameterized test cases self-documenting without requiring external test case specification files. The template literal syntax aligns values in columns, supports any serializable type (numbers, strings, objects, arrays), and generates test titles from the first row's column headers — a `%s` placeholder in the title string is replaced with the serialized value of each column. Compared to the array-of-arrays syntax (`test.each([[1, 2, 3], ...])`), the template literal form is significantly more readable at the point of definition and produces clearer failure messages when a specific case fails, since the column header names appear in the test output.

```typescript
// pricing.test.ts — template literal test.each for business rule coverage
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { calculateDiscount } from '../src/pricing/discount-engine';

describe('calculateDiscount', () => {
  test.each`
    tierName       | annualRevenue  | loyaltyYears | expectedRate
    ${'Bronze'}    | ${10_000}      | ${1}         | ${0.05}
    ${'Silver'}    | ${50_000}      | ${2}         | ${0.10}
    ${'Gold'}      | ${100_000}     | ${3}         | ${0.15}
    ${'Platinum'}  | ${250_000}     | ${5}         | ${0.20}
    ${'Enterprise'}| ${1_000_000}   | ${7}         | ${0.25}
    ${'New'}       | ${0}           | ${0}         | ${0.00}
  `(
    '$tierName tier ($loyaltyYears yrs, $$annualRevenue revenue) → $expectedRate discount',
    ({ annualRevenue, loyaltyYears, expectedRate }) => {
      const result = calculateDiscount({ annualRevenue, loyaltyYears });
      expect(result.rate).toBeCloseTo(expectedRate, 2);
    }
  );

  test.each`
    input                                       | errorMessage
    ${{ annualRevenue: -1, loyaltyYears: 1 }}   | ${'annualRevenue must be non-negative'}
    ${{ annualRevenue: 1000, loyaltyYears: -1 }}| ${'loyaltyYears must be non-negative'}
  `('throws for invalid input: $input', ({ input, errorMessage }) => {
    expect(() => calculateDiscount(input)).toThrow(errorMessage);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The template literal `test.each` syntax requires TypeScript to infer the row type from the first data row (the header row defines column names but not types), which means TypeScript will widen numeric literal types to `number` and string literals to `string` — there is no way to constrain a column to a union type like `'Bronze' | 'Silver'` without a type assertion in the test body. If the test callback requires a specific union type for a parameter, use the array-of-tuples syntax with an explicit type annotation instead: `test.each<[TierName, number, number, number]>([...])`. Additionally, the template literal form does not support `async` generators or `describe.each` with complex nested structures — for deeply nested parameterization, compose `describe.each` with `test.each` using the array syntax. [official]

### Pattern 316 — GitHub Actions `concurrency` Group with `github.workflow + github.ref` for Per-Branch Deduplication Across Workflow Files [official]

When multiple workflow files trigger on the same events (`push`, `pull_request`), each file's `concurrency:` group must encode both the workflow name and the branch ref to prevent a concurrency collision where one workflow's `cancel-in-progress` group cancels a run from a different workflow on the same branch. The canonical pattern uses `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` as the concurrency group key, ensuring that CI workflow runs and deploy workflow runs for the same branch operate in separate concurrency groups and do not cancel each other. Omitting `github.workflow` from the group key is a subtle misconfiguration that manifests as intermittent cancellations when two workflows with identical `concurrency.group` values race on the same branch.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: ['**']
  pull_request:
concurrency:
  # Unique per workflow + branch combination
  # Without ${{ github.workflow }}, deploy.yml shares this group and gets cancelled
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true   # Cancel stale CI runs; safe because CI is idempotent

---
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false  # Never cancel in-progress deploys — data integrity risk

---
# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: Release
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']
concurrency:
  # Tags have unique refs — cancel-in-progress: false is belt-and-suspenders here
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `github.ref` in the concurrency group means that two separate pushes to different branches never interfere with each other — which is the desired behavior for CI. However, for scheduled workflows (`on: schedule:`) that should only have one run at a time regardless of branch, using `github.ref` will allow multiple concurrent scheduled runs if the workflow is manually triggered on different branches simultaneously. For scheduled workflows, use a static group key like `${{ github.workflow }}-scheduled` without a ref component, and set `cancel-in-progress: false` to avoid cancelling a run that is partway through a weekly report or database backup. [official]

### Pattern 317 — GitLab CI `.gitlab/ci/` Directory with `include: local:` for Modular Pipeline Composition [official]

Splitting a large `.gitlab-ci.yml` into topic-specific files under `.gitlab/ci/` — `lint.yml`, `test.yml`, `build.yml`, `deploy.yml` — and composing them via `include: local:` in the root file reduces merge conflict frequency and makes it easier to reason about each pipeline stage in isolation. GitLab processes `include:` directives before evaluating `extends:` and `!reference:`, so shared job templates defined in `.gitlab/ci/templates.yml` are available to all included files. The pattern mirrors the multi-file Terraform module convention and is used by GitLab's own internal platform teams (documented in their public `gitlab-org/gitlab` repository).

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml — root orchestration only; no job definitions
include:
  - local: .gitlab/ci/lint.yml
  - local: .gitlab/ci/test.yml
  - local: .gitlab/ci/build.yml
  - local: .gitlab/ci/security.yml
  - local: .gitlab/ci/deploy.yml

variables:
  NODE_VERSION: '22'
  DOCKER_DRIVER: overlay2

stages:
  - lint
  - test
  - build
  - security
  - deploy

# .gitlab/ci/test.yml
.test-base:
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine
  cache:
    key:
      files: [package-lock.json]
    paths: [node_modules/]
  before_script:
    - npm ci --ignore-scripts

unit-tests:
  extends: .test-base
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm run test:unit -- --reporter=junit --outputFile=junit-unit.xml
  coverage: '/Lines\s*:\s*(\d+\.?\d*)%/'
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: junit-unit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml

integration-tests:
  extends: .test-base
  stage: test
  services:
    - postgres:16-alpine
  variables:
    POSTGRES_DB: test_db
    POSTGRES_USER: test_user
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test_pass
    DATABASE_URL: postgresql://test_user:test_pass@postgres/test_db
  script:
    - npm run test:integration -- --forceExit
```

**Tradeoff.** GitLab evaluates `include: local:` files at pipeline creation time by fetching each file via the GitLab API — on self-managed GitLab instances with high CI load, the pipeline creation latency increases proportionally with the number of included files (approximately 200-400ms per file on busy instances). For pipelines with more than 20 included files, consolidate small files (e.g., merge `lint.yml` and `format.yml` into `quality.yml`) to stay under 10 `include:` directives. Additionally, variables defined in the root `.gitlab-ci.yml` `variables:` block are available in included files, but variables defined inside included files are not automatically available in the root file or other included files — use `!reference [.template, variables]` to share variable sets across included files without duplicating them. [official]

### Pattern 318 — Vitest `--coverage.changed` Flag for PR-Scoped Differential Coverage Enforcement [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `--coverage.changed` (stable in Vitest 4.1, available as `coverage.changed: true` in config), which restricts coverage thresholds to lines, branches, and functions that are part of the current Git diff rather than the entire codebase. This enables a "coverage ratchet" approach in large legacy codebases where setting a global 80% threshold is impractical (the codebase is at 45%), but enforcing 80% coverage on all newly written or modified code is both achievable and desirable. The flag uses `git diff` against the configured `coverage.changedSince` ref (defaults to the merge base with `main`) to compute the changed-line mask before applying threshold checks.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — differential coverage for PR enforcement
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'cobertura'],
      reportsDirectory: 'coverage',
      // Only enforce thresholds on lines changed in this branch
      changed: process.env.CI_COVERAGE_MODE === 'differential',
      // If changed: true, compare against merge base with main
      // changedSince defaults to auto-detected merge base
      thresholds: {
        // These apply only to changed lines when changed: true
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        'src/**/*.stories.tsx',
        'src/**/index.ts',       // barrel files — no logic to cover
        'src/generated/**',
      ],
    },
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — differential vs global coverage modes
- name: Run tests with differential coverage on PRs
  run: |
    if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" = "pull_request" ]; then
      CI_COVERAGE_MODE=differential npx vitest run --coverage
    else
      npx vitest run --coverage  # global thresholds on main branch push
    fi
```

**Tradeoff.** `--coverage.changed` requires a clean Git history with an accessible merge base — on shallow clones (`fetch-depth: 1`), `git diff` against the merge base may fail or produce an empty diff, causing the flag to fall back to reporting 100% coverage (no changed lines → all thresholds trivially satisfied). Always use `fetch-depth: 0` or a targeted `fetch-depth` that includes the full branch history when using differential coverage in CI. Additionally, the `changed` flag counts coverage by lines in the diff, not by test quality — a change that only modifies comments or import statements will show 100% differential coverage trivially, and a change that adds 1 line of logic covered by an existing test will show 100% even if no new test was written. Use differential coverage as a floor, not a measure of test quality. [official]

---

### Pattern 319 — Jest `--shard` (Native, Jest 30) + `--ci` for First-Class Parallel Sharding Without Third-Party Plugins [official]

Jest 30 (June 2025) introduced native `--shard=<index>/<total>` support, matching the interface already available in Playwright and Vitest and eliminating the need for community plugins like `jest-circus-runner` shard extensions or `jest-shard`. Combined with `--ci` (which enables deterministic test ordering and disables watch mode) and `--coverageProvider=babel` (Jest 30's default), native sharding integrates directly with the Jest test sequencer's deterministic file ordering — each shard receives the same subset of files across identical environments, ensuring reproducible results. Jest 30's 37% speed improvement and 77% memory reduction (from the `unrs-resolver` migration and `babel-plugin-transform-barrels`) make sharding more cost-effective since each shard starts faster and holds less memory per worker.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/jest-sharded.yml
name: Jest Tests (Sharded)
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  jest:
    name: Jest Shard ${{ matrix.shard }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: ['1/4', '2/4', '3/4', '4/4']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - run: |
          npx jest \
            --ci \
            --shard=${{ matrix.shard }} \
            --coverage \
            --coverageDirectory=coverage/${{ matrix.shard }} \
            --coverageReporters=json \
            --reporters=default \
            --reporters=jest-junit
        env:
          JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_DIR: reports/
          JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME: junit-${{ strategy.job-index }}.xml
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: coverage-shard-${{ strategy.job-index }}
          path: |
            coverage/
            reports/
          retention-days: 1

  merge-coverage:
    needs: jest
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: always()
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: artifacts/
          pattern: coverage-shard-*
          merge-multiple: true
      - run: npx nyc merge artifacts coverage/merged-coverage.json
      - run: npx nyc report --reporter=lcov --reporter=text-summary --temp-dir=coverage
```

**Tradeoff.** Jest's native `--shard` splits by file count, not by execution time — like Playwright's default sharding, this produces uneven shard durations when test files vary widely in runtime. Jest 30's `--testSequencer` option (which accepts a custom sequencer class) can be used to implement time-based sharding by reading a previously recorded `--json` report's `testResults[].perfStats.runtime` values and distributing files to shards by total runtime rather than count. This requires a two-run bootstrap (first run records timings, subsequent runs use them), but reduces shard wall-time variance from ±60% to ±10% in real-world test suites with 10+ long integration test files. The `unrs-resolver` in Jest 30 also changes module resolution behavior for some non-standard `exports` field configurations — test after upgrading if any tests import workspace packages with unusual `exports` maps. [official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 46

**#174** [community] GitHub Actions `actions/cache@v4` silently skips saving the cache when the job is cancelled mid-run — the post-step cache save only executes if the job completes (success or failure), not if it is cancelled via `concurrency.cancel-in-progress`. WHY: GitHub Actions post-steps (cleanup hooks registered by actions) are skipped on job cancellation to prevent long-running teardown from blocking the runner; `actions/cache` registers its save logic as a post-step, so a job cancelled by a newer push never persists its partial `node_modules` cache. This causes a cold-start spiral on high-activity branches where fast pushes trigger `cancel-in-progress` on every run before the cache save step executes, meaning every run starts from scratch. The fix is to use `actions/cache/save@v4` as an explicit step with `if: always()` before the end of the job, rather than relying on the post-step save.

**#175** [community] Playwright `test.beforeAll()` hooks that throw an error cause all tests in the `describe` block to be marked as "passed" in some CI JUnit reporters rather than "skipped" or "failed" — the JUnit XML produced by `@playwright/test`'s built-in `junit` reporter marks tests in a failed `beforeAll` suite as `<testcase>` nodes with no `<failure>` child, which many CI systems (Jenkins, GitLab) interpret as passing tests. WHY: Playwright's JUnit reporter emits test results for tests that were never run as absent `<failure>` elements (equivalent to pass) rather than as `<skipped>` elements, because the Playwright test runner marks them as "interrupted" internally — a status that the JUnit reporter does not map to a standard JUnit outcome. This can cause a green CI pipeline despite a critical `beforeAll` failure (e.g., database connection failure) that prevented all integration tests from running. The fix is to add a `--reporter=list` reporter alongside `--reporter=junit` so the console output captures the `beforeAll` failure visibly, and check for zero test counts in JUnit XML as a separate CI validation step.

**#176** [community] GitLab CI `cache:policy: pull` on a job that runs before the cache-populating job in a pipeline (due to `needs:` reordering) will download a stale or empty cache — `cache:policy: pull` skips the cache upload step entirely, so if a rescheduled or parallel pipeline places a `pull`-only job before the `push`-only job, the `pull` job receives the previous pipeline's cache. WHY: GitLab's cache is keyed by `cache.key` and populated at the end of jobs with `policy: push` or `policy: pull-push`; the cache is a pipeline-external artifact stored in GitLab's object storage, meaning job scheduling order within a pipeline does not guarantee that `push` jobs run before `pull` jobs when `needs:` creates a DAG that violates the sequential stage assumption. Teams that convert `policy: pull-push` to `policy: pull` / `policy: push` splits for performance optimization discover that flaky pipeline reruns (which skip completed stages) can cause `pull`-only jobs to receive empty caches. The mitigation is to always include a `policy: pull-push` fallback job that runs early in the pipeline to guarantee cache population before downstream `pull`-only jobs execute.

**#177** [community] Vitest `--pool=vmThreads` with `vi.mock()` factory functions that import Node.js built-in modules (e.g., `import { readFileSync } from 'fs'` inside a `vi.mock()` factory) can throw `ERR_VM_MODULE_NOT_EVALUATED` on Vitest 3.x when the factory is evaluated in the VM context before the module graph is ready. WHY: Vitest's `vmThreads` pool runs each test file in an isolated VM context using Node.js's experimental `vm.Module` API; `vi.mock()` factories are hoisted and evaluated synchronously before the VM module graph finishes evaluation, and importing Node.js built-ins from inside a synchronous VM factory triggers the `NOT_EVALUATED` error because `vm.Module` defers built-in binding resolution. The error is non-deterministic (depends on load order) and does not appear in `--pool=threads` (the default), causing CI flakiness that is impossible to reproduce locally unless `VITEST_POOL=vmThreads` is explicitly set. The fix is to use dynamic `import()` inside the factory (making it `async`) or switch to `--pool=forks` for files with complex `vi.mock()` factories that import built-ins.

**#178** [community] Jest `--globalSetup` and Vitest `globalSetup` both support returning a teardown function, but Jest silently ignores errors thrown inside the returned teardown function in `--ci` mode — a `EADDRINUSE` error from a test server that failed to close causes `jest --ci` to exit with code 0 rather than 1, hiding infrastructure leaks in CI. WHY: Jest's `--ci` flag alters error handling in several undocumented ways to ensure CI environments get a clean exit; one side effect is that teardown function errors in `globalSetup` modules are caught and logged as warnings rather than re-thrown as process-fatal errors. This means a test suite that leaves a TCP server running on port 4000 will not fail the CI job — but subsequent CI runs on the same runner will fail with `EADDRINUSE` when the next run tries to start the server on the same port. The fix is to explicitly call `process.exit(1)` inside the teardown function's `catch` block, or to use Vitest (which correctly propagates teardown errors as fatal even in `--run` mode) for new test infrastructure.

| 317 | GitLab CI `.gitlab/ci/` directory with `include: local:` for modular pipeline composition | [official] | Topic-scoped YAML files reduce merge conflicts; root file orchestrates only — keep include count under 10 to minimize pipeline creation latency |
| 318 | Vitest `--coverage.changed` for PR-scoped differential coverage enforcement on legacy codebases | [official] | Changed-line threshold enforcement only; requires `fetch-depth: 0` for accurate merge-base detection — use as floor, not quality measure |
| 319 | Jest 30 native `--shard` + `--ci` for first-class parallel sharding without third-party plugins | [official] | File-count sharding; custom `--testSequencer` for time-based distribution — verify `unrs-resolver` compatibility with workspace `exports` maps |
| Gotcha #174 | `actions/cache@v4` post-step save skipped on job cancellation — cold-start spiral on high-activity branches | [community] | Use explicit `actions/cache/save@v4` step with `if: always()` rather than relying on post-step registration |
| Gotcha #175 | Playwright `test.beforeAll()` failures produce passing JUnit XML entries for unrun tests | [community] | Add `--reporter=list` alongside JUnit; validate non-zero test counts in JUnit XML as a separate CI gate |
| Gotcha #176 | GitLab CI `cache:policy: pull` receives stale cache when `needs:` DAG places it before the `push` job | [community] | Include a `pull-push` fallback job early in pipeline to guarantee cache population before `pull`-only consumers run |
| Gotcha #177 | Vitest `vmThreads` pool throws `ERR_VM_MODULE_NOT_EVALUATED` for `vi.mock()` factories importing Node built-ins | [community] | Make factory `async` with dynamic `import()` for built-ins, or switch to `--pool=forks` for affected test files |
| Gotcha #178 | Jest `--ci` silently swallows `globalSetup` teardown errors, hiding infrastructure leaks from CI exit codes | [community] | Explicitly call `process.exit(1)` in teardown `catch` blocks, or use Vitest which correctly propagates teardown errors as fatal |

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 320 — GitHub Actions `actions/cache` `save-always` for cache persistence independent of job outcome [official]

The `save-always` input (added in `actions/cache@v4`) instructs the cache action to execute its save post-step even when the job fails, unlike the default behavior where cache saves are skipped on failure. This is particularly valuable for package manager caches in jobs that include tests — if the test step fails after `npm ci` has successfully populated `node_modules`, the cache is saved and subsequent retry runs start warm rather than cold. Combining `save-always: true` with a tightly scoped `key` that includes the lockfile hash prevents stale cache from masking legitimate failures. The option is distinct from using `actions/cache/save@v4` as an explicit step: `save-always` also fires on `continue-on-error: true` step failures within the same job, whereas an explicit `actions/cache/save@v4` with `if: always()` only fires at the step level.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.npm
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-npm-
          save-always: true        # persist cache even when test step fails
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test              # cache is saved regardless of this step's outcome
```

**Tradeoff.** `save-always: true` can persist a cache populated with incorrect or partially installed packages if `npm ci` itself fails partway through (e.g., a native build failure mid-install). Always use an exact `key` that incorporates the lockfile hash so a corrupted partial cache does not match subsequent runs; the mismatch forces a clean install while the `restore-keys` fallback still provides a warm partial hit for the unchanged dependency subset. Do not use `save-always` for caches that include build artifacts with embedded timestamps, as these will grow unboundedly across failed runs.

### Pattern 321 — GitHub Actions `filter-paths` pattern for conditional job execution in monorepos [official]

GitHub Actions `on.push.paths` and `on.pull_request.paths` filter entire workflow triggers, but `paths-filter` (the `dorny/paths-filter` action, now a de-facto standard) performs per-job path filtering inside a workflow, enabling a single workflow file to selectively run jobs based on which parts of a monorepo changed. A matrix-driven approach combined with `paths-filter` eliminates the combinatorial explosion of per-package workflow files. The action outputs boolean variables (e.g., `changes.api`, `changes.ui`) consumed by subsequent jobs via `needs` output expressions and `if:` conditions. As of mid-2025, GitHub's native `paths` filter at the workflow level does not support per-job granularity — `paths-filter` fills this gap by running as a lightweight step and computing change sets against the merge base.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/monorepo-ci.yml
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      api: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.api }}
      ui: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.ui }}
      e2e: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.e2e }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dorny/paths-filter@v3
        id: filter
        with:
          filters: |
            api:
              - 'packages/api/**'
              - 'packages/shared/**'
            ui:
              - 'packages/ui/**'
              - 'packages/shared/**'
            e2e:
              - 'e2e/**'
              - 'packages/api/**'
              - 'packages/ui/**'

  test-api:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.api == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm test --workspace=packages/api

  test-ui:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.ui == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm test --workspace=packages/ui

  e2e:
    needs: [changes, test-api, test-ui]
    if: |
      always() &&
      needs.changes.outputs.e2e == 'true' &&
      !contains(needs.*.result, 'failure')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npx playwright test
```

**Tradeoff.** `dorny/paths-filter` uses the PR merge base for pull requests and the push comparison SHA for pushes — if a PR is opened from a branch with a diverged history (common when rebasing), the comparison base may be older than expected, causing more paths to be flagged as changed than necessary. This produces false-positive job runs (never false-negatives, which would be dangerous), so the tradeoff favors safety over efficiency. For repositories using squash merges exclusively, set `base: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}` explicitly to avoid the diverged-history issue. The `always()` guard in the E2E `if:` condition is essential: without it, the E2E job is skipped entirely when upstream jobs are skipped (not failed), preventing the required jobs check from completing.

### Pattern 322 — GitLab CI `rules:changes:compare_to` for accurate branch-relative change detection [official]

GitLab CI `rules:changes` without a `compare_to` key compares the current pipeline's changes against the parent commit — on a feature branch with multiple commits, only the most recent commit's diff is evaluated, causing jobs to be skipped even when earlier commits in the branch modified relevant files. The `compare_to` key (introduced in GitLab 15.3) specifies a branch or tag as the comparison base, enabling accurate monorepo job filtering across an entire feature branch. Using `compare_to: refs/heads/main` ensures that any commit in the MR branch that touches monitored paths triggers the job, matching developers' mental model of "this job runs if my branch changes this package".

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

test:api:
  stage: test
  script:
    - cd packages/api && npm ci && npm test
  rules:
    - changes:
        paths:
          - packages/api/**/*
          - packages/shared/**/*
        compare_to: refs/heads/main   # compare entire branch against main
      when: on_success
    - when: never

test:ui:
  stage: test
  script:
    - cd packages/ui && npm ci && npm test
  rules:
    - changes:
        paths:
          - packages/ui/**/*
          - packages/shared/**/*
        compare_to: refs/heads/main
      when: on_success
    - when: never

# Always run linting regardless of path changes
lint:
  stage: test
  script: npm run lint
  rules:
    - when: always
```

**Tradeoff.** `compare_to` requires that the referenced branch (`refs/heads/main`) is fetched in the runner's git clone — GitLab runners perform a shallow clone by default (`GIT_DEPTH: 20`), which may not include the `main` tip if the branch was created from a commit more than 20 ancestors back. Set `GIT_DEPTH: 0` or `GIT_FETCH_EXTRA_FLAGS: --deepen=50` at the job level to ensure the comparison base is available. On self-managed GitLab instances with large repositories, `GIT_DEPTH: 0` causes noticeable pipeline start latency (8–30 seconds for repositories with 50k+ commits); a `GIT_DEPTH: 100` is usually sufficient for team workflows with short-lived feature branches.

### Pattern 323 — Playwright `test.step()` for structured trace hierarchy in long E2E flows [official]

Playwright's `test.step()` function wraps logical sub-operations inside a test with named steps that appear as collapsible nodes in the HTML report and trace viewer. Unlike simply writing comments in test code, `test.step()` records precise timing for each sub-operation, captures any assertion failures with the step name in the error message, and groups screenshots/network activity by step in the trace. For long checkout or registration flows where a single test exercises 15+ interactions, step nesting reduces mean time-to-diagnosis for CI failures by surfacing exactly which named step failed without needing to decode line numbers from a 200-line test file.

```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('complete checkout flow', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('navigate to product', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Widget Pro' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('add to cart', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to Cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-count')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  await test.step('proceed to checkout', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'View Cart' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to Checkout' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/checkout');
  });

  const orderId = await test.step('complete payment', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('confirmation-banner')).toBeVisible();
    return page.getByTestId('order-id').textContent();
  });

  // step return values are available in the outer test scope
  expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ORD-\d{8}$/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.step()` adds a small overhead per step (approximately 0.5ms for the instrumentation wrapping) that is negligible in UI tests but can add up in tests with hundreds of programmatic steps (e.g., data seeding loops). More importantly, `test.step()` does not isolate side effects — a failure inside a step does not trigger automatic cleanup; the test author must still manage `page.close()` and fixture teardown. Nested `test.step()` calls (steps within steps) produce a tree structure in the trace viewer, which is very readable for 2–3 levels but becomes difficult to navigate beyond 4 levels of nesting; flatten deeply nested step hierarchies into helper functions with their own top-level steps instead.

### Pattern 324 — Vitest `workspace` configuration for multi-package monorepo test isolation [official]

Vitest's workspace configuration (the `vitest.workspace.ts` file at the monorepo root) defines multiple named projects, each with independent configuration, environment, and setup files. Unlike running `vitest` per-package with separate commands, the workspace mode shares a single Vitest process across all projects, enabling cross-project coverage merging, unified watch mode, and a single HTML report. Each project can override `environment` (`node`, `jsdom`, `happy-dom`), `setupFiles`, `globals`, and `resolve.alias` independently, allowing a backend package to run in `node` environment while a React component package runs in `happy-dom` in the same test invocation.

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts (monorepo root)
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    test: {
      name: 'api',
      root: './packages/api',
      environment: 'node',
      setupFiles: ['./test/setup.ts'],
      globalSetup: ['./test/global-setup.ts'],
      include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
      coverage: {
        include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
        exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/generated/**'],
      },
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name: 'ui',
      root: './packages/ui',
      environment: 'happy-dom',
      setupFiles: ['./test/setup.ts'],
      include: ['src/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}'],
      globals: true,
      coverage: {
        include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
        exclude: ['src/**/*.stories.tsx', 'src/generated/**'],
      },
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name: 'shared',
      root: './packages/shared',
      environment: 'node',
      include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
    },
  },
]);
```

**Tradeoff.** Vitest workspace mode shares the main Vite transform pipeline across all projects — if two projects have conflicting Vite plugin configurations (e.g., one uses `@vitejs/plugin-react` with `jsxRuntime: 'classic'` and another needs `jsxRuntime: 'automatic'`), the workspace will silently apply one configuration to both. Per-project `plugins` arrays in the workspace file do not fully isolate Vite plugin state when plugins use module-level singleton caches. For projects with deeply conflicting Vite configurations, use `vitest run --project api` and `vitest run --project ui` as separate CI steps and merge coverage reports with `nyc merge` rather than relying on the workspace coverage merge.

### Pattern 325 — GitHub Actions `environment` + `deployment_status` webhook for progressive delivery gating [official]

GitHub Actions environment protection rules (required reviewers, wait timers, deployment branch policies) integrate with the `deployment_status` event to create a programmable progressive delivery gate. A workflow that deploys to a `staging` environment automatically creates a GitHub deployment object; the deployment's status transitions (`pending` → `in_progress` → `success`/`failure`) are observable via `deployment_status` events, enabling a separate "smoke test" workflow to trigger automatically when staging deployment succeeds and report back via the Deployments API. This creates a native GitHub-tracked audit trail of every deployment attempt and its associated test results, visible in the repository's Deployments tab and linkable from PRs.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml
name: Deploy to Staging
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: staging
      url: https://staging.example.com   # shown in PR deployment status widget
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Deploy application
        run: ./scripts/deploy.sh staging
        env:
          DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DEPLOY_KEY }}

---
# .github/workflows/smoke-test-staging.yml
name: Smoke Test Staging
on:
  deployment_status:               # triggers on any deployment status change
jobs:
  smoke:
    if: |
      github.event.deployment_status.state == 'success' &&
      github.event.deployment.environment == 'staging'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run smoke tests against staging
        run: npx playwright test --config=playwright.smoke.config.ts
        env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ github.event.deployment_status.target_url }}
      - name: Update deployment status
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            await github.rest.repos.createDeploymentStatus({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              deployment_id: context.payload.deployment.id,
              state: 'failure',
              description: 'Smoke tests failed',
            });
```

**Tradeoff.** The `deployment_status` trigger fires for every environment in the repository — if the same repository has `staging`, `production`, and `preview` environments, the smoke-test workflow must explicitly filter `github.event.deployment.environment == 'staging'` or it will run for all deployment status changes including preview deployments from PRs. The `target_url` field in `deployment_status` is only populated if the deployment workflow explicitly sets `environment.url`; without it, `BASE_URL` will be empty. GitHub's required-reviewers protection on environments only applies to `workflow_dispatch` and `push`-triggered deployments — `deployment_status`-triggered workflows bypass environment protection rules entirely, so smoke-test workflows should not use protected-environment secrets.

---

### Pattern 326 — GitLab CI `parallel:matrix` for cross-platform and cross-version test matrices [official]

GitLab CI `parallel:matrix` generates a matrix of jobs from an array of variable combinations, analogous to GitHub Actions `strategy.matrix`. Unlike the top-level `parallel: N` (which creates N identical jobs), `parallel:matrix` injects distinct variable sets into each parallel job, enabling cross-platform (Linux, macOS, Windows via `tags:`) and cross-version (Node 20, 22, 24) matrices without duplicating job definitions. Job names are automatically suffixed with variable values for identification in the pipeline graph, and `needs:` can reference a specific matrix cell by name for dependent downstream jobs.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
test:
  stage: test
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - NODE_VERSION: ['20', '22', '24']
        OS: ['linux']
      - NODE_VERSION: ['22']
        OS: ['macos']
  tags:
    - ${OS}
  script:
    - node --version
    - npm ci
    - npm test -- --ci --reporters=jest-junit
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
    expire_in: 1 week
  variables:
    JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME: junit-${NODE_VERSION}-${OS}.xml

# Reference a specific matrix cell in a downstream job
deploy:
  stage: deploy
  needs:
    - job: "test: [22, linux]"    # GitLab auto-generates this job name format
      artifacts: false
  script: ./deploy.sh
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

**Tradeoff.** `parallel:matrix` job names are auto-generated as `jobname: [val1, val2]` — the exact format depends on the order of variable declarations in the matrix, and GitLab does not guarantee alphabetical ordering of variables in the job name suffix. If a `needs:` reference uses a hard-coded job name like `"test: [22, linux]"` and the variable declaration order changes, the pipeline breaks with a `needs` validation error at pipeline creation time (not at runtime), which can be difficult to debug. Prefer using `needs:` with `pipeline:` trigger jobs or avoiding matrix cell `needs:` references; instead, use a fan-in job with `needs: ["test"]` (matching all matrix cells) when any matrix result suffices for the downstream gate.
